snappy: Annual report US public companies must file with the SEC — comprehensive view of business, risk, and financials.
detail: Required under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Sections include business description, risk factors, MD&A (management discussion and analysis), audited financial statements, executive compensation, and legal proceedings. Filed 60-90 days after fiscal year-end depending on company size. Distinct from the glossy annual report sent to shareholders. The quarterly counterpart is the 10-Q; the 8-K reports material events between quarters.
plain: The detailed annual filing US public companies must give the SEC — the most comprehensive public document about a company's business and finances.

snappy: Strike convention — option struck so the call's delta is 0.25 (or put's is -0.25).
detail: FX vol surfaces are usually quoted at 25-delta call, 25-delta put, and ATM. The 10-delta points add wing detail for stress tests. 25-delta points sit roughly one standard deviation out-of-the-money — far enough to be meaningfully out-of-money, close enough to have decent liquidity. Most listed and OTC FX option flow concentrates around these points.
plain: A common way of choosing how far out-of-the-money an option is set — used in currency markets to quote the price of standard contracts.

snappy: Highest credit rating — minimal default risk.
detail: Sovereign AAAs: US (S&P downgraded 2011), Germany, Netherlands, Switzerland, Singapore. Corporate AAAs are rare — Microsoft and Johnson & Johnson have held it; most companies sit at AA or A. AAA structured products were the cornerstone of pre-2008 securitisation — many turned out to be deeply mispriced. Carries the tightest credit spreads. Downgrades make headlines.
plain: The top mark a bond can get — given to borrowers seen as almost certain to pay you back.

snappy: Bond backed by non-mortgage consumer or commercial receivables.
detail: Auto loans, credit cards, student loans, equipment leases, and more. Tranched into rated bond classes similar to MBS structures. The 2 trillion US ABS market is dominated by auto and credit card issuance from banks and captive finance companies. ABS held up better than RMBS in 2008 because underwriting was tighter and the underlying assets shorter-dated and easier to repossess.
plain: A bond backed by a pile of consumer loans like car loans, credit cards, or student loans — investors earn the borrowers' repayments.

snappy: Foreign company's shares packaged for US trading — held by a US bank in custody.
detail: Lets US investors trade non-US stocks without dealing with foreign exchanges or currencies. JPMorgan, BNY Mellon, Citi, and Deutsche Bank are the major depositary banks. Three sponsorship levels: Level 1 (OTC, light disclosure), Level 2 (US exchange listing, SEC reporting), Level 3 (capital-raising via new shares). Many large foreign companies (Alibaba, Toyota, Novartis, Unilever) trade in the US via ADRs.
plain: A way for Americans to buy a foreign company's shares without using overseas exchanges — a US bank holds the real stocks.

snappy: Market-maker risk that the counterparty has better information.
detail: Core risk in market-making: you quote a two-way price, informed traders pick off the side that's mispriced. Adverse-selection costs grow with bid-ask spread (compensation) and shrink with quote-update speed. Dark pools that don't filter informed flow can suffer extreme adverse selection. Information asymmetry economics underpin most market-making profit/loss dynamics.
plain: The risk that the person you're trading with knows more than you do — they only trade with you when it's bad for you.

snappy: MBS guaranteed against credit loss by a government-sponsored enterprise (GSE).
detail: Issued by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae. The GSE guarantees principal and interest, removing credit risk for the investor — but leaving prepayment and rate risk. Treated as 'Treasury-like' for regulatory capital and pension mandates. The Fed bought trillions of agency MBS during QE programs; runoff post-2022 has placed pressure on mortgage spreads. Roughly 9 trillion outstanding.
plain: A bond made of US home loans where a US government-owned company effectively insures investors against homeowner defaults.

snappy: Side of a trade that took liquidity — opposite of the resting (passive) side.
detail: If a buy order lifts a resting offer, the buy is the aggressor. Trade reporting includes aggressor flags. Aggressor data is critical for inferring order-flow toxicity, sentiment, and price-impact patterns. HFT firms quote aggressively only when their models indicate favourable expected value. Buy-side TCA scrutinises aggressor versus passive fill mix as an execution-quality dimension.
plain: The side of a trade that grabbed an existing price someone else was offering — the one who pulled the trigger first.

snappy: EU regulation for alternative investment funds — hedge funds, private equity, real estate funds.
detail: Effective 2013. Manager registration, capital requirements, leverage limits, transparency obligations. Allows EU and non-EU AIFM to market across the EU via passport (subject to conditions). Stricter than US Form ADV/Form PF in some respects, lighter in others. Brexit forced UK managers into national private-placement regimes for EU marketing. AIFMD II amendments in 2024 add delegation and loan-fund rules.
plain: A European rulebook for funds that take bigger risks than ordinary mutual funds — hedge funds, private equity, real-estate funds.

snappy: Fed framework adopted 2020 — tolerates above-target inflation to make up for below-target periods.
detail: Replaced the previous symmetric 2 percent target with an averaging approach. Aimed at preventing prolonged ZLB risk by letting actual inflation run above 2 percent after extended periods of undershooting (most of post-2008 era). Adopted Aug 2020. Criticised in retrospect as contributing to the 2021-22 inflation overshoot — by signalling tolerance for higher inflation, gave the Fed less urgency in tightening when prices started rising. Currently being internally reviewed.
plain: A US central bank approach that lets prices rise faster than usual for a while, to make up for years when they rose too slowly.

snappy: Buy-side framework that allocates orders across multiple brokers' algos and measures performance.
detail: Each order randomly (or systematically) routed to one of several broker algos; performance compared via TCA. Removes broker selection bias and isolates execution quality. Standardised by buy-side traders to extract better execution from competing brokers. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPM, and others compete for algo-wheel allocations. Common in modern institutional equity execution.
plain: A computer system big investors use to spread orders across multiple banks' trading robots and track which one trades best.

snappy: Excess return over a benchmark, adjusted for risk — measure of investment skill.
detail: Jensen's alpha (1968): observed return minus CAPM-predicted return. Positive alpha signals stock-picking or timing skill. Persistent alpha is rare and contested. After fees, most active mutual funds underperform benchmarks (SPIVA reports). Hedge fund alpha typically small after fees and survivorship bias corrections. Modern factor models often reattribute 'alpha' to factor exposures, suggesting much active outperformance is factor beta in disguise.
plain: Returns from a fund manager's skill — the extra money earned beyond what the market itself would have delivered for the same risk.

snappy: Lightweight industrial metal — packaging, aerospace, construction, transport.
detail: LME-listed aluminium is the benchmark. Production is electricity-intensive (4 percent of global power consumption); aluminium prices closely track power costs. China produces 60 percent of global aluminium. The 2022 European energy crisis forced widespread European smelter closures. Demand growth driven by EV lightweighting and electrification. Carbon-intensity differences across producers create premium markets for 'green' aluminium.
plain: A light, silver-coloured metal used in cans, planes, and cars — its price rises and falls with electricity costs and demand from China.

snappy: Option exercisable any time up to and including expiration.
detail: Standard for single-stock equity options (most listed options on US stocks). Early exercise rarely optimal — typically only justified by dividends (for calls) or deep in-the-money status (for puts on illiquid names). American options can be valued via binomial trees or finite-difference methods; closed-form solutions don't exist. The name has nothing to do with geography.
plain: An option you can use at any point before its expiry date — most US single-stock options work this way.

snappy: Multi-factor extension of CAPM — expected return depends on multiple risk factor exposures.
detail: Stephen Ross's 1976 framework. Foundation for modern factor models. APT itself doesn't specify which factors matter — empirical work fills that in. Fama-French and successors built on APT logic. The 'no-arbitrage' principle: if two portfolios have the same factor exposures, they must have the same expected return. Underpins modern asset-pricing research and factor-investing practice.
plain: A theory that an investment's expected return depends on its exposure to several big risk forces, not just one overall market move.

snappy: Risk-free profit from simultaneous buying and selling of related instruments.
detail: Pure arbitrage: same security trading at different prices on different exchanges (rare in modern markets). Statistical arbitrage: short-term pricing relationships expected to revert. Convertible arbitrage: long convertible bonds, short the stock and bond components. Capital structure arbitrage: long one debt class, short another. Modern markets have shrunk most pure arb opportunities to milliseconds via HFT.
plain: Earning a small risk-free profit by buying something cheap in one place and selling it more expensively somewhere else — instantly.

snappy: Currency and banking crisis that started in Thailand and swept East Asia in 1997-98.
detail: Triggered when Thailand abandoned its USD peg in July 1997 (THB had been overvalued; capital flight forced the float). Contagion hit Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, Philippines. Local-currency depreciation crushed dollar-denominated debt holders; banking systems collapsed; IMF bailouts followed with painful conditions. Lasting effects: massive reserve accumulation across Asia, ASEAN+3 cooperation, the rise of EM local-currency bond markets.
plain: A 1997-98 panic that started in Thailand and swept Asia — currencies collapsed, banks failed, and many countries needed bailouts.

snappy: Option whose payoff depends on the average price of the underlying over a period — not the final price.
detail: Common in commodity hedging (averages match physical exposure over a delivery period), FX hedging (smooths out month-end rate spikes), and structured products. Average can be arithmetic or geometric, fixed-strike or floating-strike. Lower premiums than vanilla options because averaging dampens volatility. Asian options got their name because they were popularised in Tokyo trading in the 1980s.
plain: An option whose payoff is based on the average price of a stock or other Underlying over a period, not its final price.

snappy: Lowest price at which a seller is currently willing to sell an asset.
detail: Other half of bid-ask spread. The 'best offer' is the lowest among multiple sellers. Market orders to buy execute at the offer. Often called 'offer' interchangeably. The spread between bid and offer is the dealer's compensation for providing liquidity. Wider spreads in illiquid securities; pennies in major equities. EU/UK markets sometimes use 'offer' instead of 'ask' as the convention.
plain: The lowest price a seller is willing to accept right now — what you pay if you want to buy immediately.

snappy: Company buys back a large chunk of shares from an investment bank immediately — bank covers via market.
detail: Investment bank delivers shares immediately, then buys them in market over weeks or months. Locks in capital return faster than open-market repurchase. Common when companies want to retire shares quickly (rebalancing leverage post-spin, accelerated EPS impact). Typically 3-9 month execution windows. The investment bank takes execution risk; pricing usually tied to VWAP over the buying period.
plain: A deal where a company buys back a big chunk of its own stock instantly through a bank, which sources the shares over time.

snappy: Anything of value owned by a person or company — generates future economic benefit.
detail: Three broad categories: financial (cash, bonds, stocks), real (property, equipment), intangible (patents, brand value). Total US household financial assets approach 100 trillion dollars (2024). Bank balance sheets distinguish between trading-book and banking-book assets, each with different accounting and regulatory treatment. Foundation of every financial statement and balance-sheet analysis.
plain: Anything of value that someone owns — cash, a house, a stock, a bond, even a patent or a brand name.

snappy: Spread over the swap curve that prices a bond at par when its coupon is converted to floating.
detail: Mechanics: investor buys the bond and enters a fixed-to-floating swap, converting the bond's fixed coupon into SOFR-plus-spread. ASW measures the spread on the floating leg that makes the package zero-cost at inception. Used by bank treasuries to compare across instruments on a uniform floating-rate basis. Differs from Z-spread by the convexity correction and bond price effects.
plain: The extra yield a bond gives over a standard floating reference rate, once its fixed coupon is swapped into floating payments.

snappy: Option struck close to the current price of the underlying.
detail: Strictly: strike equals spot. Loosely: strike within a small range of spot. ATM options have the highest time value, highest gamma, and roughly 0.5 delta (or -0.5 for puts). Most option volume concentrates in at-the-money and just-out-of-money strikes. ATM volatility is the headline implied-vol number quoted for any expiry.
plain: An option whose Strike Price is right around the current price of the Underlying — neither cheap nor deep underwater.

snappy: Bank capital instrument that converts to equity or gets written down if regulatory ratios breach.
detail: Created post-2008 under Basel III to provide loss-absorbing capital that doesn't dilute existing equity in normal times. Counts as Tier 1 capital. The March 2023 Credit Suisse rescue wiped out 17 billion of AT1 to zero while equity holders got partial payment — broke the conventional capital-stack hierarchy and sent shockwaves through the AT1 market. Yields demanded subsequently widened by hundreds of basis points.
plain: A bank bond that gets wiped out or converted to stock if the bank runs into trouble — protecting taxpayers from another bailout.
An option whose Strike Price sits right at the current Underlying price — exercising it today would break even.
snappy: Option whose strike is at or very near the current underlying price.
detail: ATM options carry the highest time value because uncertainty about whether they'll end in-money is greatest. The vol-smile minimum typically sits at ATM. ATM-forward (strike equal to the forward price, not spot) is the standard quoting convention for FX and swaption vol. Greeks like delta sit near 50 for ATM calls. ATM is where retail and institutional options flow concentrates.

snappy: Buying both a Call option and a Put option at the same at-the-money Strike Price — pure volatility exposure.
detail: Standard quote for FX implied volatility: dealers price the ATM straddle and quote its vol, which becomes the headline vol number for that tenor. Delta-neutral at inception (call delta plus put delta sums to zero). Gains if the underlying moves a lot, loses if it stays still. Combined with risk reversals and butterflies, straddles let dealers build the full FX Volatility Surface.
plain: Buying one call and one put at the same Strike Price — a bet that the Underlying will move a lot, in either direction.

snappy: Non-exchange trading venue registered with the SEC under Reg ATS.
detail: Includes dark pools, ECNs, and crossing networks. Roughly 50 ATSs operate in US equities. Form ATS-N requires public disclosure of operations. Subject to SEC rule changes proposed in 2022-2024 that would tighten oversight. ATSs allow flexibility in market structure without full exchange status — lower regulatory burden but no listing role and limited quote-display privileges.
plain: A trading venue in the US that isn't a full stock exchange — includes dark pools and other private matching systems.

snappy: Maximum number of shares a company is allowed to issue under its charter.
detail: Set in the corporate charter; can be increased with a shareholder vote. Distinct from outstanding shares (already issued) and float (publicly tradable). Boards typically keep authorised well above outstanding to allow flexibility for future issuance — stock-based compensation, acquisitions, secondary offerings. Disclosed on the balance sheet and in 10-K filings.
plain: The maximum number of stocks a company is allowed to issue under its own rulebook — usually more than it has actually issued.

snappy: ABS backed by auto loans or leases — the largest non-mortgage ABS sector.
detail: Roughly 250 billion outstanding in the US. Pool of 30,000-100,000 auto loans, weighted-average life of 1-3 years. Prepayments come from car sales, refinancing, and total losses. Default and loss rates correlate with employment and used-car prices. Performed remarkably well in 2008 (better than MBS) but stressed in 2020 before COVID-era stimulus and supply-chain car-price spikes flipped used-car values upward.
plain: A bond backed by a pool of car loans or leases — investors get paid as drivers make their monthly repayments.

snappy: Structured note that gets early-redeemed if the underlying is at or above an observation level on coupon dates.
detail: Pays a fixed coupon if the underlying is above the call barrier on observation dates; otherwise rolls forward, potentially with memory of unpaid coupons. If the underlying falls below a knock-in barrier, the investor takes equity-like downside at maturity. Massive product class in Europe and Asia — over 500 billion outstanding globally. Investor effectively sells volatility and downside risk for an enhanced coupon.
plain: An investment that pays a chunky coupon and ends early if a stock holds above a chosen level — but loses money if it crashes.

snappy: Testing a strategy on historical data to evaluate its performance.
detail: Essential for systematic strategy development. Pitfalls: data-mining bias (testing too many strategies), look-ahead bias (using future information), survivorship bias (using only surviving stocks), transaction-cost neglect. Walk-forward analysis: split data into training and out-of-sample test sets. Cross-validation. Most backtests overestimate live trading performance — a 2x reduction is rule of thumb. Standard in quant research.
plain: Replaying a trading strategy on years of past data to see how it would have done — a way to test ideas before risking money.

snappy: Futures price below spot — usually means scarcity or strong demand for prompt delivery.
detail: The opposite of contango. Curve slopes downward. Common in commodities with seasonal demand (heating oil in winter), supply disruptions (oil after the 2022 Russia-Ukraine invasion), or storage costs that exceed convenience yield. Long futures holders earn positive roll yield, rolling cheaper. Backwardation is a generally bullish signal for the spot commodity — physical market is tight.
plain: When today's price of something like oil is higher than the price for delivery later — usually means there's a shortage right now.

snappy: Post-crisis resolution tool — bank's bondholders and shareholders absorb losses rather than taxpayers.
detail: Triggered when a bank is failing or likely to fail. Resolution authority writes down equity, AT1, Tier 2, then potentially senior debt in a specified order. The 2017 Banco Popular resolution in Spain wiped out 2 billion euros of equity and AT1; the 2023 Credit Suisse wipe-out of AT1 was a partial bail-in. Designed to make resolution credible without state aid.
plain: A rule that forces a failing bank's investors and bondholders to take losses first, instead of taxpayers paying for a rescue.
When a government or central bank rescues a failing Bank with taxpayer money — the alternative to letting it collapse and risk wider damage.
snappy: Government rescue of a failing institution — taxpayer funds absorb losses.
detail: Famous bailouts: 2008 TARP (700 billion US programme rescuing AIG, GM, banks), UK Northern Rock and RBS rescues, the 2010-2012 eurozone sovereign bailouts (Greece, Ireland, Portugal). Post-crisis bail-in rules aim to shift losses to private creditors before taxpayers. Politically toxic but often deemed necessary to prevent systemic collapse. Distinct from bail-in, where shareholders and bondholders absorb losses without taxpayer money.

snappy: Comprehensive accounting of a country's international economic transactions.
detail: Three components: current account (trade, services, income, transfers), capital account (capital flows), and the financial account (changes in reserves). Always balances by accounting identity; persistent imbalances reflect underlying economic dynamics. BoP crises occur when capital inflows reverse abruptly — Asian 1997, Russia 1998, Argentina 2001. IMF programs typically address BoP crises.
plain: The full record of money flowing in and out of a country — trade, services, investments, everything added up.
The UK's central bank — sets sterling interest rates, supervises Banks, and prints British banknotes.
snappy: The UK's central bank — sets Bank Rate, oversees financial stability.
detail: Founded 1694. Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate eight times yearly. Mandate: 2 percent inflation target plus secondary objectives (employment, growth) since 1997 independence. Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA, within the BoE) supervises banks and insurers; Financial Policy Committee (FPC) targets system-wide stability. Played a critical role in the 2022 gilt crisis after the Truss mini-budget, restoring market function via temporary asset purchases.

plain: Japan's central bank — pioneered the world's longest run of near-zero interest rates and is still the most cautious major central bank.
snappy: Japan's central bank — pioneer of zero rates, QE, and yield curve control.
detail: Founded 1882. Policy Board meets eight times yearly. Held interest rates at zero or negative from 1999 to March 2024. Pioneered modern QE (2001-2006, then 2013-onwards), yield curve control (2016-2024), and ETF purchases. The March 2024 exit from negative rates ended a 17-year era. BoJ owns over half of outstanding JGBs. Yen weakness reflects persistent rate differentials with other developed economies.

snappy: Option that activates or extinguishes if the underlying crosses a barrier level.
detail: Four flavours: knock-in (activates on touch), knock-out (extinguishes on touch), up-and-in, down-and-out. Cheaper than vanilla options because part of the time the holder doesn't own anything. Heavily used in structured products and FX hedging. Pricing handles path-dependence — analytical solutions for some types, Monte Carlo for others. Barrier breaches in stressed markets create discontinuous payoff jumps that hedgers fear.
plain: A bet on a stock or other Underlying that only pays off — or stops working — if the price hits a chosen Strike Price.

snappy: First currency in a pair quote — the one being priced.
detail: In EUR/USD, EUR is the base — the rate tells you how many dollars you'd pay for one euro. Conventions are sticky: EUR is always base against everything else; GBP is base against most things except EUR; USD is base against most non-major currencies. When the base currency strengthens, the pair's price rises. Reading FX news requires keeping the base straight.
plain: The first currency in a Currency Pair quote — the rate tells you how many of the second currency one of these buys.

snappy: Post-2008 global bank capital and liquidity rules from the Basel Committee.
detail: Finalised 2010-2017, implementation extending through 2028 in some jurisdictions. Key additions over Basel II: higher and better-quality capital (CET1 minimum 4.5 percent), capital conservation and countercyclical buffers, liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR), leverage ratio. Final 'Basel III Endgame' (Basel 3.1) standardises risk-weights with internal-models constraints. US implementation finalised 2024 for major banks.
plain: Global rules that force banks to hold thicker safety cushions of capital and cash after the 2008 crash.

snappy: Final Basel III revisions — restricts internal-model use, introduces output floors.
detail: Finalised by BCBS in 2017. Caps internal-model RWA benefits to 72.5 percent of standardised RWA (output floor). Restricts internal models for low-default portfolios. Implementation began 2023 in EU, 2025-2028 in UK. US 'Basel III Endgame' proposal 2023, finalised mid-2024 with significant pushback from large banks claiming it would constrain lending. Phase-in through 2028.
plain: A tightening of the global banking rulebook that limits how much banks can lower their own capital using internal computer models.

snappy: Tiny unit traders use for yields and spreads — one one-hundredth of a percent.
detail: One basis point (often 'bp' or 'bip', pronounced 'beep') equals 0.01 percent. A 25 bp Fed hike is a quarter-percent move. Credit spreads, central-bank moves, swap rates, mortgage points — every fixed-income conversation runs in bps because percentage-of-a-percentage is too clumsy. 'Came in twelve wider' means the spread widened by twelve basis points.
plain: A tiny unit traders use for rates and yields — one hundredth of one percent. A quarter-point rate cut equals 25 of these.

snappy: Falling market — typically 20-plus percent below a recent high.
detail: Average post-WWII US bear market: 13 months, 35 percent S&P decline. Notable bears: 1929-32 (89 percent decline), 1973-74 (48 percent), 2000-02 (49 percent), 2007-09 (57 percent), 2020 (34 percent), 2022 (25 percent). Bear-market psychology: denial, anger, fear, capitulation. Sometimes followed by bear-market rallies that retest lows.
plain: A long, deep slide in prices — usually defined as a fall of 20 percent or more from a recent peak.

snappy: Yield curve trade or shift where long yields rise faster than short yields.
detail: Typical when inflation expectations rise sharply or when the Fed signals it will let inflation run hot before tightening. The 2003 Greenspan 'measured pace' communication triggered a notorious bear steepener. Long bonds underperform short bonds. Opposite: bull flattener, when long yields fall and the curve flattens (typical of growth slowdowns).
plain: A move in the bond market where long-term rates jump up faster than short-term ones — typically when investors fear inflation.

snappy: Anecdotal economic survey from the twelve Federal Reserve districts — published eight times yearly.
detail: Each Federal Reserve Bank surveys local business contacts, lenders, and industry experts. Released two weeks before each FOMC meeting. Captures qualitative regional economic trends not in headline statistics. Often early indicator of changes in consumer behaviour, labour markets, real-estate conditions. Watched by macro analysts for ground-level signal complementing top-down data. Less market-moving than minutes but useful for nowcasting.
plain: A booklet the US central bank publishes eight times a year, summing up what businesses across the country are seeing on the ground.

snappy: Option exercisable on a set of pre-specified dates — between European and American.
detail: Common for OTC swaptions (the right to enter a swap) and callable bonds (issuer's embedded option). 'Bermudan' because it sits between European (one date) and American (every date). Pricing uses backwards-induction through the exercise dates. Issuer-callable corporate bonds and mortgage callability are economically Bermudan options.
plain: An option you can use only on a handful of specific dates — somewhere between a strict European option and a flexible American option.

snappy: Broker's duty to seek the most favourable terms reasonably available for customer orders.
detail: Codified in FINRA Rule 5310 and MiFID II (Europe). Factors: price, speed, likelihood of execution, settlement, total transaction cost. Broker reports (Rule 605/606 in US, RTS 27/28 in Europe) disclose execution quality publicly. Best-execution standards have intensified with retail commission compression and scrutiny of PFOF. Robinhood and others have faced regulatory action over execution-quality concerns tied to PFOF.
plain: A broker's legal duty to get the best deal reasonably possible for a customer's order — not just any deal.

snappy: Stock's sensitivity to market moves — slope of regression against market return.
detail: Market index beta = 1.0 by definition. High-beta stocks (tech 1.3+) amplify market moves; low-beta stocks (utilities 0.5) dampen them. Negative beta is rare (gold mining stocks occasionally). Historic beta uses past returns; forward beta predicts. Used in CAPM, factor models, portfolio risk decomposition. The 'low-beta anomaly' — low-beta stocks outperforming risk-adjusted — is one of the persistent findings in empirical finance.
plain: How much a stock swings when the market swings — a beta of 1 mirrors the market; a beta of 2 swings twice as much.

snappy: Portfolio constructed to have zero net beta to the market — equal long and short market exposure.
detail: Standard hedge-fund category. Long-short equity, market-neutral pairs, equity stat arb. Aims for absolute returns independent of market direction. Generally lower returns and lower volatility than long-only equity. The 2007 Quant Quake (August 2007) hit market-neutral hedge funds particularly hard as positions unwound simultaneously. Industry has matured; volatility lower than 2008-09 extremes.
plain: A portfolio built so that overall market moves don't help or hurt it — bets win or lose based on the manager's stock-picking alone.

snappy: Highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for an asset.
detail: Half of the bid-ask spread. The 'best bid' is the highest among multiple buyers; sub-best bids stack behind in the order book. Market orders to sell execute at the bid. Lifting the offer means buying at the offer; hitting the bid means selling at the bid. NBBO (National Best Bid and Offer) is the consolidated bid across US equity venues.
plain: The highest price a buyer is willing to pay right now — what you'd get if you wanted to sell immediately.

snappy: Gap between what buyers offer and sellers accept — the dealer's cut.
detail: Quoted as the difference between bid (where a market-maker will buy) and offer (where they'll sell). Tightens with volume and competition; widens around news, illiquid hours, or stress. A penny S&P 500 spread costs retail almost nothing; a fifty-cent emerging-market bond spread is the trader's bread and butter. Regulators (MiFID II in Europe, Rule 605 in the US) require disclosure as a proxy for execution quality.
plain: The small gap between the price buyers are offering and the price sellers want — the cost of trading in and out instantly.

snappy: Large unit of an FX quote — the digits before the decimal point.
detail: EUR/USD at 1.0850 has 'big figure' 1.08; a move to 1.0950 is a 'big figure' move. Used in trader shorthand: 'EUR-USD is 50/55 in the figure' means 1.0850 bid / 1.0855 offered. Big-figure changes are visually meaningful — round-number levels often act as support or resistance because algos and option strikes cluster there.
plain: The whole-number part of a foreign exchange rate — the digits before the decimal, used as quick trader shorthand.

snappy: Discrete option-pricing model — underlying moves up or down each timestep with assigned probabilities.
detail: Published 1979. Build the tree of possible price paths backward from expiry, computing option value at each node. Handles American exercise naturally (compare hold vs exercise at each node). Converges to Black-Scholes as timesteps approach infinity. Used heavily for teaching and for callable-bond pricing. Trinomial trees (three branches per step) converge faster and handle some path-dependent products better.
plain: A method for pricing an option by mapping out every possible up-or-down step the Underlying could take between now and expiry.

snappy: Rare, high-impact event that is hard to predict and rationalised in hindsight.
detail: Coined by Nassim Taleb (2007 book). The 2008 financial crisis, 2020 pandemic, 2022 Ukraine invasion arguably fit. Reframes risk management: focus less on predicting probability of extreme events (impossible), more on building robustness to surprises. Critics argue 'black swan' has become overused — some events labelled black swans were predictable in advance.
plain: A rare disaster nobody saw coming that turns out to be huge — explained as obvious only after the fact.

snappy: Foundational option-pricing model — risk-neutral valuation via Brownian-motion underlying.
detail: Published 1973 by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes; extended by Robert Merton. Scholes and Merton won the 1997 Nobel Prize (Black died in 1995). Assumes log-normal returns, constant volatility, no dividends, continuous trading, risk-free rate hedging. Real markets violate every assumption — but the framework persists as the canonical reference. Implied volatility is the 'fudge factor' that lets traders use the model despite its flaws.
plain: The famous 1973 formula that gave traders the first reliable way to assign a fair price on an option.

snappy: Large transaction negotiated off the public order book — minimises market impact.
detail: Equity block thresholds: NYSE 10,000+ shares, Nasdaq similar. Block trades cross between institutional buyers and sellers via block-trading desks, dark pools, or RFQ networks. Treasury block trades go via interdealer brokers (Cantor Fitzgerald, BGC). Block flow is critical for pension funds and asset managers handling million-share orders. Detection: trade prints at sizes far above typical retail orders.
plain: A very large order arranged privately between big investors, away from the public market — to avoid moving the price.

snappy: Diversified commodity benchmark — 24 commodities with capping rules.
detail: Operated by Bloomberg. Roll methodology: third Friday before each month's contract expiry. Caps single-commodity weights at 15 percent and sector weights at 33 percent — limits oil dominance. Used as benchmark by many commodity funds and ETFs. Total return version includes collateral return on cash backing the futures positions. Long-running multi-billion benchmark for diversified commodity exposure.
plain: A widely watched basket tracking the prices of 24 raw materials together — from oil and gold to corn and copper.

snappy: Multi-currency investment-grade bond benchmark spanning developed markets.
detail: Combines US Aggregate, Pan-European, and Asia-Pacific aggregates. Total market value approaches 70 trillion dollars (notional). Provides global IG fixed-income exposure for institutional benchmarks. Hedged-USD versions strip FX risk. Various sub-indexes for specific exposures (Bloomberg Global Aggregate ex-Treasury, ex-Government, etc.). Operated by Bloomberg Index Services.
plain: A giant basket of high-quality bonds from around the world — the most-followed benchmark for global bond investors.

snappy: Broad US investment-grade taxable bond benchmark — the bond Agg.
detail: Roughly 13,000 securities: US Treasury securities, agency MBS, IG corporate bonds, ABS, CMBS. Market-value weighted. Originally Lehman Brothers Aggregate; renamed Bloomberg Barclays after acquisitions, now simply Bloomberg US Aggregate. Tracked by ishares Core US Aggregate bond ETF (AGG), Vanguard Total bond Market (BND). Multi-trillion indexed against. Duration around 6 years; yield reflects mixed Treasury and credit composition.
plain: The main scorecard for the US bond market — covers Treasury securities, mortgages, and high-grade company debt.

snappy: Japan's central bank — global pioneer of unconventional monetary policy.
detail: Implemented QE first in 2001 (years before other major banks). Maintained zero or negative rates for nearly all of 2000-2024. Owns roughly half of all outstanding JGBs and significant ETF holdings (around 7 percent of TOPIX market cap). Exited negative-rate policy and YCC March 2024 after inflation finally returned to target. Now slowly normalising — first major central bank to hike after the pandemic-era easing.
plain: Japan's central bank — famous for keeping interest rates near zero for over twenty years before slowly raising them in 2024.

snappy: Loan packaged as a tradable security — pays coupons until maturity, then principal back.
detail: Issuer (government, corporate, agency) sells bonds to raise capital; investors lend in exchange for coupon payments and repayment at maturity. Quoted as a percentage of par (100 = par; 95 = below par). Trading happens mostly OTC through dealer networks, not on exchanges. The US Treasury market is the largest and most liquid in the world — roughly 27 trillion dollars outstanding as of 2024.
plain: A loan you make to a company or government — they pay you interest, then return your money on a fixed date.

snappy: Accounting value of the company — assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet.
detail: Per-share book value equals total shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding. P/B ratio (price-to-book) compares market value to book value. Banks and insurers trade close to book because their assets are largely financial; tech and brand-driven companies trade at multiples of book because their value sits in intangibles not on the balance sheet. Tangible book value excludes goodwill and intangibles.
plain: What a company would be worth on paper if it sold every Asset, paid off every debt, and handed shareholders the rest.

snappy: Resampling technique generating statistical estimates without parametric assumptions.
detail: Bradley Efron (1979). Resample with replacement from observed data to create alternative samples; compute statistics on each; build empirical distribution. Used for confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, model validation without distributional assumptions. Block bootstrap preserves time-series dependence. Common in modern empirical finance and quant strategy validation.
plain: A statistical trick where you re-sample your data many times to estimate how confident you can be in a number, without needing extra assumptions.
The inflation rate the bond market is pricing in — calculated from the gap between regular and inflation-protected Treasury yields.
snappy: Yield gap between nominal Treasury securities and TIPS — the market's implied future inflation rate.
detail: If a 10-year Treasury yields 4.5 percent and the matching 10-year TIPS yields 2.0 percent, the 10-year breakeven is 2.5 percent — the inflation rate at which both bonds would deliver the same return. Quoted by maturity (2-year, 5-year, 10-year, 30-year breakevens). You'll hear breakevens cited in every Fed communications post-mortem, since they're the cleanest market-implied inflation expectation.

snappy: North Sea crude benchmark — global pricing reference, especially for non-US trade.
detail: Quoted in dollars per barrel. ICE-listed Brent futures are the global benchmark, used in pricing roughly two-thirds of internationally traded crude. Lighter and sweeter than many EM grades but heavier than WTI. Brent-WTI spread reflects North Sea supply, US pipeline constraints, and global vs continental dynamics. Historically WTI traded above Brent by a few dollars; flipped in 2011 with the US shale boom.
plain: A type of crude oil drilled in the North Sea — its price is the world's most quoted benchmark for oil.

snappy: Intermediary that executes trades on behalf of clients, charging commission or spread.
detail: Agency model: the broker matches the client order with the best venue and takes a commission. Principal model: the broker takes the other side of the trade from inventory and earns the spread. Most US retail brokers (Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood) now charge zero commission and earn primarily from PFOF and net interest. Institutional brokers also add research, prime brokerage, and securities lending. Regulated by FINRA in the US, FCA in the UK, and ESMA-coordinated regimes across the EU.
plain: A firm that buys and sells investments on your behalf — earns either a commission per trade or a margin built into the price.
A maths model for random wandering — used to describe how stock prices drift up and down unpredictably over time.
snappy: Random-walk model with continuous paths — foundational stochastic process in finance.
detail: Named after botanist Robert Brown's 1827 observation of pollen jiggling in water; formalised mathematically by Einstein and Wiener. Geometric Brownian motion is the assumption behind Black-Scholes option pricing. Real markets deviate from pure Brownian motion (jumps, fat tails, vol clustering) — modern models add jumps (Levy processes) and stochastic vol to capture realism. Still the starting point for most pricing theory and risk modelling.

plain: The EU's rulebook for winding up failing Banks without using taxpayer money — losses get pushed onto Shareholders and certain Bondholders first.
snappy: EU framework forcing bank shareholders and bondholders to absorb losses before any state aid.
detail: Effective 2015. Establishes resolution authorities, bail-in tools, MREL requirements (minimum loss-absorbing capacity). The March 2023 Credit Suisse rescue applied a version of bail-in: 17 billion of AT1 was wiped out before equity, sparking AT1 market turmoil. BRRD2 (2019) refined the framework. EU SRM (Single Resolution Mechanism) implements BRRD for significant eurozone banks. Together with TLAC, the cornerstone of post-crisis bank resolution.

snappy: Yield curve flattening driven by long yields falling faster than short yields.
detail: Typical of growth scares: investors pile into long bonds for safety, pulling long yields down while the Fed hasn't moved yet. Long bonds outperform short bonds. Repeatedly seen in 2024 around recession-fear episodes. Opposite of bear steepener. The 'bull' label means falling yields (bonds rallying); 'flattener' means the curve flattens.
plain: A move in the bond market where long-term rates fall faster than short-term ones — typically when investors fear a slowdown.

snappy: Rising market — typically 20-plus percent above a recent low.
detail: Often used for equity markets but applies broadly. Average post-WWII US bull market: 60 months, 175 percent S&P gain. Recent bulls: March 2009 to February 2020 (132 percent gain), 2020 lows to current. Sentiment shifts during bull markets: skepticism, hope, optimism, euphoria. Famous bull-market peaks: 1929 (Depression), 2000 (dot-com), 2007 (financial crisis). Each ends differently.
plain: A long, sustained rise in prices — usually defined as a gain of 20 percent or more from a recent low.

snappy: Settlement enforcement — buyer purchases failed-to-deliver securities in the market, bills the seller.
detail: Triggered when a seller fails to deliver securities by settlement deadline. The buyer purchases shares from any seller in the market, and the original seller must reimburse the cost difference. SEC Reg SHO mandates close-out within specific timeframes. CSDR (EU equivalent) imposes similar buy-in regime. Discourages chronic failure to deliver and protects buyers.
plain: When a seller fails to deliver shares on time, the buyer purchases them on the open market and bills the seller for the cost.

snappy: Company buys back its own shares — reduces share count, returns cash to shareholders.
detail: Two forms: open-market repurchase (gradual purchases over time) and tender offers (one-time large buys). S&P 500 buybacks routinely exceed 900 billion annually. 2022 inflation Reduction Act imposed 1 percent excise tax on net buybacks. Compared to dividends as a method of returning capital — buybacks are more tax-efficient and flexible. Often boost EPS mechanically by reducing share count denominator.
plain: When a company spends its own cash to repurchase its own stocks — leaving fewer shares and a bigger slice for each remaining holder.

snappy: Net stock buybacks as a percentage of market cap — shareholder return via share-count reduction.
detail: Companies returned roughly 950 billion to S&P 500 shareholders via buybacks in 2022 — more than dividends. Buybacks shrink share count, mechanically boosting EPS and dividend-per-share if total dividend pool is constant. The 'shareholder yield' (dividend yield plus buyback yield) is a broader payout measure than dividend yield alone. The 2022 US inflation Reduction Act introduced a 1 percent excise tax on net buybacks.
plain: The percentage of a company's value that it returns to shareholders by buying back its own stocks each year.

snappy: 40 largest French-listed companies — France's main equity index.
detail: LVMH, TotalEnergies, L'Oréal, Sanofi, Hermès are major weights. Heavy luxury-goods, energy, and pharma exposure. Operated by Euronext. The French headline equity index for political and economic commentary. CAC 40 ETFs and futures support trading. Higher correlation with European peers (DAX, Eurostoxx 50) than with US equity benchmarks.
plain: The headline French stock index — 40 big companies including LVMH, L'Oréal, and TotalEnergies.

snappy: Process of fitting model parameters to observed market prices.
detail: Daily for option-pricing desks: load market quotes for vanilla options across strikes and tenors, solve for the model parameters that minimise pricing errors. Calibration accuracy determines exotic-option pricing quality. Local-vol models calibrate exactly to vanillas; stochastic-vol models trade exact fit for better dynamics. Volatility-surface arbitrage exploits calibration errors between desks.
plain: Adjusting a pricing model's settings until it matches what's actually trading in the market — done daily on option desks.
A contract that pays off if a stock or other Underlying rises above an agreed price — used to bet on gains or capture upside.
snappy: Option giving the holder the right to buy the underlying at the strike price before expiry.
detail: Buyers of calls profit when prices rise; sellers ('writers') collect premium and lose if the stock spikes. Covered calls — selling calls against shares you own — are a popular income strategy. Speculative call buying drove the GameStop and meme-stock rallies of 2021. Single-stock and index calls are the most-traded equity derivative products, with billions of dollars notional changing hands daily on CBOE and other exchanges.

snappy: Option giving the right to buy the underlying at a strike price by expiry.
detail: Long call: holder buys, pays premium, profits if underlying rallies above strike plus premium. Short call (naked): writer collects premium, unlimited loss potential if underlying rallies — covered calls offset by owning the underlying. Common in hedging and speculation. American calls on dividend-paying stocks can be optimal to exercise early just before ex-dividend dates; European calls cannot be early-exercised.
plain: An option giving you the right to buy a stock or Underlying at a chosen price — pays off if the price goes up.

snappy: Option series that pays out when a floating interest rate rises above a fixed strike.
detail: A series of caplets, one per reset period of the underlying floating leg. Each caplet pays max(floating rate minus strike, 0) on notional. Used to cap borrowing costs on Floating Rate loans — corporates buy caps to hedge variable-rate debt. Trades over-the-counter under an ISDA Master Agreement. Vol surface typically fit with the SABR Model. Cheaper than locking into a fixed rate up front because there is no protection if rates stay below the strike.
plain: A contract that pays the buyer whenever a floating interest rate climbs above an agreed level — a way to set a ceiling on borrowing costs.

snappy: Net cross-border capital flows — direct investment, portfolio investment, banking flows.
detail: By accounting identity, capital account mirrors current account (with errors and omissions). Capital flows into US — Chinese, Japanese, Saudi reserves into Treasury securities; foreign equity into US tech — fund US current-account deficit. Reversals can be sharp: 1998 Asian crisis, 2020 March COVID flight. Capital controls aim to limit volatility but distort allocation.
plain: A country's record of money flowing in and out for investments — buying foreign companies, lending across borders, that sort of thing.

snappy: 2.5 percent CET1 buffer above minimum — constrains distributions when breached.
detail: Mandatory under Basel III. If a bank's CET1 falls into the buffer zone (below 7 percent total), restrictions on dividends, buybacks, and bonus payments kick in proportional to the breach depth. Designed to ensure banks rebuild capital naturally through retained earnings rather than forced capital raises during stress. Sits above the 4.5 percent CET1 minimum.
plain: An extra capital cushion banks must hold above the minimum — dipping into it triggers limits on dividends and bonuses.

snappy: Government restrictions on cross-border money flows — for stability or political reasons.
detail: Common in EM during crises: Malaysia 1998 (Asian crisis), Iceland 2008 (banking crisis), Greece 2015 (deposit flight), Russia 2022 (sanctions response). Forms include deposit reserve requirements, currency mismatches, outright bans on FX purchases, foreign-investment ceilings. The IMF historically opposed controls; the 2010s shifted to acknowledging temporary, targeted controls as macro tools. Tobin tax proposals are an academic relative.
plain: Rules a government enacts to limit how much money can flow in or out of the country — usually during a crisis.

snappy: Theoretical model relating expected return to beta — the foundational asset-pricing equation.
detail: Expected return equals risk-free rate plus beta times market risk premium. Published 1964-66 by Sharpe Ratio, Lintner, Mossin. Single-factor model — every asset's expected return depends only on market beta. Empirical evidence shows CAPM systematically under-prices low-beta stocks and over-prices high-beta — leading to multi-factor extensions. Still the cornerstone of academic finance and undergraduate textbooks. Sharpe Ratio won 1990 Nobel.
plain: A textbook formula that says a stock's expected return depends on how risky it is compared to the overall market.

snappy: Tradable permit to emit one tonne of CO2 — issued under cap-and-trade schemes.
detail: EU ETS EUAs are the largest credit market. Voluntary markets (REDD+ forest conservation, renewable-energy credits) operate separately at lower prices and with weaker integrity controls. Cap-and-trade schemes shrink credit supply over time, lifting prices. Critics argue carbon markets allow polluters to outsource action; supporters cite EU ETS achieving real emission reductions cost-effectively.
plain: A tradable permit that lets a company release one tonne of carbon dioxide — designed to make polluting expensive and cutting emissions profitable.

snappy: Borrow a low-yield currency, invest in a high-yield one — pocket the rate differential.
detail: Classic example: borrow JPY at 0.1 percent, invest in AUD at 4 percent, earn the 3.9-percent gap as carry. Works in calm markets; explodes in stress (2008 AUD/JPY fell 50 percent in months). Risk: the funding currency rallies in a flight-to-safety, wiping out months of carry in days. Hedge funds and macro strategies systematically run carry baskets, sized to risk metrics like volatility-adjusted carry.
plain: Borrowing money in a country with low interest rates and investing it where rates are higher — pocketing the difference.

snappy: Company sells a minority stake in a subsidiary via IPO, retaining majority control.
detail: Distinct from spin-off (which separates entirely). Parent receives cash from IPO proceeds; carved-out entity gets a public market valuation. Notable examples: AT&T's Vrio, Lambda's IPO in 2023. Sometimes precursor to full spin-off — parent crystallises valuation, then later distributes remaining stake. Tax treatment more complex than tax-free spin-offs.
plain: When a company sells a slice of one of its divisions to public investors, but keeps majority control of it.

snappy: CME-owned exchange listing grain and bond futures — home of corn, wheat, soybeans.
detail: Founded 1848 as the first US futures exchange. Merged with CME in 2007. Lists CBOT corn (/ZC), wheat (/ZW), soybeans (/ZS), and also 30-year US Treasury bond futures (/ZB) and 10-year T-Note (/ZN). Trading hours extended overnight for global access. Historic Chicago grain-trading floor closed in 2015; trading now electronic via Globex.
plain: A historic Chicago exchange where corn, wheat, soybean, and US government bond Futures are traded — now part of CME.

snappy: Fed annual stress test for largest US banks — assesses capital adequacy under stress scenarios.
detail: Introduced 2011. Banks submit capital plans (dividend, buyback proposals) for Fed review. Fed runs banks' balance sheets through severely adverse scenarios. Quantitative pass/fail (now replaced by Stress Capital Buffer in 2020). Forces banks to maintain capital adequate for prescribed stress scenarios. Now integrated with the annual Dodd-Frank Stress Test (DFAST).
plain: The US central bank's annual exam where the biggest banks have to prove they could survive a severe recession.

snappy: Clearing house standing between buyer and seller — guarantees each trade's settlement.
detail: Major CCPs: LCH (interest-rate swaps, equity, FX), ICE Clear Credit (CDS), CME Clearing (futures, swaps), Eurex Clearing (European derivatives), DTCC NSCC (US equities). Counterparty risk concentrated at the CCP, mitigated by initial margin, default fund, and skin-in-the-game. Designated SIFMU (Systemically Important Financial Market Utility) status by FSB.
plain: A safety hub that sits between every buyer and seller — if one side defaults, the hub makes the other side whole.

snappy: Variable capital buffer that regulators raise in boom times and release in stress.
detail: Basel III tool. Set by national regulators between 0 and 2.5 percent of RWA. US Fed has kept CCyB at zero throughout. UK PRA raised UK CCyB to 2 percent in mid-2023, signalling concerns about leverage. Released in stress to give banks capital headroom to keep lending. Designed to lean against the credit cycle.
plain: A capital cushion regulators raise during boom times and release in busts — leans against the credit cycle.

snappy: Securitisation of bonds (corporate, MBS, ABS) — infamous for its role in the 2008 crisis.
detail: Pool of debt securities tranched by seniority — investors got the spread differential and ratings benefits. Synthetic CDOs used CDS to gain exposure without owning bonds. The 2008 crisis exposed massive mispricing in mortgage-backed CDOs and CDOs-squared (CDOs of CDOs). Post-crisis the CDO market shrank dramatically; CLOs (CDOs of leveraged loans) survived and grew, but mortgage CDOs largely disappeared.
plain: An investment built by pooling bonds or loans and chopping them into slices of different risk — infamous for blowing up in 2008.

snappy: Insurance contract on a bond's default — buyer pays premium, seller pays out on credit event.
detail: Buyer pays the seller a quarterly premium (the spread) over the contract's term; if the reference name suffers a credit event, the seller pays out the face value minus recovery. Standardised 2009 reforms moved most CDS to central clearing at LCH and ICE. The single-name CDS market shrank dramatically post-Dodd-Frank as flows moved to index CDS (CDX, iTraxx). ISDA defines credit events and runs auctions.
plain: An insurance contract on a bond defaulting — the buyer pays a regular premium, and the seller pays out if the borrower fails.

snappy: ISDA-administered auction that determines the recovery rate after a CDS credit event.
detail: Triggered when a Credit Determinations Committee rules a credit event occurred. Two-stage auction: initial bidding sets a midpoint price, then a final 'open interest' phase where dealers transact bonds at the determined recovery. Roughly 100 auctions have been held since 2005. Famous cases: Lehman (8.625 cents on the dollar), Greek 2012 restructuring (21.5 cents), Sears 2018 (16 cents).
plain: An auction that decides how much insurance buyers get paid after a borrower defaults — usually a percentage of what they were owed.

snappy: Annual premium paid to insure a bond against default — basis points on notional.
detail: Buyer pays a quarterly premium (the spread), seller pays out if the reference name defaults. A 200 bp CDS on a ten-million notional costs two hundred thousand a year. Spreads widen when default looks more likely. iTraxx (Europe) and CDX (US) indexes track baskets. Blew out during the 2008 Lehman crisis and the 2023 SVB stress. Post-2009 reforms moved most trades to central clearing at LCH and ICE.
plain: The annual cost of insuring a bond against default — wider numbers mean the market thinks default is more likely.

snappy: Basket of 125 North American CDS contracts — the most-traded credit derivatives benchmark.
detail: Two main sub-indexes: CDX IG (investment grade) and CDX HY (high yield). Roll every six months as composition refreshes. Replaced single-name CDS as the primary credit-risk-transfer venue post-2009 — daily volumes in the tens of billions. Used to hedge corporate bond portfolios, express macro credit views, and arbitrage against single-name CDS. Cleared at ICE Clear Credit.
plain: A basket of 125 North American company default-insurance contracts traded as a single instrument — the standard tool for hedging US credit risk.

snappy: Operational autonomy of central banks from political interference.
detail: Empirical evidence supports independent central banks delivering lower inflation. Fed enjoyed strong independence through Volcker (anti-inflation push) and Greenspan-Bernanke eras. Trump administration verbally pressured Powell (2018-2020). BoE has full operational independence (since 1997). ECB has very high independence (constitutionally enshrined). Turkey's central bank independence eroded under Erdoğan, contributing to lira crisis. Indispensable for credible inflation targeting.
plain: A central bank's freedom to set interest rates without politicians ordering it around — generally produces lower, steadier inflation.

snappy: Highest-quality bank capital — common stock plus retained earnings.
detail: Minimum 4.5 percent of risk-weighted assets under Basel III, plus conservation buffer (2.5 percent), countercyclical buffer (variable), G-SIB surcharge (1-3.5 percent). Total CET1 requirement for largest banks: roughly 10-13 percent. Absorbs losses first; protects depositors and senior creditors. Tracked by every bank earnings release.
plain: The highest-quality form of bank safety capital — common stock plus retained profits, the first money to absorb losses.

snappy: OTC contract that pays the price difference of an underlying without owning it.
detail: Popular in Europe and Asia for retail traders to get leveraged stock or FX exposure. Banned for US retail by the SEC. Cash-settled, no physical delivery. Traded against the broker as counterparty rather than on an exchange. The 2021 GameStop episode highlighted CFD risks — brokers like IG and Plus500 saw extreme retail losses. Spread plus financing cost is the broker's revenue.
plain: A contract that pays the price change of a stock without you owning it — popular with retail in Europe, banned in the US.

snappy: Dodd-Frank-created US agency enforcing consumer-financial-products rules.
detail: Established 2011. Oversees mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, debt collection, student loans. Independent funding through Fed (constitutional challenges to that funding model unsuccessful at Supreme Court 2024). Returned billions in restitution to consumers for predatory lending, illegal fees, deceptive marketing. Frequently in political crosshairs — Republican administrations push for restructuring; Democrats expand authority.
plain: A US government agency created after 2008 to protect ordinary people from unfair fees, predatory loans, and shady financial-product marketing.
The US watchdog that polices futures and most derivatives — sets the rules for commodity, rate, and FX contracts.
snappy: US regulator for commodity, futures, and most OTC derivative markets.
detail: Created in 1974, the CFTC oversees CME, ICE, and other US derivatives venues. Sets position limits, runs enforcement actions for manipulation and spoofing, and writes Title VII Dodd-Frank rules on cleared OTC swaps. Jurisdiction overlaps with the SEC on security-based swaps. You'll hear CFTC named in market-structure debates, in commitment-of-traders reports, and after any spoofing or manipulation case.

snappy: Private-sector USD large-value payment system — operated by The Clearing House.
detail: Handles roughly 1.8 trillion dollars daily. Uses real-time multilateral netting rather than gross settlement — more efficient than Fedwire. Final settlement at end of day via Fedwire. Operated by major US banks. Together with Fedwire, handles vast majority of US dollar wholesale payments. Foundation of US financial plumbing.
plain: A private US system that moves trillions in payments between big banks daily — settles at end of day rather than instantly.

snappy: Pre-set rule that halts trading when prices move beyond a threshold.
detail: Three-tier S&P 500 circuit breakers: Level 1 (7 percent decline, 15-minute halt), Level 2 (13 percent, 15-minute halt), Level 3 (20 percent, halt for the day). Single-stock LULD (Limit Up Limit Down) bands tighter still. Triggered multiple times during March 2020 pandemic selloff. Designed to give participants time to assess information during disorderly moves. Critics argue they can amplify volatility by pulling liquidity around triggers.
plain: An automatic rule that halts trading when prices fall too far too fast — to give panicked investors a chance to catch their breath.

snappy: Cleared derivatives settle through a central counterparty; bilateral settle directly between parties.
detail: Dodd-Frank and EMIR mandated clearing for most standardised IRS and CDS post-2012. Clearing concentrates counterparty risk in clearing houses (LCH, CME, ICE), backed by member default-funds and initial margin. Bilateral trades use ISDA Master Agreement plus CSA collateral. Cleared trades benefit from netting across all clearing-house members. Most new OTC swap volume is cleared; exotic and non-standardised trades remain bilateral.
plain: Two ways a derivatives trade can settle — through a central safety hub (cleared) or directly between the two parties (bilateral).

snappy: Bank or broker authorised to clear trades through a specific CCP — their customers' trades pass through them.
detail: Major clearing members: JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Citi, Barclays, BNP Paribas. Customers must use a clearing member to access central clearing. Clearing members post initial margin to the CCP, fund their share of the default fund, and assume liability for their customers' obligations. CCP eligibility requires significant capital and operational sophistication.
plain: A bank or broker authorised to route trades through a central safety hub — pays in if any of its customers defaults.

snappy: International CSD based in Luxembourg — competitor to Euroclear.
detail: Subsidiary of Deutsche Börse. Handles roughly 8 trillion euros in custody. Stronger in German and Asian fixed-income markets than Euroclear. Provides international settlement for sovereign bonds, corporate bonds, equities, and increasingly investment funds. Has been expanding T2S participation in EU CSD harmonisation.
plain: A European institution based in Luxembourg that holds bonds and shares safely on behalf of investors and settles trades between them.

snappy: Series of forward-starting options — locks in periodic gains.
detail: Each leg resets the strike at the beginning of its period. Used in structured products as 'ratcheted' return profiles — investor locks in gains period-by-period without giving them back. The 1999 LTCM-era cliquet craze created huge vol-surface exposures that surfaced losses for dealers during the 2000 vol spike. Now standard in equity structured products and exotic FX hedges.
plain: A chain of small options that lock in gains period by period — investors keep early profits even if the market falls later.

snappy: Securitisation of leveraged loans — bonds backed by a pool of bank loans, tranched by seniority.
detail: Market grew to roughly 1.2 trillion in 2024. Pool of 100-300 senior secured loans from LBOs and corporate borrowers. Tranches from AAA down to equity, paying different yields. CLOs are the largest buyer of leveraged loans globally — bank loan markets effectively depend on CLO demand. Tested in 2008 (held up better than CDOs), again in March 2020 (volatile but resilient). Managers actively rotate the pool.
plain: A pool of risky business loans sliced into different-quality bonds — investors choose how much risk they want for how much return.

snappy: ISDA Master Agreement provision triggering immediate termination and netting of all trades upon default.
detail: Critical legal protection for derivatives counterparties. On default, all outstanding trades terminate, net market value is calculated, and a single payment determines the final claim. Enforceable in major jurisdictions through specific legal opinions. Without close-out netting, gross derivative exposures would create massive counterparty risks. Crisis-tested through Lehman 2008 — close-out worked as designed.
plain: A legal trick where, if one party defaults, every trade between the two firms gets cancelled and combined into a single net payment.

snappy: FX settlement utility that eliminates Herstatt risk — both legs of a trade settle simultaneously.
detail: Founded 2002 in response to the 1974 Herstatt Bank collapse, where banks paid out one side of FX trades before failing on the other. CLS settles 18 currencies, processing roughly 2 trillion dollars daily through payment-versus-payment (PVP). Eliminates principal risk between settlement and receipt. Members include the biggest global banks; their customers settle indirectly via members. The plumbing nobody outside FX operations notices.
plain: A worldwide plumbing system that settles foreign-exchange trades so neither side can pay first and lose out if the other goes bust.

snappy: MBS backed by commercial mortgages — office, retail, hotel, multi-family.
detail: Pool of 50-100 large commercial loans, tranched by seniority and rating. Distinct from RMBS because commercial mortgages don't prepay freely (yield-maintenance clauses lock in lender economics). The 2020-22 office crisis hammered CMBS valuations: vacancy rates spiked, refinancing dried up, several major office loans defaulted. Roughly 700 billion outstanding. SEC oversight; ratings from Moody's, S&P, KBRA.
plain: A bond backed by mortgages on offices, hotels, shopping malls, and apartment buildings — hit hard during the 2020 office crisis.

snappy: World's largest derivatives exchange — futures on rates, equity indexes, FX, energy, agriculture, and metals.
detail: Formed by Chicago Mercantile Exchange's merger with CBOT (2007) and NYMEX/COMEX (2008). Lists Eurodollar (now SOFR) futures, E-mini S&P 500 futures, WTI crude, gold, corn, and soybeans. Clears through CME Clearing. Operates the Globex electronic platform almost 24 hours. Publishes Term SOFR and the FedWatch tool tracking implied policy probabilities. The benchmark venue for nearly all US listed futures.
plain: The world's biggest exchange for futures contracts — everything from corn to the price of a barrel of oil trades there.
A bundle of home loans cut into slices with different repayment timing, so investors can pick fast-paying or slow-paying tranches.
snappy: Pool of MBS cash flows tranched into pieces with different prepayment and maturity profiles.
detail: Takes a pool of mortgage-backed securities and slices the cash flows so different tranches get principal at different speeds. Common structures: planned amortisation class (PAC) bonds get predictable cash flows, support tranches absorb prepayment variability, IO/PO strips separate interest from principal. CMOs let investors with specific duration or convexity needs target their preferred slice. Mostly issued out of agency MBS pools today.

snappy: Yuan traded outside mainland China — distinct exchange rate from onshore CNY.
detail: Hong Kong is the dominant CNH centre; London, Singapore, and Taipei also active. CNY trades within a daily band set by the PBoC's fixing; CNH floats more freely. The CNY-CNH spread widens during stress (capital flight pressure) and tightens in calm. CNH market includes spot, forwards, NDFs, options, and bonds (dim sum bonds). Critical plumbing for non-Chinese investors seeking yuan exposure.
plain: Chinese yuan traded outside mainland China — mostly in Hong Kong — at a price that floats more freely than the tightly managed mainland rate.

snappy: Placing trading servers in the same data centre as the exchange matching engine.
detail: Reduces network latency from milliseconds to microseconds. NYSE Mahwah, Nasdaq Carteret, CME Aurora are the major co-location sites. Costs tens of thousands of dollars per month per cabinet. HFT firms invest heavily in co-location plus FPGA hardware to minimise tick-to-trade latency. Regulators have raised fairness concerns but allow co-location as standard practice.
plain: Renting space inside an exchange's data centre so your trading computer sits right next to the market's — saving precious microseconds.

snappy: Carbon-rich solid fuel used primarily for electricity generation.
detail: Major pricing references: Newcastle thermal (Asia), Rotterdam (Europe), Central Appalachian (US). Demand peaked globally around 2014; in retreat from gas and renewables in OECD economies, but China and India still expanding. 2022 European energy crisis briefly revived coal demand as gas supplies were squeezed. Carbon-pricing schemes (EU ETS) penalise coal generation. Futures traded on ICE and CME.
plain: A black, carbon-rich rock burned to make electricity — global demand is shrinking in rich countries but still growing in China and India.

snappy: Chocolate raw material — concentrated supply in West Africa.
detail: Ivory Coast and Ghana produce roughly 60 percent of global supply. ICE-listed cocoa futures (London for European delivery, NYC for US). Prices surged to record 10,000+ dollars per tonne in early 2024 — quadruple historical averages — as West African disease and weather damaged crops. Climate change and aging tree stocks create structural supply concerns. Cocoa demand grows roughly 2-3 percent annually; supply struggles to keep pace.
plain: The bean that becomes chocolate — mostly grown in West Africa, with prices spiking to record highs in 2024 after crop damage.

snappy: Tropical bean — Arabica (premium) and Robusta (mass-market) varieties.
detail: ICE-listed Arabica (Coffee C) is the premium benchmark; Robusta on London ICE. Brazil produces roughly 40 percent of global Arabica; Vietnam dominates Robusta. Arabica prices spiked to record highs in 2024 on Brazilian drought and frost concerns. Specialty coffee market (premium grades) developing alongside the commodity market with separate pricing dynamics. Climate change is a real long-term threat — Arabica's growing range is shrinking.
plain: The world's most-traded soft drink raw material — Brazil grows most of the premium kind, Vietnam most of the cheaper variety.

snappy: Two non-stationary time series whose linear combination is stationary — they share a long-run equilibrium.
detail: Engle-Granger test (1987 Nobel) is the standard cointegration test. Used in pairs trading: identify stocks/instruments that tend to revert to a long-run ratio. The pairs trade buys the underpriced side and shorts the overpriced side, profiting from convergence. Statistical arbitrage shops run hundreds of cointegrated pairs simultaneously. Famous example: gold versus gold miners; Coca-Cola versus Pepsi.
plain: When two prices wander up and down but always tend to drift back to a fixed relationship — used to spot pairs trades.

snappy: CME-owned division for precious-metals and copper futures — gold and silver benchmark.
detail: Originally the Commodity Exchange of New York. Merged with NYMEX in 1994; under CME Group since 2008. Lists gold (/GC), silver (/SI), copper (/HG), platinum, palladium. Physically deliverable in principle, mostly financially settled. Gold and silver delivery warrants from COMEX-registered warehouses (HSBC, JP Morgan, Brinks) form the physical market backbone. Daily settlement prices are key benchmarks.
plain: A New York exchange where gold, silver, and copper Futures are traded — the main place those metals are priced globally.

snappy: Standard equity — full voting rights, dividend eligibility, residual claim.
detail: What most people mean when they say 'stock'. One vote per share, dividends paid only after preferred holders get theirs, last in line for residual value on liquidation. Trades on exchanges. Companies typically issue one class of common stock, though many tech companies (Google, Meta, Snap) issue two or three classes with different voting rights — see dual-class share structures.
plain: Standard ownership shares — one vote each, a slice of any dividends, and whatever's left if the company is wound down.

snappy: Process that nets offsetting derivative trades — reduces gross notional without changing net risk.
detail: Run by TriOptima and other providers in cycles across cleared and bilateral books. Pre-2008 derivatives notional outstanding compressed dramatically post-crisis — global IRS notional fell from over 500 trillion peak to roughly 400 trillion as duplicate trades got terminated. Reduces leverage ratio drag, operational risk, and balance-sheet usage. Routine for banks active in cleared swap markets.
plain: A clean-up process where banks cancel out matching derivative trades against each other — shrinks paperwork without changing real risk.

snappy: Risk from large exposure to a single name, sector, geography, or risk factor.
detail: Pension funds limit single-name equity exposure to 5-10 percent typically. Bank lending concentrated in single industries (commercial real estate, energy) historically caused failures. The 2023 SVB collapse: concentrated tech-VC client base, long-duration asset book — twin concentration risks. Basel large-exposure regime limits single-counterparty bank exposure to 25 percent of Tier 1 capital. Diversification is the main mitigation.
plain: The danger of having too much money tied to a single name, industry, or country — eggs all in one basket.

snappy: Futures price above spot — usually means storage costs or surplus inventory.
detail: Crude oil in storage-glut periods sits in contango: a one-month forward trades above near-month, the curve sloping upward. Holders of long futures roll into pricier contracts each month, paying the 'roll yield' penalty. The April 2020 negative WTI episode was contango taken to extremes — storage was so full that nearby contracts went negative. ETF investors in commodity products learn about contango the hard way.
plain: When today's price of something like oil is lower than the price for delivery later — usually means there's too much sitting in storage.

snappy: Bank capital bond that converts to equity (or gets written down) on a regulatory trigger.
detail: Synonym for AT1 in European bank usage. Trigger usually a CET1 ratio falling below 5.125 percent (or 7 percent for higher-trigger CoCos). Mechanism: convert to common equity (dilutes existing shareholders, recapitalises bank) or principal write-down (creditors lose, equity holders preserved). Designed to absorb losses without taxpayer bailout. Performed as intended in some bank rescues, controversially in Credit Suisse.
plain: A bank bond that turns into stock or gets written off if the bank's safety cushion drops too low — a built-in shock absorber.

snappy: Implicit benefit of holding physical commodity inventory vs holding a futures contract.
detail: Drives the relationship between spot and futures. Physical holders have flexibility — they can use the commodity, deliver to short sellers, profit from local shortages. The convenience yield equals interest rate plus storage cost minus the futures-spot basis. When convenience yield exceeds storage cost, the curve goes into backwardation. Common in heavily-used commodities (oil, gas) with thin spot inventories.
plain: The unspoken benefit of physically owning a commodity right now — flexibility to use it, sell it, or cash in on local shortages.

snappy: Bond that can convert into equity at a fixed ratio — debt with embedded call option.
detail: Issuer benefits from lower coupon (the conversion option is part of the compensation); investor benefits from upside participation. Issued primarily by mid-cap growth companies and stressed names. The convert market spiked during 2020-21 SPAC and growth-stock issuance. Pricing decomposes into bond floor plus conversion value plus implied option vol. Convertible arb funds run the dominant pricing edge.
plain: A bond that can be swapped into a fixed number of the company's stocks — combines bond safety with share-price upside.

snappy: How a bond's duration itself changes as yields move — the second-order kicker.
detail: Duration alone is a first-order approximation. Convexity captures the curvature: positive convexity (most non-callable bonds) means the price gains more on a rate drop than it loses on an equivalent rise — good for the holder. Mortgage-backed securities have negative convexity because prepayment shortens duration in rallies, the dreaded MBS hedge flow that whipsaws Treasury markets.
plain: How a bond's price curves with interest-rate moves — usually a bit lopsided in the holder's favour for ordinary bonds.

snappy: Industrial base metal — wiring, plumbing, construction, electrification.
detail: Nicknamed 'Dr Copper' for its perceived ability to diagnose the global economy — strong copper demand signals industrial expansion. Quoted in dollars per pound (US) or dollars per tonne (LME). China consumes roughly half of global copper. Electrification, EVs, and renewable grids drive structural demand growth. Surged to 5 dollars per pound in 2021-22; supply constraints from declining ore grades and project delays keep prices structurally elevated.
plain: An industrial metal used in wiring, plumbing, and electric cars — nicknamed Dr Copper because its price often predicts the global economy.

snappy: Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices — proxy for underlying inflation trend.
