detail: More stable signal of price pressures because food and energy are highly volatile. Most central banks focus on core (or 'underlying') inflation for policy decisions. Critics note core can underestimate inflation when food and energy rise persistently. Variants: trimmed-mean inflation (exclude top and bottom outliers), median CPI, sticky-price CPI. Cleveland Fed publishes multiple alternative measures.
plain: Inflation excluding food and fuel — strips out the two most volatile categories to show what's really going on underneath.

snappy: Globally largest crop by volume — feed, food, ethanol, industrial uses.
detail: CME-listed corn futures (/ZC) are the benchmark. US is the largest producer (Iowa, Illinois, Nebraska). Roughly 40 percent of US corn goes to ethanol production. Brazil's second corn crop (safrinha) increasingly significant. USDA WASDE monthly report drives prices. Drought, heat stress, and planting-progress reports move corn 2-5 percent on release.
plain: The world's biggest crop by tonnage — used for animal feed, sweeteners, and US ethanol fuel.

snappy: Statistical measure of how two variables move together — ranges from -1 to +1.
detail: Critical input to portfolio construction, factor models, hedging. Equity correlation rises in stress (the 'correlation goes to 1' phenomenon) — exactly when diversification is most needed. Spurious correlations common with short samples. Correlation doesn't imply causation (famous statistical caveat). Rolling correlations capture time variation; copulas extend beyond simple correlation. The 2008 mortgage CDO debacle exposed catastrophic correlation-model failures.
plain: A score from minus one to plus one showing how two things move together — plus one is in sync, minus one perfect opposites.

snappy: Weekly CFTC report breaking down futures positions by trader category.
detail: Published Fridays for positions as of the prior Tuesday close. Categories: commercial hedgers (producers/users), managed money (hedge funds and CTAs), other reportables, non-reportables (small specs). Watched closely for signals of extreme positioning — when managed money is at record long, often a contrarian sell signal. Available across crude, gas, gold, currencies, equities, and rates contracts.
plain: A weekly US government release showing who's holding what in Futures markets — traders watch it for extreme positioning signals.

snappy: Natural fibre for textiles — competes with synthetic fibres (polyester).
detail: ICE-listed cotton futures (/CT) are the benchmark. US, China, India, Brazil are top producers. Cotton prices closely correlate with global GDP — apparel demand reflects discretionary spending. Synthetic fibres now dominate global fibre consumption; cotton holds roughly 25 percent share. ESG concerns around water-intensive cultivation (Aral Sea desiccation by Soviet cotton growing) drive sustainability initiatives.
plain: The fluffy plant fibre that becomes T-shirts and jeans — competes with cheaper synthetic fibres like polyester.

snappy: Party on the other side of a financial transaction.
detail: Critical concept for derivatives, repo, securities lending. Counterparty risk: the other party may default before settlement. Mitigations: central clearing (interposes a CCP), netting agreements (ISDA), collateral (CSA), credit limits, monitoring. Pre-2008, OTC derivatives counterparty risk was largely unmonitored. Dodd-Frank and EMIR forced standardisation and clearing. Lehman 2008 demonstrated cascading counterparty failures.
plain: The person or institution on the other side of a financial trade or contract — the one who owes you, or whom you owe.
The danger that whoever you've made a deal with goes bust before paying what they owe — and you're left chasing what's left.
snappy: Risk that the other side of a contract defaults before settling its obligations.
detail: Drove the 2008 panic — Bear Stearns and Lehman counterparties scrambled to close exposures. Central clearing (mandatory for most swaps under Dodd-Frank Title VII) substitutes a CCP for bilateral risk. For uncleared trades, ISDA CSAs require daily variation margin and initial margin posting. CVA (credit valuation adjustment) prices counterparty risk into derivative fair value. You'll hear it on every trading desk and in every bank stress test.

snappy: Interest payment a bond pays at fixed intervals — usually twice a year.
detail: Set at issuance as a percentage of face value: a 4 percent coupon on a thousand-dollar bond pays forty dollars annually, typically twenty every six months. Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic interest and are sold at deep discount instead. The term comes from physical bonds that had paper coupons clipped off and presented for payment — now all electronic.
plain: The interest payment a bond sends its holder, usually every six months — often expressed as a percentage of the bond's face value.

snappy: Arbitrage condition: forward FX rate equals spot adjusted for the interest-rate differential.
detail: Mathematically, forward equals spot times (1 plus quote rate) divided by (1 plus base rate). When CIP holds exactly, there's no arbitrage between investing in one currency and hedging back to another. Persistent CIP deviations since 2008 — the 'cross-currency basis' — reflect post-crisis bank funding constraints. The USD basis widens during stress as global banks scramble for dollars.
plain: A pricing rule saying the forward exchange rate must reflect the gap between the two countries' interest rates — otherwise free money would be possible.

snappy: Measure of inflation based on a basket of consumer goods and services.
detail: BLS-published monthly in the US. Components: housing (shelter is largest at over 30 percent), food, energy, medical care, transportation. Headline CPI includes everything; core CPI excludes food and energy (more stable signal). Year-over-year and month-over-month changes both watched. UK uses RPI alongside CPI. Inflation surge 2021-22 took US headline CPI to 9 percent peak; back near 3 percent by 2024.
plain: A monthly score of how much a basket of everyday shopping costs compared to a year ago — the main inflation number people watch.

snappy: Difference between refined product prices (gasoline, distillates) and crude oil — refining margin.
detail: Classic 3-2-1 crack: three barrels of crude in, two of gasoline plus one of distillate out — refining margin per crude barrel. Widened to record levels in summer 2022 as global refining capacity shortages collided with sanctions on Russian product exports. Refiners use crack-spread futures to lock in margins; speculators trade them as direct macro views on global product balances.
plain: The profit a refinery makes turning crude oil into petrol and diesel — watched as the gauge of refining health.

snappy: Currency peg that adjusts gradually over time — a controlled depreciation or appreciation.
detail: Used by countries managing inflation differentials without abandoning the peg discipline. China ran a managed crawling peg/band against USD from 2005-2015. Vietnam, Nicaragua, and historically Brazil used crawling pegs to handle inflation. Distinct from a hard peg (fixed) and a free float (market-determined). Bands around the central rate let the currency wiggle without breaking the regime.
plain: An exchange rate that's not fixed but isn't free either — the central bank lets it drift slowly in a chosen direction.

snappy: Historical commodity index — first published 1957, the dean of commodity benchmarks.
detail: Currently the Refinitiv/CoreCommodity CRB Index (RJ-CRB). 19 commodities with fixed component weights: energy 39 percent, agriculture 41 percent, base metals 13 percent, precious metals 7 percent. Rebalanced periodically. Tracked by iPath series and other commodity products. Less actively traded than GSCI or BCOM but the longest-running commodity benchmark.
plain: The oldest commodity basket benchmark — tracks 19 raw materials and has been published since 1957.

snappy: EU directive translating Basel bank capital rules into European law.
detail: First version 2006, currently CRD VI (2023). Paired with CRR (Capital Requirements Regulation) — the directive sets supervision principles while the regulation sets harmonised rules. Together they implement Basel III/IV in the EU: minimum capital ratios, leverage ratio, liquidity coverage, large-exposure limits. CRD also covers governance, supervisory powers, and remuneration (bonus caps). The UK adopted CRR/CRD pre-Brexit and now diverges slightly.
plain: The EU's set of bank capital rules — translates the international Basel standards into European law banks must follow.

snappy: ABS backed by revolving credit-card receivables — short-dated, high-yielding.
detail: Pool of credit-card balances from a single issuer (Capital One, Citi, Amex). Master trust structures let issuers add and remove receivables over time. Weighted-average life of 2-5 years. Charge-off rates run 2-4 percent in calm times, spiking in recessions. Post-2008 issuance recovered; modern deals carry low spreads reflecting strong collateral performance and frequent issuer stress tests.
plain: A bond backed by people's credit-card balances — investors earn the interest as cardholders pay down what they owe.

snappy: Term structure of an issuer's credit spread across maturities — like a yield curve but for credit.
detail: Normally upward-sloping: longer-dated bonds carry larger credit spreads to compensate for default-probability accumulation over time. Inverted credit curves (short spreads above long) signal acute distress — Lehman's curve inverted before bankruptcy. Single-name CDS quotes by tenor (1y, 3y, 5y, 7y, 10y) build the curve. The 5y CDS is the benchmark liquidity point.
plain: A picture of how much extra yield a borrower must pay over different time horizons — usually higher for longer-dated debt.
Insurance-style contract that pays off if a company or country fails to pay its debts — used to hedge credit exposure or bet against borrowers.
snappy: Derivative that pays out if a referenced borrower defaults — credit insurance, in effect.
detail: Buyer pays an annual premium to the seller; if the reference entity defaults, the seller pays par minus recovery value. Pioneered by JPMorgan in the 1990s, exploded pre-2008, then shrunk dramatically. Standardised by ISDA. Single-name CDS on major issuers and indexes (CDX, iTraxx) are the main flavours. AIG's 2008 collapse was driven by CDS sold on mortgage securities. Mostly centrally cleared post-Dodd-Frank.

snappy: ISDA-defined trigger for CDS payout — bankruptcy, failure to pay, or restructuring.
detail: Bankruptcy: court filing or analogous proceeding. Failure to Pay: missed payment over a grace period. Restructuring: terms changed to creditors' disadvantage (debt exchange, maturity extension, coupon reduction, principal write-down). Restructuring as a credit event is less common in US contracts post-2009; standard in Europe. Determination by ISDA's Credit Determinations Committee, made of major dealer and buy-side firms.
plain: An official trigger — like a missed payment or bankruptcy — that activates a Credit Default Swap and forces a payout.

snappy: Movement of an obligor's credit rating up or down — drives bond price changes outside of yield curve moves.
detail: Standard rating-agency transition matrices show one-year probabilities: an A-rated obligor has roughly a 1 percent chance of upgrade to AA, 2 percent of downgrade to BBB, 96 percent of staying A. Long-horizon transitions compound through migration matrices. Bank IFRS 9 provisioning explicitly uses migration to project expected losses. Migration risk is the credit equivalent of duration risk for fixed-income portfolios.
plain: When a borrower's credit grade moves up or down — even without default, an upgrade or downgrade swings the value of their bonds.

snappy: Letter grade assigned by a rating agency to a bond issuer or specific debt instrument.
detail: Three majors: S&P, Moody's, Fitch. Scales: AAA to D (S&P/Fitch), Aaa to C (Moody's). Issuer ratings differ from instrument ratings (subordinated debt is rated lower than senior). Ratings drive eligibility for index inclusion, regulatory capital, and pension mandates. The 2008 crisis exposed rating-agency conflicts of interest with structured products; Dodd-Frank tried to reduce regulatory reliance on ratings but the change has been gradual.
plain: A letter grade from a rating agency saying how likely a borrower is to repay — AAA is safest, D means already in default.

snappy: Extra yield a corporate bond pays over a comparable-maturity Treasury — compensation for default risk.
detail: Quoted in basis points. A 10-year corporate at 5.50 percent with the 10-year Treasury at 4.30 percent has a 120 bp spread. Tighter spreads reflect either credit improvement or risk appetite; wider spreads signal stress. The Bloomberg US Aggregate Corporate Index spread is the headline IG gauge; the high-yield equivalent OAS is its junk counterpart. Spreads gapped to crisis levels in 2008, 2020, and 2022.
plain: The extra yield a company bond pays over a same-maturity government bond — compensation for the risk the company might miss payments.
A multi-year deal to swap loan payments in one currency for payments in another — like trading a yen loan for a dollar loan.
snappy: Swap exchanging principal and interest in two different currencies — typically 1-30 year tenors.
detail: Distinct from a short-dated FX Swap — cross-currency swaps run for years and exchange interest payments along the way as well as principal at start and end. Used by multinationals to fund overseas operations in local currency without taking FX risk, and by banks to manage cross-border balance sheets. The cross-currency basis (the deviation from covered interest parity) is priced into these swaps. You'll hear them quoted on any global treasury or corporate funding desk.

snappy: Currency pair that doesn't include the US dollar — EUR/GBP, EUR/JPY, GBP/CHF.
detail: Derived from each currency's USD rate: EUR/JPY equals EUR/USD divided by USD/JPY... no, actually multiplied, since JPY is on the bottom of USD/JPY. Triangular arbitrage keeps cross rates consistent with major-pair rates. The most-traded crosses are EUR/JPY, EUR/GBP, and AUD/JPY. Spreads on crosses are wider than majors because dealers have to hedge through two USD legs.
plain: An exchange rate between two currencies that doesn't include the US dollar — like euro-to-yen or pound-to-Swiss-franc.

snappy: Anonymous matching engine — buyers and sellers cross at a reference price (usually midpoint).
detail: Examples: Liquidnet, Posit, Bloomberg POSIT, MS Pool. Periodic auctions or continuous crossing. Reference price typically NBBO midpoint, removing the half-spread cost. No public quote display — institutions match large orders without leaking information. Crossing networks are technically a form of dark pool, often distinguished by their continuous-auction crossing mechanism rather than continuous matching.
plain: A private system that matches big buy and sell orders anonymously at a fair midpoint price — without showing them to the open market.
Raw petroleum pumped from the ground — refined into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and the chemical building blocks of plastics.
snappy: Unrefined petroleum traded globally — the world's most-traded commodity.
detail: Two main benchmarks: WTI (US, light-sweet, delivered Cushing OK) and Brent (North Sea, waterborne). OPEC+ coordinates supply among major exporters. Global daily production around 100 million barrels. Sub-grades vary by API gravity (density) and sulphur content. Refineries process crude into product slates tuned to local demand. Geopolitical events (Middle East tensions, Russia sanctions) and OPEC+ decisions dominate price moves.

snappy: ISDA annex governing collateral posting — eligible types, thresholds, and timing.
detail: Specifies eligible collateral (typically cash plus Treasury securities), thresholds below which no collateral is posted, minimum transfer amounts, and dispute resolution. Daily MTM produces collateral movements under CSA terms. Sophisticated CSAs differentiate between currency, tenor, and asset class. The post-2016 'IM Big Bang' rolled out two-way initial margin requirements for non-cleared derivatives across major asset managers, banks, and corporates.
plain: A standard add-on contract between two derivatives partners that spells out who posts cash or collateral to whom, and when.

snappy: Institution holding securities in electronic form — the registry and settlement layer.
detail: DTC for US equities. Euroclear (Belgium) for international bonds. Clearstream (Luxembourg) for European bonds and equities. Each jurisdiction has its own CSD for local securities. CSDs handle ownership records, dividend payments, and settlement. Settlement happens by book entry — physical certificates rare. CSDs are designated SIFMUs by global regulators.
plain: A specialist institution that holds stocks and bonds in electronic form on behalf of investors — and updates records when ownership changes.

snappy: EU rules on settlement discipline, cash penalties for failed trades, and CSD harmonisation.
detail: Enacted 2014. Two main pillars: (1) authorisation and supervision of CSDs (Euroclear, Clearstream, and others), (2) the Settlement Discipline Regime — mandatory cash penalties on failed equity, bond, and ETF trades, in force since February 2022. Mandatory buy-ins were watered down after industry pushback. Operates alongside Reg SHO and SEC Rule 204 in the US.
plain: The EU rulebook for how securities settle — punishes trades that fail to settle on time with cash penalties.
Money issued by a country — dollars, euros, yen, pounds — used to price goods, savings, and trades within and across borders.
snappy: A nation's money — the medium of exchange and unit of account.
detail: The dollar dominates global trade and reserves (roughly 58 percent of central-bank holdings, IMF data). The euro, yen, pound, Swiss franc, Canadian and Australian dollars round out the major freely-traded currencies. Emerging-market currencies face periodic crises when external financing dries up. Currency strength reflects interest rates, trade balances, political stability, and capital flows. You'll hear it in any cross-border deal, earnings announcement, or macro discussion.

snappy: Strictest form of peg — domestic money supply fully backed by foreign reserves.
detail: Hong Kong's USD-pegged HKD has been a currency board since 1983: every HKD in circulation is backed by HKD7.75 of US dollar reserves. Argentina ran one 1991-2001 (pegged to USD) — collapsed in the 2001 crisis. Estonia, Lithuania ran them en route to euro. Eliminates central-bank discretion entirely; trades sovereignty for monetary stability.
plain: The strictest type of currency peg — every unit of local money must be backed by foreign reserves held in the central bank's vault.

snappy: Rapid currency depreciation driven by capital flight, sometimes triggering wider economic collapse.
detail: Pattern: capital flows reverse, FX reserves drain defending the currency, depreciation accelerates, dollar-denominated debt costs explode, inflation spikes, recession follows. 1992 ERM crisis (GBP, ITL forced out), 1994 Mexican peso, 1997-98 Asian crisis (THB, IDR, KRW), 1998 Russia, 2001 Argentina, 2018 Turkey. Pegged regimes are particularly vulnerable. IMF rescue packages typically follow.
plain: A sudden collapse of a country's currency — investors flee, reserves run out, and the economy often plunges into recession.

snappy: Two currencies quoted against each other — the price says how much of the quote currency buys one unit of the base.
detail: EUR/USD at 1.0850 means one euro buys 1.0850 US dollars. The base currency is first (EUR), the quote currency is second (USD). 'Major pairs' (EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD, NZD/USD) account for most volume. Cross pairs exclude USD (EUR/JPY, GBP/CHF). Exotic pairs include emerging-market currencies (USD/TRY, USD/ZAR).
plain: Two currencies quoted against each other — the price tells you how many of the second you'd need to buy one of the first.

snappy: Pricing deviation from covered interest parity in FX swap markets — reflects funding stress.
detail: Persistent negative cross-currency basis for USD funding since 2008 (despite CIP arbitrage incentives). EUR-USD basis hit -100 bps in March 2020 stress. Reflects post-crisis bank balance-sheet constraints and limits to arbitrage. Watched by macro traders as a stress indicator. The 'basis' here is the cross-currency basis spread, distinct from the basis-point unit.
plain: A small pricing gap in foreign-exchange swap markets that shouldn't exist in theory — when it widens, it usually signals bank funding stress.

snappy: Fixed exchange rate against another currency, maintained by central-bank intervention.
detail: Hong Kong dollar pegged to USD (since 1983), Saudi riyal pegged to USD, Danish krone pegged to EUR. The central bank stands ready to buy or sell its currency at the peg rate, using FX reserves to defend it. Pegs collapse when reserves run out or when the peg becomes economically untenable — Argentina abandoned its USD peg in 2002, the Swiss removed the EUR cap in 2015.
plain: A fixed exchange rate one country chooses to keep against another's — defended by the central bank using its foreign reserves.

snappy: Net international trade in goods, services, income, and transfers — broad measure of external balance.
detail: Surplus: country saves more than invests, accumulates foreign assets. Deficit: country invests more than saves, accumulates foreign liabilities. US has run persistent current-account deficit since 1990 (around 3-4 percent of GDP). China, Germany, Japan have run surpluses. Persistent imbalances build up to financial-system pressure and currency adjustment. The 2008-09 crisis partly reflected unsustainable US-China imbalance unwinding.
plain: A country's net earnings from selling goods and services abroad, minus what it buys in — a broad measure of trade balance.

snappy: Annual coupon income divided by current bond price — simple yield.
detail: A 5 percent coupon bond trading at 95 has current yield of 5.26 percent (5 over 95). Misses two things YTM captures: the gain or loss to maturity, and the time value of intermediate coupons. Useful as a quick income check for the buy-and-hold investor but not a true total-return measure. Most quoted in retail brokerage screens; institutional desks use YTM.
plain: A bond's annual coupon divided by its current market price — a rough income score that ignores any gain or loss at maturity.

snappy: Bank that holds securities on behalf of investors — separate from trading and clearing.
detail: Major custodians: State Street, BNY Mellon, Citi, JPMorgan, Northern Trust, BNP Paribas, HSBC. Combined trillions in assets under custody. Service includes: safekeeping, trade settlement, corporate-action processing, income collection, securities lending, fund administration. The 1995 Barings Bank collapse partly stemmed from inadequate custody segregation. Post-Madoff (2008), regulators tightened custodian-investor segregation rules.
plain: A bank that keeps stocks and bonds safe on behalf of investors and handles the paperwork when they're bought, sold, or pay dividends.

snappy: Adjustment to derivative fair value reflecting counterparty default risk.
detail: Banks deduct CVA from gross derivative values — what you'd get if no counterparty default minus what you actually expect. CVA reflects expected loss = PD x LGD x exposure. Largest dealers have dedicated CVA desks managing aggregate counterparty exposure with CDS, equity, and FX hedges. CVA gain/loss volatility was a major P&L source 2008-2015. Basel III specifically charges capital against CVA volatility.
plain: An accounting deduction that reduces a derivative's value to reflect the chance the other side might default before paying.

snappy: Bank important to its home country's financial system but not at global G-SIB level.
detail: Domestic regulators designate D-SIBs. US D-SIB regime gives Category II-IV banks specific capital surcharges and stress-test treatment. EU D-SIB framework similar. Smaller banks below the D-SIB threshold get lighter regulation. The threshold matters: when SVB grew above the Category IV threshold in 2021, additional supervisory expectations would have applied — its 2023 failure prompted EGRRCPA-rollback critiques.
plain: A bank important enough that its failure would shake its own country's economy — but not big enough to threaten the world.

snappy: Trading venue where orders are not publicly displayed — large blocks cross without market impact.
detail: Operated by banks (Credit Suisse Crossfinder, Morgan Stanley MS Pool), exchanges (NYSE Block, Nasdaq), and independent operators (Liquidnet, Investment Technology Group). Dark pools represent roughly 12-15 percent of US equity volume. Trade prints to consolidated tape with a delay; quotes don't show on order books. Critics argue dark pools fragment price discovery; supporters cite reduced market impact for institutional orders.
plain: A private trading venue where big institutions can buy and sell large blocks of stock without showing their hand to the public market.

snappy: 40 largest German-listed stocks — German equity benchmark.
detail: Total-return index by default (dividends reinvested) — unusual among major indexes. Expanded from 30 to 40 constituents in 2021 to broaden representation. SAP, Siemens, Mercedes, Volkswagen, Allianz are major weights. Auto, chemicals, industrials heavy. Operated by Deutsche Börse. The 2020 inclusion of Wirecard, just before its fraud collapse, embarrassed Deutsche Börse and triggered methodology reforms.
plain: Germany's main stock index — 40 large companies including SAP, Siemens, Mercedes, and Allianz.
Valuing a company by adding up all the cash it's expected to generate in future years — shrunk to today's value.
snappy: Valuation method computing present value of projected future cash flows.
detail: Foundational valuation technique. Forecast free cash flows for an explicit period (typically 5-10 years), add a terminal value beyond that, discount everything back to today using the weighted average cost of capital. Sensitive to assumptions about growth, margins, and the discount rate — small input changes swing valuations by tens of percent. Equity research analysts publish DCF models to justify price targets. You'll hear 'DCF' cited in any equity research note or M&A valuation discussion.

snappy: Failure to make a contractual debt payment when due.
detail: Triggers acceleration clauses (full principal owed immediately) and cross-default provisions on the issuer's other debt. ISDA determines whether a credit event has occurred for CDS purposes. Three forms: missed payment, bankruptcy filing, distressed exchange (forced restructuring offered at discount). Sovereign defaults: Russia 1998, Argentina 2001, Greece 2012 (debt exchange), Sri Lanka 2022. Corporate default rates spike in recessions.
plain: A borrower's failure to pay back what they owe on time — triggers penalties, lawsuits, and sometimes bankruptcy.

snappy: Pool of clearing-member contributions standing behind a CCP's defaulter losses.
detail: Sized to cover losses from the simultaneous default of the two largest clearing members under extreme stress. Funded by clearing members proportional to their cleared volume and risk. The 'mutualisation' layer of the default waterfall — losses spread across surviving members after defaulter's initial margin is exhausted. Major CCPs hold default funds in the low single-digit billions.
plain: A safety pool that all the members of a clearing house pay into — used to cover losses if one member goes bust.

snappy: Order in which a CCP applies financial resources to cover a defaulting member's losses.
detail: Standard sequence: defaulting member's initial margin → defaulting member's default fund contribution → CCP's own 'skin in the game' → surviving members' default fund contributions → assessment rights (force surviving members to top up). Designed so non-defaulting members aren't immediately on the hook. Real-world tests rare and limited — Lehman's bankruptcy was successfully resolved within the LCH waterfall.
plain: The set order in which a clearing house drains its safety pools to cover a defaulted member's losses — defaulter's money first, everyone else's last.

snappy: Sustained decline in the general price level — opposite of inflation.
detail: Japan experienced mild deflation/zero inflation through most of 1995-2024. The 1930s Great Depression saw severe deflation in advanced economies. Dangerous because it raises real debt burdens, encourages spending delays, and pushes economies into self-reinforcing slumps. Central banks fear deflation more than mild inflation. The 2008-09 brief deflationary scare drove the Fed to QE; pandemic-era stimulus aimed in part at preventing renewed deflation.
plain: When prices fall over time instead of rising — sounds nice, but it can paralyse an economy if people delay every purchase.

snappy: How much an option's price moves for a one-point move in the underlying.
detail: A call's delta runs from 0 (deep out-of-the-money) to 1 (deep in-the-money); puts run 0 to -1. At-the-money options sit near plus or minus 0.5. Traders use delta to hedge: short a 0.5-delta call and buy fifty shares of the underlying to neutralise directional risk. Delta-hedging keeps shifting as the underlying moves — the gamma problem — generating the buy-high-sell-low flows that bleed long-volatility books.
plain: How much an option's price changes when the Underlying moves by one dollar — the rough hedge ratio for traders.

snappy: Financial instrument whose value derives from an underlying asset, rate, or index.
detail: Categories: futures (exchange-traded), forwards (OTC), options (call/put), swaps (rate, currency, credit). Notional outstanding globally: roughly 600 trillion dollars. Used for hedging, speculation, and synthetic exposure. Post-2008 Dodd-Frank reforms forced standardised derivatives onto central clearing. The 2008 crisis was partly an opaque-derivatives crisis (mortgage CDOs, AIG's CDS book).
plain: A contract whose value depends on something else — a stock, a currency, an interest rate, a commodity, almost anything.

snappy: NYSE-listed firm formally responsible for facilitating trading in specific stocks.
detail: Replaced the legacy NYSE specialist role in 2008. DMMs provide opening and closing auction prices, supply liquidity during stress, and step in when buy-sell imbalances arise. Major DMMs: GTS, Citadel Securities, Virtu, IMC. Earn rebates and modest privileged access in exchange for liquidity obligations. The Nasdaq equivalent is the Market Maker firm assigned to each Nasdaq stock.
plain: A firm on the New York stock Exchange responsible for keeping trading orderly in specific stocks — opening prices, closing prices, providing liquidity in panics.

snappy: Statutory stress-test framework — overlaps with CCAR.
detail: Required by Dodd-Frank Section 165. Run annually by Fed for largest banks. Tests bank capital adequacy under macroeconomic stress scenarios. Mid-sized banks tested every two years post-EGRRCPA. Public disclosure of results. Effectively merged with CCAR since 2020. Stress scenarios include severely adverse, adverse, and baseline economic projections.
plain: A US bank stress test required by law — checks whether the biggest banks could survive a severe recession.

snappy: Middle distillate fuel — used for trucks, trains, ships, and as heating oil.
detail: Global benchmarks: ICE Gas Oil (European), NYMEX ULSD (US). Diesel demand correlates with industrial activity — manufacturing, freight, agriculture. Diesel crack spreads (vs Brent) hit record highs in 2022 amid sanctions on Russian product exports and refining capacity tightness. Marine fuel transitioned post-2020 to IMO-2020 low-sulphur specs, restructuring global diesel/HSFO markets.
plain: A fuel made from crude oil that powers trucks, trains, ships, and farm machinery — its price tracks industrial activity closely.

snappy: Option that pays a fixed amount if the underlying finishes above (or below) the strike — zero otherwise.
detail: All-or-nothing payoff. A digital call on AAPL with 200 strike pays 1 dollar if AAPL ends above 200, zero otherwise. Cheap to buy, easy to understand, popular in structured products. The retail 'binary option' craze (2010s) saw widespread fraud — regulators (FCA, ASIC) banned retail binaries. Institutional digital options remain legitimate but cleared through OTC channels with regulated counterparties.
plain: An option that pays a fixed amount if the Underlying ends above (or below) the Strike Price — and nothing otherwise. All-or-nothing.
When a company issues new shares, every existing holder owns a slightly smaller slice — like adding water to a glass of juice.
snappy: Reduction in existing shareholders' ownership stake when a company issues new shares.
detail: Triggers: secondary equity offerings, employee stock options vesting, warrant exercises, conversions of convertible bonds. Companies report 'fully diluted' share counts in earnings to show worst-case dilution. Heavy dilution typically weighs on share prices. Buybacks act as the opposite — reducing share count, concentrating ownership. Investors watch dilution metrics like share-count growth in earnings reports.

snappy: Company lists existing shares on an exchange without raising new capital.
detail: No underwriters, no new share issuance, no traditional roadshow. Existing shareholders simply sell into the public market starting day one. Spotify (2018), Slack (2019), Coinbase (2021), Roblox (2021) used direct listings. Recently extended to allow new share issuance simultaneously. Saves underwriter fees but provides less price stability than traditional IPOs.
plain: A way for a company to list its existing stocks on a public exchange without raising new money or using underwriters.

snappy: Bond trading below par — usually because its coupon lags current market rates.
detail: A 2 percent coupon bond in a 4 percent yield environment trades at a discount: the skimpy coupon makes the bond less valuable than face value. Holders pay less upfront and recoup the gap when face value is repaid at maturity. Original-issue discount (OID) bonds are issued below par on purpose. T-bills are pure discount instruments — no coupon, just gap to face.
plain: A bond trading for less than the amount the issuer will repay at maturity — usually because its coupon is below current market rates.
The interest rate used to translate future cash payments into today's value — higher discount rates make future cash worth less now.
snappy: Rate used to convert future cash flows into present value.
detail: Central in DCF valuation, bond pricing, and option pricing. Different uses: risk-free rate plus risk premium for equity valuation, swap curve for derivative pricing, Treasury yields for bond discounting. The Fed's 'discount rate' is also the specific rate at which the Fed lends to banks via the discount window — separate from the broader concept. Lower discount rates inflate present values (the long-duration tech rally of the 2010s rested partly on falling discount rates).

snappy: Fed's traditional lending facility for banks needing emergency short-term funding.
detail: Three tiers: primary credit (healthy banks), secondary credit (weaker banks), seasonal credit (small banks with cyclical needs). Borrowing carries stigma — banks fear signalling weakness to counterparties — so usage is usually minimal except in crises. The March 2023 Bank Term Funding Program added a Discount Window-adjacent emergency facility after SVB. Primary credit rate is typically set 25 bp above IORB.
plain: The US central bank's emergency cash counter for banks that suddenly need short-term funding — but using it can look like a sign of weakness.

snappy: Decline in the rate of inflation — inflation still positive but slowing.
detail: Distinct from deflation (negative inflation). The 2022-2024 process where US CPI dropped from 9 percent to 3 percent was disinflation. Soft-landing disinflation (without recession) is the policy goal — historically rare but achieved 2022-2024 in the US. Sticky-price components (services, shelter) typically lag goods disinflation, so the last mile to 2 percent is hardest.
plain: When prices are still rising, but more slowly than before — the goal central banks pursue without tipping the economy into recession.

snappy: Sell index volatility, buy single-stock volatility — profits if correlation falls.
detail: Decomposes index vol into single-stock vol times correlation. When correlation drops (stocks move idiosyncratically), realised index vol falls below the weighted average of single-stock vols, profiting the dispersion seller. Reverses when correlation spikes (typical of crashes). Hedge funds run systematic dispersion books. Sized in vega terms across the components.
plain: A bet that individual stocks will move in different directions even if the overall index stays calm — profits when correlation drops.

snappy: Spreading investments across uncorrelated assets to reduce portfolio risk.
detail: Modern portfolio theory (Markowitz 1952): optimal portfolios maximise return per unit of risk via diversification. International stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities offer different return drivers. Correlation matters — assets that move together don't diversify each other. Stress periods often see correlations rise toward 1 — 'diversification disappearing when you need it most'. The classic 60/40 portfolio (60 percent stocks, 40 percent bonds) is the canonical diversified portfolio.
plain: Spreading your money across many investments that don't all move together — so a fall in one can be offset by gains in another.

snappy: Cash payment from a corporation to its shareholders — slice of profits returned.
detail: Paid out of retained earnings, typically quarterly in the US (annually in some other markets). Decided by the board; can be cut or eliminated. Companies signal stability via dividend continuity — the 'Dividend Aristocrats' have raised payouts for 25+ consecutive years. Special dividends are one-off larger payouts. Stock dividends pay shares instead of cash. Most US dividends are taxed at preferential long-term capital-gains rates.
plain: A cash payout a company sends its shareholders, usually every three months — a slice of profits returned rather than reinvested.

snappy: Annual dividend as a percentage of share price — equity income measure.
detail: A 50-dollar stock paying a 2-dollar annual dividend has a 4 percent yield. Compared to bond yields as part of equity-versus-fixed-income allocation. Utility stocks and REITs typically have the highest yields (3-6 percent); growth stocks often pay nothing. Yields rise either by dividend increases or by share-price drops — a soaring yield can be a warning sign of falling price rather than improving payouts.
plain: Annual dividend payments divided by the current stock price — how much income you'd earn each year as a percentage of what you paid.

full: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
snappy: 2010 US legislation overhauling financial regulation in response to the 2008 crisis.
detail: Signed July 2010. Established CFPB, Financial Stability Oversight Council, Volcker Rule restrictions on bank prop trading, Title VII mandatory clearing for standardised OTC derivatives, swap-dealer registration, position limits, and SEF trading mandates. Repealed parts of Glass-Steagall hadn't already been gone. Partial rollback under the 2018 Trump administration EGRRCPA Act loosened rules for smaller banks.
plain: A sweeping US law passed in 2010 to fix problems the 2008 crash exposed — tougher bank rules, new agencies, more transparent derivatives.

snappy: Economy adopts a foreign currency (usually USD) for domestic transactions.
detail: Ecuador (since 2000), El Salvador (2001), Panama, Zimbabwe (2009-2019). Full dollarisation eliminates monetary sovereignty: no central bank policy rate, no exchange rate. 'Partial dollarisation' is common in high-inflation economies — domestic deposits and contracts denominated in USD alongside the local currency. Reverses only with major political will (Zimbabwe relaunched ZWL in 2019).
plain: When a country gives up its own currency and uses the US dollar (or another foreign one) for everyday transactions instead.

snappy: Chart of individual FOMC members' rate projections — released quarterly with the SEP.
detail: Each member places a dot at their projected fed funds target rate at year-end for the current year, next two years, and longer run. Markets infer the FOMC's collective median view from the dot distribution. The longer-run dot is the median estimate of r-star (neutral rate). Famous market-moving dot shifts: December 2018 (rate-cut signals), September 2021 (hike-bringing-forward signals), September 2024 (steeper rate-cut path).
plain: A chart of where each US central-bank policymaker individually expects interest rates to be in a year, two years, and the long run.

snappy: 30 large US companies, price-weighted — the oldest US stock index.
detail: Launched 1896 by Charles Dow. Price-weighted (not market-cap-weighted) — a 1-dollar move in any stock contributes equally to the index. UnitedHealth, Goldman, Microsoft, Apple are heavy weights despite different market caps. Less representative than S&P 500 but more recognised by retail and media. Crossed 40,000 in 2024. Tracked by SPDR DIA ETF.
plain: An iconic US stock index of 30 major companies — launched in 1896 and quoted on every newscast, though smaller than the S&P 500.
A Barrier option that only activates if the Underlying price falls and hits the chosen barrier level.
snappy: Knock-in barrier option that activates only if the underlying falls through the barrier level.
detail: Mirror of up-and-in. Pays nothing unless the underlying drops far enough to hit the lower barrier. A directional bet on a downward move large enough to clear the barrier. Used in puts to cheapen the premium. Popular in credit-linked notes and protective structures where the buyer wants to pay less for cover that only kicks in during a real selloff.

plain: A Barrier option that automatically expires worthless if the Underlying price falls and hits the chosen barrier level.
snappy: Knock-out barrier option that extinguishes if the underlying falls through the barrier level.
detail: Cheaper than a vanilla option because it stops working in scenarios the holder doesn't care about — or where the seller doesn't want to pay. Used in protective hedges where cover is only needed above a certain level. Pricing handles the discontinuity at the barrier. Popular in FX (a long EUR-call with a knock-out below spot) and equity structured products.

snappy: Peak-to-trough decline in portfolio value during a specific period.
detail: Measured from each high-water mark forward. A portfolio at 100 drops to 80 then recovers — 20 percent drawdown. Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall over the entire history. Used as a risk measure alongside volatility — drawdown captures investor experience better than annualised volatility. Behavioural impact: investors panic on big drawdowns regardless of long-term return.
plain: How far a portfolio has fallen from its highest point — the most painful measure of risk for the person holding it.

snappy: Company-sponsored plan letting shareholders reinvest dividends into additional shares automatically.
detail: Often offered without commissions and sometimes at modest discounts to market price. Major dividend payers (Coca-Cola, J&J, Procter & Gamble) operate DRIPs that have built long-term wealth for patient shareholders. Tax treatment: dividends still taxable when received, even if reinvested. Useful for compounding long-term but creates tax-lot tracking complexity. Most modern brokers offer broker-administered reinvestment with similar economics.
plain: A scheme that automatically uses your Dividend payouts to buy more stocks in the same company — small amounts that compound over time.

snappy: US CSD subsidiary of DTCC — holds and settles US equities and corporate bonds.
detail: Founded 1973. Holds nearly all US-listed securities in book-entry form (95-plus percent). Daily settlement value approximately 5 trillion dollars across DTC, NSCC, and FICC subsidiaries. Survived 2008 stress with minimal disruption. Currently transitioning systems to support T+1 settlement and explore T+0 capabilities.
plain: The main US institution that holds stocks and bonds in electronic form and settles trades between investors and brokers.

snappy: Federal Reserve's legal mandate — maximum employment plus stable prices.
detail: Established by 1977 Federal Reserve Reform Act. Most other major central banks (ECB, Bank of England) have price stability as primary mandate; employment is secondary. The dual mandate occasionally creates tension — high inflation with low unemployment (2022) requires policy choices weighing both objectives. Fed Chairs publicly emphasise both in press conferences and Congressional testimony.
plain: The US central bank's twin job by law — keep prices stable and keep unemployment low. Sometimes those goals pull in opposite directions.

snappy: Share structure with multiple voting classes — typically founders retain control via supervoting shares.
detail: Google's GOOG (Class C, no votes) versus GOOGL (Class A, 1 vote) versus founder-held Class B (10 votes each). Meta, Snap, Pinterest, and many tech IPOs use similar structures. Critics argue it entrenches founders and weakens governance; supporters say it lets founders make long-term decisions free from quarterly pressure. S&P 500 has accepted dual-class since 2017; FTSE rules tightened then relaxed.
plain: A setup where founders hold a special class of stock with extra voting power, letting them keep control of the company they built.

snappy: How much a bond's price moves for a one-percent rate shift, expressed in years.
detail: Macaulay duration is the weighted-average time to cash flows. Modified duration is what traders quote — a seven-year-duration bond loses roughly seven percent if yields rise one percent. Effective duration handles callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities. Portfolio managers target duration to express macro views; index funds match the benchmark duration to track. Long-duration assets got hammered in 2022 as the Fed hiked 525 basis points.
plain: How sensitive a bond's price is to a change in interest rates — measured in years. Longer duration means bigger price swings.

snappy: Dollar P&L hit from a one-basis-point yield move — the rates trader's primary risk metric.
detail: Calculated from duration times price times 0.0001. A position with a hundred-thousand-dollar DV01 makes or loses that amount per basis point. Quoted in millions for big books. Used to size trades to risk limits, to compare positions across instruments, and to hedge: matching DV01s between cash bonds and swaps neutralises first-order rate risk. The 'PV01' variant is essentially the same number from the present-value direction.
plain: How many dollars a bond position gains or loses if interest rates move by one basis point — the rates trader's main risk gauge.

snappy: Adjustment for the bank's own default risk — gains if own credit deteriorates.
detail: Counterintuitive: if a bank's own CDS spread widens, its derivative liabilities are worth less in fair-value terms, producing accounting gains. Headed banks book DVA gains/losses in income statement under fair-value accounting. The 2011 European sovereign crisis saw major banks book multi-billion DVA gains on their own widening credit spreads — controversially. Excluded from regulatory capital calculations.
plain: An accounting quirk where a bank's own derivative liabilities look smaller as its credit gets worse — making bad news look like profit.

snappy: Settlement mechanism where securities and cash change hands simultaneously.
detail: Eliminates principal risk: neither party can deliver without receiving. Standard for most securities settlement worldwide via CSDs. Three DvP models (BIS classification): Model 1 (gross trade-by-trade simultaneous), Model 2 (gross securities, net cash), Model 3 (net both). Most modern systems (DTC, Euroclear, Clearstream) use Model 2 or 3 for efficiency.
plain: A settlement design where shares and cash change hands at exactly the same instant — so neither side risks paying and getting nothing.

snappy: ICE-published trade-weighted index of the US dollar against six major currencies.
detail: Weights: EUR 57.6 percent, JPY 13.6, GBP 11.9, CAD 9.1, SEK 4.2, CHF 3.6 (fixed since 1973). Quoted to two decimals — DXY at 105 means the dollar is 5 percent stronger than the 1973 baseline. Used as a quick read on dollar strength; included in many macro models. Tracks broad dollar direction but is heavy on European exposures and excludes major partners like CNY, KRW, INR.
plain: A score of the US dollar's strength against six major currencies — a popular shorthand for how strong or weak the dollar is.

snappy: Expected outstanding exposure at the moment of default.
detail: For amortising loans, EAD is straightforward — it's the remaining balance. For revolving credit facilities, EAD models the expected drawdown at default time (typically higher than current outstandings as defaulting companies often draw down before bankruptcy). For derivatives, EAD accounts for potential future exposure. Used in Basel regulatory capital calculations with PD and LGD.
plain: An estimate of how much a borrower will actually owe at the moment they default — used to calculate banks' safety capital.

full: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, Amortisation
snappy: Operating earnings before non-cash and financing charges — proxy for cash generation.
detail: Strips out capital-structure choices (interest), tax differences, and accounting policies (depreciation) to give a cleaner read on operating performance. Heavily used in M&A and leveraged finance (debt covenants are usually written against EBITDA). Critics describe it as 'earnings before bad stuff' — it can flatter unprofitable companies. Adjusted EBITDA further excludes 'one-offs', which can become permanent in some serial reporters' hands.
plain: A company's profits before deducting interest, taxes, and accounting wear-and-tear charges — a rough proxy for cash generation.
The central bank for countries using the euro — sets eurozone interest rates and supervises the biggest European Banks.
snappy: Central bank for the 20-country eurozone — sets policy rates, oversees major banks.
detail: Founded 1998, based in Frankfurt. Governing Council (six executive board members plus 20 national central bank governors) sets monetary policy. Mandate: price stability defined as 2 percent inflation. Negative deposit rate from 2014 to 2022. Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) directly supervises 100+ significant eurozone banks. Bond-buying programs (APP, PEPP) ran through 2022; balance sheet now in steady runoff.

snappy: Electronic system matching buy and sell orders from multiple participants.
detail: Pioneered by Instinet in the 1970s; Island, Archipelago, BATS dominated the 2000s. Reg ATS regulates ECNs as Alternative Trading Systems. ECN inventors (Joshua Levine, William Lupien) reshaped US equity markets by undercutting exchange-floor middlemen. Many original ECNs merged into today's exchanges: Archipelago became NYSE Arca, BATS became Cboe BZX. Distinct from dark pools by displaying quotes.
plain: An electronic system that lets multiple investors place orders to buy or sell, then automatically matches them up — pioneered modern fast trading.

snappy: Daily volume-weighted median rate at which banks lend reserves to each other overnight.
detail: Published daily by the New York Fed using transaction-level data from brokered fed funds trades. Stays inside the FOMC's target range thanks to IORB (ceiling) and ON RRP (floor). EFFR is what fed funds futures settle to. With reserves abundant, the interbank fed funds market is much smaller than pre-2008 — most volume is GSE lending to banks rather than bank-to-bank.
plain: The average overnight interest rate US banks actually charge each other — the score the US central bank tries to control.

full: Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act
plain: A 2018 US law that loosened some of the post-2008 banking rules — particularly for mid-sized banks below the largest tier.
snappy: 2018 US law rolling back parts of Dodd-Frank for mid-sized banks.
detail: Signed by Trump in May 2018. Raised the systemic-bank threshold from 50 billion in assets to 250 billion, exempting many regional banks from the toughest stress tests and capital rules. Critics blame the rollback for contributing to the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failure — SVB had grown above the old threshold but stayed below the new one. You'll hear EGRRCPA cited in any debate about regulating banks the size of SVB or Signature.

snappy: US weekly snapshot of crude oil, gasoline, and distillate stocks — moves oil prices.
detail: Published Wednesdays at 10:30 AM Eastern by the Energy Information Administration. Surprise builds or draws move WTI 1-3 dollars per barrel on release. Includes inventories, production, imports, exports, and refinery utilisation. The American Petroleum Institute (API) publishes a competing report Tuesday evenings, watched as a preview. Distilled into weekly traders' notes globally.
plain: A weekly US government release showing how much crude oil and petrol is sitting in tanks — oil prices jump on surprises.

snappy: Wholesale market where electricity is bought and sold — settles in real time across grids.
detail: Major hubs: PJM, ERCOT (Texas), CAISO (California), MISO (Midwest), Nord Pool (Europe). Day-ahead markets fix prices for the next 24 hours; real-time balancing markets clear last-minute imbalances. Texas ERCOT February 2021 winter storm produced 9,000-dollar-per-MWh prices for days; Australia's 2022 NEM crisis saw similar extremes. Renewable penetration drives more negative-price episodes.
plain: The wholesale market where power is bought and sold for delivery into the grid — prices can swing wildly between calm and crisis days.

snappy: Mid-income, mid-development economies — distinct from advanced (DM) and frontier markets.
detail: MSCI's EM index defines the universe for most allocators: China, India, Brazil, Mexico, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Korea, Taiwan, and others. Approximately 24 countries, 1,400 stocks. EM equity, bond, and currency markets carry higher beta to global risk sentiment than DM. The 'EM' label is increasingly contested for large economies like China and Korea, but MSCI's classification drives indexed flows so it sticks.
plain: Mid-income, fast-developing countries like Brazil, India, Mexico, and South Africa — their stocks and bonds tend to swing more than rich-country ones.

snappy: EU's post-2008 derivatives regulation — mandates clearing, reporting, and risk mitigation.
detail: Enacted 2012, in force 2013. Counterpart to Dodd-Frank Title VII in the US. Three core mandates: clearing eligible OTC derivatives at authorised CCPs, reporting all derivative trades to trade repositories, and risk mitigation requirements (collateral, dispute resolution) for non-cleared derivatives. EMIR REFIT (2019) simplified reporting; EMIR 3.0 (2024) increased EU CCP requirements.
plain: The European Union's rulebook for derivatives trading after the 2008 crash — forces standard contracts to be cleared and all of them to be reported.
The old daily benchmark for overnight euro lending between banks — replaced by ESTR in 2019.
snappy: Defunct overnight euro benchmark — succeeded by ESTR in 2019.
detail: Published from 1999 to January 2022 by the European Money Markets Institute. Calculated from real interbank lending transactions reported by a panel of large euro-area banks. The 2017 benchmark scandal pushed EU authorities to replace EONIA with the ECB-administered ESTR, which is built from a broader transaction base. Trillions of euro derivative contracts were transitioned during the cutover. You'll hear EONIA mentioned in legacy bond covenants and pre-2022 swap documentation.

snappy: Net income divided by shares outstanding — corporate profitability per share.
detail: Most-watched single number on earnings releases. Companies report basic EPS (using outstanding shares) and diluted EPS (including potential shares from options and convertibles). Adjusted EPS excludes one-offs like restructuring charges; GAAP EPS includes everything. Stock prices move sharply when reported EPS beats or misses consensus estimates. Buybacks mechanically increase EPS by shrinking the denominator.
plain: A company's profit divided by its total stocks — the most-watched number on every quarterly earnings release.

snappy: Ownership stake in a company — residual claim after debts are paid.
detail: Equity-holders get whatever's left after creditors are made whole — the residual claim. In exchange they get voting rights (usually) and unlimited upside if the business grows. Public equity trades on stock exchanges as shares; private equity is owned by founders, employees, and investment firms. Global public equity market cap is roughly 110 trillion dollars (2024).
plain: Ownership in a company. One share is one tiny slice — millions of shares add up to the whole company's value.

snappy: Futures contract on an equity index — most liquid equity derivative.
detail: CME's E-mini S&P 500 futures (/ES) are the most-traded equity contract in the world — over a trillion dollars notional daily during active sessions. NDX, Russell 2000, Dow, MSCI futures also active. Used for index hedging, portfolio rebalancing, futures-vs-cash arbitrage, and synthetic equity exposure. Quarterly expirations (March, June, September, December). Settle to a special opening rotation price.
plain: A Futures contract on a basket of stocks like the S&P 500 — the deepest way to bet on the overall market.

snappy: Contract to buy or sell shares at a set price by a set date.
detail: Listed on options exchanges (CBOE, ISE, BOX in the US) in standard contracts of 100 shares. Vanilla flavours: American-style (exercisable any time) for single stocks, European-style (only at expiry) for most index options. Used to hedge, speculate, or generate income (covered calls). US-listed retail options volume hit record levels in 2021-22; institutional flow dominates index options.
plain: A contract giving you the right to buy or sell a single company's stocks at a fixed price — usually 100 shares apiece.

snappy: Extra return investors demand for holding equities over risk-free bonds.
detail: Historically 4-6 percent over long horizons for US equities versus Treasury securities. Drives equity valuation: discount rate equals risk-free rate plus ERP times beta (CAPM). Implied ERP can be back-solved from current market valuations; surveyed ERP comes from investor polls. The Fed Model compared equity earnings yield to bond yield as a relative-value gauge. ERP varies with risk appetite — collapses in bubbles, widens in crises.
plain: The extra return investors demand for taking the risk of owning stocks instead of safe government bonds — historically about four to six percent.

snappy: Total return on an equity for periodic cash payments — usually LIBOR-replacement-plus-spread.
detail: Used by hedge funds for leveraged equity exposure (prime brokerage), by corporates for share buybacks structured as accelerated programs, by funds for tax or regulatory arbitrage. The 2021 Archegos collapse was effectively a margin call on equity total-return swaps gone catastrophically wrong — Credit Suisse and others lost over 10 billion combined. ISDA-documented OTC contracts.
plain: A contract that pays you the total return of a stock in exchange for regular cash payments — gives exposure without buying shares.

snappy: Lowest-priority slice of a structured product — absorbs first losses, gets residual cash flow.
detail: Unrated, highest yield. In a CLO, the equity tranche is typically 8-12 percent of the deal and pays cash flow after all senior tranches are serviced. Equity-tranche IRRs of 15-25 percent in normal markets, deeply negative in stress. Held by hedge funds, family offices, CLO managers themselves (alignment), and structured-credit funds. Often retained by issuer in regulatory 'skin in the game' contexts.
plain: The riskiest slice of a structured product — takes the first losses, but gets paid most generously if everything goes well.

snappy: ECB-published overnight unsecured euro borrowing rate — euro-area equivalent of SOFR (but unsecured).
detail: Calculated from actual transactions reported by 50-plus large euro-area banks. Replaced EONIA in October 2019 as the recommended euro overnight benchmark. ESTR is unsecured (interbank borrowing), unlike SOFR which is collateralised by Treasury securities. Underlies euro OIS swaps and after LIBOR was retired euro derivatives. ECB publishes ESTR daily by 9:00 CET.
plain: An overnight benchmark interest rate for euro borrowing — built from real bank transactions and used to price euro derivatives after LIBOR was retired.

snappy: Standardised derivatives traded on regulated exchanges with central clearing.
detail: Includes futures (CME, ICE, Eurex), listed options (CBOE, ISE), and exchange-traded swaps. Standardised contracts, daily margining, central clearing reduce counterparty risk. Distinct from OTC derivatives (bilateral, customised). The shift from OTC to ETD has been a regulatory priority post-2008 — Dodd-Frank pushed many cleared OTC trades into futures-like cleared structures, blurring lines.
plain: A Derivative bought and sold on a regulated exchange with daily margining — safer and more standardised than private OTC deals.

snappy: Investment fund traded on an exchange like a stock.
detail: Tracks an index, sector, theme, or actively managed strategy. Major issuers: BlackRock ishares, Vanguard, State Street SPDR, Invesco. Tax-efficient structure via in-kind creation/redemption avoids capital-gains distributions. Global ETF AUM exceeds 12 trillion dollars (2024). The 2024 launch of US spot Bitcoin ETFs (IBIT, FBTC, others) attracted tens of billions in months.
plain: An investment fund traded on a stock exchange like a single share — usually tracks an index, sector, or theme cheaply and tax-efficiently.

snappy: World's largest cap-and-trade scheme — covers EU power, industry, aviation.
detail: Launched 2005. Companies must surrender allowances (EUAs) matching their CO2 emissions; shortfalls require buying allowances. The cap shrinks annually toward 2030/2050 targets. EUA prices: roughly 5 euros per tonne in 2017, 80-90 in 2024, briefly above 100 in early 2023. Industries on the system: power, steel, cement, aluminium, refining, aviation (intra-EU). Phase 4 runs 2021-2030.
plain: Europe's giant carbon market — power plants and heavy industry must buy permits to release CO2, and the supply shrinks each year.

snappy: Frankfurt-based derivatives exchange — Europe's largest for interest-rate and equity-index futures and options.
detail: Owned by Deutsche Börse. Flagship contracts: Bund and Bobl futures, Euro Stoxx 50 options, single-stock options on European blue chips. The sole exchange for Euro-denominated long-rate futures benchmarks. Clears through its own CCP (Eurex Clearing). Pre-Brexit, competed directly with London-based LIFFE; now central to ESMA's push for euro-denominated clearing to migrate to the eurozone.
plain: Frankfurt's main derivatives exchange — the biggest European venue for trading futures and options.

snappy: Daily benchmark for euro interbank lending — still in use after LIBOR was retired reform.
detail: Published by the European Money Markets Institute (EMMI) using a hybrid methodology (transactions where possible, market-based estimates where not). Tenors from 1 week to 12 months. Underlies trillions in euro-denominated mortgages, swaps, and corporate loans. Survived the LIBOR reforms by overhauling methodology in 2019. ESTR (Euro Short-Term Rate) is the overnight risk-free complement.
plain: A daily benchmark interest rate for euro lending — used as the reference for trillions in euro mortgages, loans, and Derivatives.

snappy: Largest international CSD — clears trillions in bonds and equities, mostly EU-related.
detail: Based in Brussels. Settles roughly 1 quadrillion euros in transactions annually. Holds custody of nearly 40 trillion euros in securities. Russian sanctions in 2022 immobilised approximately 200 billion euros of Russian central bank assets at Euroclear — politically and legally complex. Sister institution Euroclear Bank handles cross-border eurobond settlement.
plain: A Belgian institution that holds bonds and shares safely for international investors — Europe's biggest record-keeper of who owns what.

snappy: CME-listed futures on three-month USD LIBOR — discontinued after 2023 LIBOR cessation.
detail: Once the most liquid interest-rate futures contract in the world — trillions of notional weekly. Replaced by SOFR futures after the formal LIBOR cessation in June 2023. Last Eurodollar futures contracts expired in 2023. The name comes from dollar-denominated deposits held offshore (originally in London) — historically the underlying for LIBOR.
plain: Contracts that once let traders bet on future US interbank lending rates — replaced by SOFR-based versions after a benchmark scandal.

snappy: Option exercisable only at expiration — no early exercise.
detail: Standard for index options (SPX, RUT, etc.) and most OTC FX options. Simpler to value than American options — Black-Scholes assumes European exercise. Avoids the assignment risk that complicates American option positions. Most exotic options (barriers, digitals, Asians) are European-style. The 'European' label is convention, not geographic.
plain: An option you can only use on its expiry date — no early exercise. Standard for most index options.

snappy: 19 EU countries (now 20 with Croatia 2023) using the euro as common currency.
detail: Created 1999 with 11 founding members. ECB sets common monetary policy. Common currency but separate fiscal policies — chronic tension during sovereign-debt crisis 2010-12 (Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Spain). 'Single currency, multiple sovereigns' design flaw partially addressed by ESM (2012) and OMT (Mario Draghi's whatever-it-takes). Banking union with Single Supervisory Mechanism (2014) further integrated.
plain: The group of 20 European countries that share the euro as their currency and the European Central Bank's monetary policy.

snappy: Whole-company valuation multiple — captures both equity and debt.
detail: Enterprise value (market cap plus net debt) divided by EBITDA. Standard for comparing companies with different capital structures — a highly levered company's P/E understates its true cost; EV/EBITDA captures the debt. Common in private equity, M&A, and credit analysis. Industry-typical multiples: industrials 8-12x, tech 15-25x, utilities 8-10x. Used in LBO pricing and equity research valuation models.
plain: A whole-company valuation score that compares what a business is worth in total — including its debts — to its annual operating profits.

snappy: Volatility estimator giving more weight to recent observations — common in trading.
detail: Variants: RiskMetrics (JP Morgan 1996) uses lambda = 0.94 for daily data. Simple, fast, transparent. Doesn't capture vol clustering as fully as GARCH but easier to implement and maintain. Used in much of bank risk-system infrastructure. Equivalent to a special case of GARCH model with constrained parameters. The standard pre-GARCH volatility model used by trading desks for decades.
plain: A way of estimating recent volatility by giving fresh data more weight than older data — a fast, simple risk-management staple.

snappy: First day a stock trades without its declared dividend — buyers don't receive the upcoming payout.
detail: Stock price typically drops by the dividend amount on the ex-date as the future right to the dividend disappears. Set by the exchange one business day before the record date under T+1 settlement. Dividend capture strategies attempt to buy just before ex-date, capture the dividend, sell after — usually unprofitable after transaction costs and tax implications.
plain: The first day a stock trades without the right to the next Dividend — buyers from this day onwards miss the upcoming payout.

snappy: Average loss in the worst-case scenarios beyond VaR.
detail: A 95-percent ES is the average loss given you're in the bottom 5 percent. Captures tail risk better than VaR (which is silent about how bad bad gets). Basel III FRTB switched market-risk capital from VaR to ES specifically because of VaR's tail-risk blindness. Heavier tails in actual market returns make ES significantly larger than VaR for the same confidence level.
plain: The average loss in the worst-case scenarios beyond a chosen threshold — captures how bad things really get in a disaster.

snappy: Date an option or futures contract ends — last day to trade or exercise.
detail: Standard monthly options expire third Friday of expiration month. Weeklies expire every Friday; SPX has daily expirations now. Futures expire at varying dates (third Friday for many indexes, mid-month for commodities). 'Triple witching' is the quarterly Friday when index options, index futures, and single-stock options all expire together — produces unusual hedging flows and intraday volatility.
plain: The date on which an option or Futures contract ends — the last day to use it or close out the position.

snappy: Risk that MBS principal returns slower than expected — typically when rates rise.
detail: The flip side of prepayment risk. As rates rise, fewer homeowners refinance (or move), so MBS principal returns are extended. Holders are locked into below-market coupons longer than modelled. Extension risk hammered MBS portfolios in 2022 as rates rose 400 bps in a year. Negative convexity captures both prepayment and extension dynamics — MBS holders lose either way.
plain: The risk that mortgage repayments come back to investors more slowly than expected — typically when interest rates rise.

snappy: Amount the issuer repays at maturity — the bond's principal.
detail: Also called 'par value' or 'principal'. Most corporate and government bonds use a thousand-dollar face value; municipal bonds often five thousand; some sovereign bonds a hundred. Coupon payments are computed as a percentage of face value, not of market price. A bond trading at 95 means 95 percent of face — for a thousand-dollar bond, that's nine hundred and fifty dollars.
plain: The amount a bond's issuer promises to repay at maturity — also the figure used to calculate coupon payments. Usually a thousand dollars per bond.

snappy: Systematic strategy targeting specific risk factors (value, momentum, quality, size, low-vol).
detail: Pioneered by Dimensional (1981) and now mainstream via ishares, Vanguard factor ETFs. Smart Beta is the marketing label. Trillions invested globally. The 2018-2022 'value drawdown' was painful for value-tilted factor funds; the 2024 recovery partially offset. Critics argue factor premiums have shrunk with capital flows; supporters note long-run statistical evidence remains. Multi-factor blends popular over single-factor exposures.
plain: Building a stock portfolio by deliberately tilting toward specific traits that have historically paid off — like value, momentum, or quality.

snappy: Daily charge imposed on a counterparty that fails to settle a trade on time.
detail: Designed to incentivise timely settlement. US Treasury fails charge introduced 2008 — 3 percent annualised on fail amount. CSDR in Europe imposes cash penalties for settlement fails. Repo and securities-lending fails carry market-rate penalties. Aggregate fails data published by Treasury and Fed; spikes in fails signal operational stress or extreme short interest in the affected security.
plain: A daily fine imposed on a trading partner who doesn't deliver stocks or bonds on time — designed to encourage smooth settlement.

snappy: Trade where the seller fails to deliver securities at settlement.
detail: Causes: counterparty default, short-selling without locating shares to borrow, operational error. Triggers buy-in procedures — the buyer can purchase shares in the market and bill the failed seller. SEC Reg SHO governs short-sale fails. Persistent FTDs in a security can flag manipulation or extreme short interest. Reported and tracked by SEC and FINRA.
plain: When a seller doesn't hand over the stocks they sold by the deadline — triggers fines and forced market purchases to fix the problem.

snappy: IG bond downgraded to HY — forced selling by IG-only mandates often follows.
detail: Notable examples: Ford and GM in 2005 (took 25 percent of HY index overnight), Kraft Heinz in 2020, Boeing's near-downgrade scare in 2020-21 (avoided). The mechanical selling creates buying opportunities for HY funds — but the downgrade often precedes further fundamental deterioration. The 'rising stars' index tracks upgrades back to IG. Pandemic-era Fed bond-buying explicitly included fallen angels.
plain: A company bond that gets downgraded from high-grade to junk — often forcing pension funds and insurers to sell, regardless of price.

snappy: Extension adding profitability and investment factors to FF3.
detail: Fama-French (2015) added robust-minus-weak (RMW) profitability factor and conservative-minus-aggressive (CMA) investment factor. Better fit than FF3 in modern data. Profitability and investment factors largely subsume the value factor's explanatory power. Adding momentum (Carhart 1997) and quality factors expands further. Modern factor investing (smart beta) typically uses five to ten factors.
plain: An upgraded version of the three-factor model — adds profitability and investment patterns to explain why some stocks beat the market.

snappy: Asset-pricing model adding size and value factors to CAPM market beta.
detail: Eugene Fama and Kenneth French (1992-93): excess return depends on market beta, size (small minus big), and value (high minus low book-to-market). Better fits historical returns than CAPM. Established that small-cap and value stocks earned premium historical returns. Spawned the 'factor zoo' of subsequent multi-factor models. Fama won 2013 Nobel partly for this work.
plain: A model from the 1990s saying a stock's returns depend on market exposure, company size, and how cheap it looks relative to its books.
US government-sponsored company that buys home loans from banks and packages them into bonds — keeps mortgage credit flowing.
snappy: US government-sponsored enterprise — second-largest buyer of US residential mortgages.
detail: Founded 1938 to support the housing market, privatised in 1968, placed in federal conservatorship in 2008 after near-collapse on subprime losses. Buys mortgages from lenders, packages them into agency MBS with a credit guarantee, and either holds or sells the resulting bonds. Roughly half of all US conforming mortgages flow through Fannie. You'll hear Fannie named alongside Freddie Mac in every housing-policy debate.

snappy: US central bank — sets short-term interest rates and regulates banks.
detail: Created 1913. Twelve regional Federal Reserve banks plus the Board of Governors in Washington. The FOMC (Board plus regional presidents) sets the federal funds rate target eight times a year. Dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices. Lender of last resort via the discount window. Supervises bank holding companies and large insurers. Chair (currently Jerome Powell) testifies twice a year to Congress under Humphrey-Hawkins. The Fed's balance sheet ballooned past 9 trillion dollars during pandemic QE and is now in slow runoff.
plain: The US central bank — sets the interest rate that drives most other US rates, and supervises the country's biggest banks.

snappy: CME futures contracts referencing the monthly average effective federal funds rate.
detail: The cleanest market-implied probability of Fed policy moves. Each contract settles to one minus the average daily EFFR during the contract month. The difference between adjacent contracts is the market's expected move at that FOMC meeting. CME publishes the FedWatch tool that translates these prices into rate-change probabilities. Heavily watched by macro traders and Fed-watchers.
plain: Contracts that let traders bet on what the US central bank's interest rate will be in coming months — the cleanest read on policy expectations.

snappy: The Fed's policy rate — what banks charge each other for overnight reserves.
detail: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range eight times a year. Since 2008 the Fed has implemented policy through interest on reserves (IORB) and the overnight reverse repo rate, which bracket the effective rate. Cuts in 2008 (from 5.25 percent to 0), hikes in 2022-23 (0 to 5.50 percent), and the path from here drive global asset prices. Watch the dot plot for the FOMC's own rate projections.
plain: The US central bank's main interest-rate lever — what banks pay to borrow from each other overnight, anchoring most other rates.
The interest rate US Banks charge each other for overnight cash — set by the Federal Reserve and the headline tool of US monetary policy.
snappy: Overnight rate US banks charge each other on reserves — the Fed's primary policy lever.
detail: Targeted by the FOMC in a range (e.g. 5.25 to 5.50 percent). The Fed steers the rate via IORB (interest on reserve balances), ON RRP, and the standing repo facility, keeping the effective fed funds rate inside its target band. Every other US dollar rate — Treasury yields, swap rates, mortgage rates, deposit rates — references it. FOMC meetings every six weeks are the highest-stakes events on the macro calendar.

snappy: Federal Reserve's real-time gross settlement system — large-value US dollar payments.
detail: Handles roughly 1 trillion dollars daily in 750,000+ payments. Used for interbank transfers, securities settlement, treasury operations. Open 21.5 hours daily. RTGS architecture means each payment settles immediately and finally — no netting. Compare with CHIPS (private-sector competitor) which uses netting. Fed-operated; payment system risk monitored closely.
plain: The US central bank's instant payment system for large bank-to-bank transfers — moves around a trillion dollars in a typical day.

snappy: US self-regulatory body overseeing broker-dealers — writes and enforces conduct rules.
detail: Independent non-governmental regulator created 2007 from NASD and NYSE Member Regulation. Licenses brokers, polices market manipulation, and enforces Rule 5310 (best execution), Rule 605/606 (execution-quality disclosure), and Rule 4210 (margin). Operates BrokerCheck and TRACE bond trade reporting. Funded by industry fees. The SEC retains ultimate authority but FINRA handles day-to-day broker-dealer supervision.
plain: The US watchdog for stockbrokers — sets the rules they must follow when handling customer trades and disciplines them for misconduct.

snappy: Coupon set at issuance and unchanged through the bond's life.
detail: The traditional bond structure: 5 percent coupon for 10 years, no resets. Investor takes interest-rate risk; issuer locks in funding cost.
