Most US Treasury securities, most corporate bonds, and most municipal bonds are fixed-rate. Compare with floating-rate notes, where the coupon resets. Fixed-rate bond prices move inversely to rates because the coupon stream stays fixed while market yields shift.
plain: A bond coupon that stays the same throughout the bond's life — the buyer locks in the income, the issuer locks in the cost.

snappy: Sudden, brief, severe market plunge followed by rapid recovery.
detail: Most famous: May 6, 2010 — Dow Jones fell 1,000 points (9 percent) in minutes, recovered most losses within 30 minutes. Triggered by an algo selling E-mini futures into thin liquidity, amplified by HFT liquidity withdrawal and stop-loss cascades. Subsequent flash crashes hit Treasury yields (October 2014), Swiss franc (January 2015), British pound (October 2016), and gold. Limit Up Limit Down rules and circuit breakers reduce but don't eliminate.
plain: A sudden, vicious price drop that reverses within minutes — usually triggered when automated traders all pull liquidity at once.

snappy: Exchange rate determined entirely by market forces — no central-bank intervention.
detail: USD, EUR, JPY, GBP all float freely. Central banks may intervene rhetorically or in extreme cases, but no formal target. Contrast with managed floats (Singapore, India intervene actively) and pegs. Free floats absorb shocks through price adjustments rather than reserve drains — the trade-off is more day-to-day volatility but no peg-collapse risk. Most developed-market currencies have floated since the 1973 Bretton Woods collapse.
plain: An exchange rate whose value is set entirely by buyers and sellers — the central bank doesn't try to defend a particular level.

snappy: Coupon that resets periodically based on a reference index — usually SOFR or EURIBOR.
detail: Floating-rate notes (FRNs) pay 'reference plus spread' — say, SOFR plus 80 basis points — with the coupon resetting quarterly or semiannually. Duration is roughly equal to the reset frequency, not the maturity, because the coupon adjusts with rates. Popular in rising-rate environments. Most corporate bank loans and many structured products are floating-rate. The 2023 LIBOR cessation forced trillions of contracts to migrate to SOFR-based equivalents.
plain: A bond coupon that resets every few months based on a reference interest rate — the buyer's payments rise and fall with market rates.

snappy: Option series that pays out when a floating interest rate falls below a fixed strike.
detail: Mirror image of a Cap. A series of floorlets paying max(strike minus floating rate, 0). Used by investors holding Floating Rate assets (loans, FRNs) to guarantee a minimum yield. Many syndicated loans embed an implicit 1 percent floor protecting lenders against zero-rate environments. Trades over-the-counter under an ISDA Master Agreement. Vol surface typically fit with the SABR Model.
plain: A contract that pays whenever a floating interest rate falls below an agreed level — a way to lock in a minimum yield on floating-rate investments.

snappy: Fed's policy-setting body — 7 governors plus 5 regional Fed presidents.
detail: Eight scheduled meetings per year. Sets the federal funds target range and chooses balance-sheet operations (QE, QT). Chair (currently Jay Powell) and Vice Chair lead. Five voting regional presidents rotate (NY Fed always votes; other 11 rotate in groups). Statements, press conferences, and Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) drive market reactions. Minutes released three weeks post-meeting.
plain: The committee at the US central bank that meets eight times a year to set interest rates and balance-sheet policy.

snappy: Detailed record of FOMC meeting discussions — released three weeks after each meeting.
detail: More detailed than the post-meeting statement. Captures range of views, internal debates, staff economic projections. Watched closely for hawk-dove signals beyond the headline statement. Sometimes shifts market expectations meaningfully when minutes reveal more hawkish or dovish internal discussion than the statement language conveyed. Heavily lawyered to avoid market-moving leaks.
plain: The detailed notes from a US central-bank meeting, released three weeks later — markets watch them for hints about future rate decisions.

snappy: SEC quarterly/annual filing required of large private fund advisers.
detail: Adopted 2011 under Dodd-Frank. Covers hedge funds, private equity, real-estate funds, securitised-asset funds. Detailed disclosures on AUM, portfolio composition, leverage, counterparty exposure, financing. Used by FSOC for systemic-risk monitoring. Confidential to the public. 2024 amendments expanded reporting requirements substantially. Form ADV (publicly available) supplements with manager-level disclosures.
plain: A confidential US filing big private-fund managers must make to regulators every quarter — discloses leverage, exposures, and investor types.

snappy: OTC agreement to buy or sell an asset at a future date for a price agreed today.
detail: Distinct from futures (exchange-traded, standardised, mark-to-market) — forwards are bilateral and customised. Settle on delivery date with cash or physical delivery. No daily margining unless governed by ISDA CSA. Used heavily in FX (corporate hedging), commodities (producer/consumer hedging), and rates (forward rate agreements). The 2008 crisis prompted regulators to push standardisation toward exchange-traded futures.
plain: A private agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date — customised, unlike standardised exchange Futures.

snappy: Central bank communication about likely future policy paths — used to influence market expectations.
detail: Two flavours: time-based (rates low until 2024), state-based (rates low until unemployment falls below X percent). The Bank of England and Fed pioneered modern forward guidance post-2008. Forward guidance creates self-fulfilling expectations — if markets price in the path, financial conditions adjust as if the policy were already implemented. Credibility-dependent: gradual phasing-out signals must be carefully managed.
plain: When a central bank signals what it's likely to do with interest rates in coming months — to shape market expectations before any actual move.

snappy: Premium or discount added to spot to get the forward FX rate.
detail: Derived from interest-rate differentials: borrow the high-rate currency, lend the low-rate one, and the forward must price arbitrage out (covered interest parity). Quoted as pips: USD/JPY at spot 150 with three-month forward points of -45 means the three-month forward is 149.55. Forwards above spot mean the base currency is at a premium; below means a discount. Tight in normal times, blow out in funding stress.
plain: The little adjustment added to today's exchange rate to get the forward rate — driven by the interest-rate gap between the two currencies.

snappy: OTC contract locking in a future short-term interest rate.
detail: Buyer pays fixed and receives floating (or vice versa) over a future period — say, three-month SOFR starting in six months. Settles in cash at the period's start based on the gap between the agreed rate and the realised reference rate. Largely supplanted by IRS after LIBOR was retired transition for longer dates, but still used at short maturities and as building blocks for swap pricing.
plain: A private contract that locks in a future short-term interest rate — useful for companies wanting to fix borrowing costs before they need to borrow.
US government-sponsored company that buys home loans, packages them into bonds, and guarantees the payments to investors.
snappy: US government-sponsored enterprise — Fannie Mae's smaller sibling in the residential mortgage market.
detail: Chartered 1970 to add competition to Fannie Mae's mortgage purchasing role. Buys conforming mortgages from lenders, securitises them into agency MBS, guarantees timely payment. Placed in federal conservatorship in September 2008 alongside Fannie. Combined Fannie-Freddie balance sheets are roughly 7 trillion dollars. Together they back most US residential mortgage credit. You'll hear them grouped under the GSE label.

snappy: Cash from operations minus capital expenditure — what's left for shareholders, debt holders, or growth.
detail: More conservative than EBITDA because it accounts for the actual capex needed to maintain the business. Sub-flavours: free cash flow to equity (after debt service), free cash flow to firm (before debt service). Discounted FCF (DCF) is the foundational valuation method. Companies report FCF in earnings releases; many investors prefer it to EPS because FCF is harder to manipulate via accounting choices.
plain: The money a company has left after paying for everything it needs to keep running and growing — what's actually available for dividends and buybacks.

snappy: Number of shares actually available for public trading — excludes insider and strategic holdings.
detail: Shares held by founders, governments, strategic partners, employee plans subject to lock-up, and treasury stock get excluded. Index providers (S&P, MSCI, FTSE Russell) weight index constituents by free-float market cap, not total market cap. A company with 100 million shares outstanding but only 30 million publicly tradable has a 30 percent free float. Low-float stocks (Snap, many crypto-related listings) are prone to extreme price moves.
plain: The portion of a company's stocks actually available for the public to buy — excludes founders, governments, and locked-up insider holdings.
A bond whose Interest payments reset every few months in line with a reference rate like SOFR — so the income tracks short-term rates.
snappy: Bond paying a coupon that resets periodically against a reference rate.
detail: US Treasury launched 2-year FRNs in 2014, referencing the 13-week T-bill rate. Corporate FRNs typically reference SOFR plus a spread, resetting quarterly. Less interest-rate-sensitive than fixed-coupon bonds because coupons rise with rates. Favoured by investors expecting rising rates or wanting cash-like exposure with a yield kicker. Lower duration but typically lower spread than fixed-coupon equivalents.

snappy: Illegally trading ahead of a client order with knowledge of the client's intent.
detail: Banned under SEC rules and FINRA conduct rules. Modern HFT firms are often accused of latency-based front-running — detecting incoming retail orders from broker order-flow payments and trading ahead. Distinct from anticipating market direction based on public information. Several settlements (Citadel Securities, Robinhood) involved disputed front-running allegations around payment for order flow.
plain: Illegally trading ahead of a client's order because you know what they're about to do — banned, but accusations come up regularly.

snappy: Markets less developed than EM — smaller, less liquid, often with capital controls.
detail: MSCI Frontier Markets index includes Nigeria, Kenya, Vietnam, Romania, Kazakhstan, Bahrain, and others — roughly 28 countries. Lower correlation with global markets, higher idiosyncratic risk, often dramatic returns (positive or negative). Liquidity constraints make institutional investing difficult. Some countries graduate to EM (UAE, Qatar 2014; Kuwait 2020); some get demoted (Argentina, Pakistan have bounced).
plain: Small, less-developed economies one tier riskier than typical emerging markets — places like Vietnam, Nigeria, and Bahrain.

full: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
plain: A global overhaul of how banks calculate the safety capital they hold against their trading books — replaces older methods with stricter ones.
snappy: Basel framework overhauling market-risk capital — replaces VaR with Expected Shortfall.
detail: Finalised by the Basel Committee in 2019 after years of post-crisis debate. Switches the market-risk capital metric from 99-percent Value-at-Risk to 97.5-percent Expected Shortfall, captures tail risk better, and stress-tests through historical periods. Tightens the boundary between trading and banking books to stop regulatory arbitrage. Implementation phased in across major jurisdictions through 2025-2026. You'll hear FRTB on bank earnings announcements under 'market risk capital' guidance.

snappy: G20 standard-setter coordinating global financial regulation post-2008.
detail: Successor to the Financial Stability Forum. Based in Basel alongside the BIS. Membership: G20 plus the EU plus standard-setting bodies (BCBS, IOSCO, IAIS). Sets policy on G-SIBs, too-big-to-fail, derivatives reform, and shadow banking. No legal authority — relies on members implementing standards domestically. Publishes the annual G-SIB list ranking the world's most systemic banks.
plain: The international body that gets the world's top financial regulators to agree on common rules — its standards usually shape national law later.

snappy: US council of senior regulators that designates systemic firms and watches systemic risk.
detail: Created by Dodd-Frank in 2010. Ten voting members chaired by the Treasury Secretary plus Fed Chair, SEC Chair, CFTC Chair, FDIC Chair, OCC, CFPB, FHFA, NCUA, and an insurance expert. Designates non-bank SIFIs, subjecting them to Fed supervision (AIG, GE Capital, Prudential, MetLife — most later de-designated). Publishes an annual report on systemic vulnerabilities. Re-tightened SIFI designation rules in 2024.
plain: A US committee that brings together the country's top financial regulators to spot risks that could shake the whole system.

snappy: 100 largest UK-listed companies by market cap — the UK equity benchmark.
detail: Established 1984. Heavy in financials, energy, mining, pharma — global businesses with London listings. Many constituents derive most revenue overseas (Shell, AstraZeneca, HSBC). Total market cap around 2 trillion pounds. Tracked by ishares Core FTSE 100 ETF (ISF). FTSE 250 covers mid-caps; FTSE All-share is the broader UK benchmark. Operated by FTSE Russell, part of LSEG.
plain: The headline UK stock index — 100 large companies including Shell, AstraZeneca, and HSBC, most earning the bulk of their revenue overseas.

snappy: Low-yield currency borrowed to finance carry positions.
detail: Traditional funding currencies: JPY (yen), CHF (Swiss franc), EUR (euro), USD (when Fed is cutting). Choice depends on the rate differential and the currency's behaviour during stress — JPY rallies in risk-off, making it a costly funding leg when carry unwinds. Mortgage-style: many corporates and households in Eastern Europe took on CHF or EUR mortgages pre-2008, then got hammered when those currencies rallied.
plain: A low-yielding currency you borrow in order to invest somewhere with higher yields — historically the Japanese yen or the Swiss franc.

snappy: Adjustment for the funding cost of uncollateralised derivative positions.
detail: Banks fund derivative collateral and unsecured positions at their own (above-Treasury) funding cost — FVA captures the gap. Less established than CVA — different banks calculate differently. Major OTC derivative valuation differences across dealers partly reflect FVA-methodology differences. FVA and CVA together can offset (a bank's FVA gain offsets the counterparty's FVA charge in mirror form).
plain: An accounting adjustment for the cost a bank pays to fund collateral on its derivatives — closely related to the controversial CVA.
The market where one country's Currency is swapped for another — turning dollars into euros, yen into pounds, and so on.
snappy: Currency trading — the world's largest market by daily turnover.
detail: Roughly 7.5 trillion dollars in daily turnover (BIS 2022 triennial survey) — bigger than all equity markets combined. Major pairs (EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD) account for most volume. London, New York, Tokyo, and Singapore are the main hubs. FX trades 24 hours weekdays. You'll hear FX desks quoted everywhere — investment banks, central banks, multinational corporates, hedge funds. The market is largely OTC; futures (CME) and listed options exist but are a smaller slice.

snappy: Central bank buying or selling its own currency in markets to influence the exchange rate.
detail: Tactics: spot transactions (most common), forward sales (off-balance-sheet), verbal intervention ('jawboning'). Effective when reserves are deep, intentions are credible, and intervention aligns with policy fundamentals. The Bank of Japan intervened twice in 2022 selling USD to support JPY (its first intervention in 24 years); the Swiss National Bank ran years of intervention to weaken the franc. G7 nations rarely intervene; EM does so routinely.
plain: When a central bank buys or sells its own currency in the open market to push its exchange rate up or down.

snappy: Contract giving the right (not obligation) to exchange one currency for another at a future date.
detail: Quoted in volatility terms rather than price — dealers say 'EUR/USD 1-year vol at 7' rather than premium in dollars. Three main flavours: vanilla calls/puts, structured products (knock-in, knock-out), and exotics (digital, barrier). Used by corporates to hedge contingent exposures (the deal might not happen), by traders to express volatility views, and by central banks to manage reserves. Settled mostly OTC.
plain: A contract giving you the right (but not the obligation) to swap one currency for another at a chosen rate on a future date.

snappy: Foreign-currency assets held by central banks — backstop for intervention, debt service, imports.
detail: Mostly USD-denominated Treasury securities (still around 58 percent of allocated reserves), with EUR, JPY, GBP, CNY making up most of the rest. China holds the largest reserve stockpile (3.2 trillion in 2024), Japan second, Switzerland fifth. Used for FX intervention, sovereign debt service, and import financing. Sanctions on Russian reserves in 2022 raised concerns about reserve-currency status and triggered some de-dollarisation flows.
plain: Foreign-currency assets a central bank stockpiles — used to defend its own currency, pay international debts, or finance imports during a crisis.

snappy: FX trade settling in two business days at the current market rate.
detail: The base of the FX market — over 7 trillion dollars in daily turnover globally (BIS 2022 survey). Most pairs settle T+2; USD/CAD and USD/MXN settle T+1. Spot rates fluctuate continuously across global trading hours, with London accounting for roughly 40 percent of volume. Dealers quote two-way prices (bid-offer) to clients; the largest pairs have spreads of a fraction of a basis point.
plain: A foreign-exchange trade that settles two business days later at the current market rate — the simplest, deepest type of currency deal.

snappy: Exchange currencies now, agree to swap them back at a fixed forward rate.
detail: Two legs: spot exchange today, reverse exchange at maturity. Used by corporates to hedge cross-currency funding, by central banks (the Fed's swap lines with the ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank of England), and by anyone wanting to synthesise foreign-currency exposure without borrowing. The 'cross-currency basis' — the forward points implied minus what covered interest parity says — became a watched stress gauge after 2008 when banks lost access to dollar funding.
plain: A pair of foreign-exchange trades — swap currencies today, swap them back at an agreed rate later. The bread-and-butter of cross-border funding.

snappy: Bank designated by FSB and BCBS as critical to global financial stability.
detail: Current G-SIB list: 29 banks across 13 jurisdictions. Five categories of surcharge from 1 percent (lowest) to 3.5 percent (highest, currently unoccupied). JPMorgan, HSBC, Citigroup, BNP Paribas in higher tiers. Annual reassessment based on size, interconnectedness, complexity, cross-jurisdictional activity, substitutability. G-SIB surcharge sits on top of regular capital requirements.
plain: A bank so large that regulators worry its failure could break the global financial system, so it must hold extra safety capital.

snappy: Rate of change of delta — how an option's delta moves as the underlying moves.
detail: Long-gamma positions buy low and sell high mechanically — as the underlying rises, delta increases, requiring the hedger to sell more; as it falls, the reverse. Positive gamma benefits from realised volatility. Dealers paid short gamma (short options) lose money in volatile markets; long gamma profits. Gamma is highest for at-the-money options near expiry, which is why short-dated options have outsized hedging flows.
plain: How quickly an option's sensitivity to price moves changes — like the steepness of a hill, not just the slope.

snappy: Dealer hedging of short call positions forces them to buy more stock as price rises — amplifies rally.
detail: Variation of short squeeze involving options. As a stock rallies into expiring call strikes, market-makers who sold those calls hedge by buying more stock to maintain delta neutrality, which pushes the price higher, requiring more buying. The 2021 GameStop episode combined classic short squeeze with gamma squeeze. Most pronounced near expiry when gamma is highest. Reverses violently if the underlying rolls over.
plain: When dealers who sold call options are forced to buy a stock as it rises, pushing the price even higher.

snappy: Time-series model for volatility — captures volatility clustering and persistence.
detail: Engle (1982) introduced ARCH; Bollerslev (1986) generalised to GARCH. Captures the fact that volatility comes in clusters (high-vol periods follow high-vol days). GARCH(1,1) is the workhorse model in finance. Used in VaR, option pricing, risk forecasting. Recent extensions: HEAVY-GARCH (with high-frequency data), realised-GARCH, multivariate GARCH. Engle won 2003 Nobel partly for ARCH.
plain: A math recipe that predicts how jumpy prices will be tomorrow based on how jumpy they have been lately.

snappy: FX equivalent of Black-Scholes — accounts for two risk-free rates (one per currency).
detail: Extends Black-Scholes by replacing the single risk-free rate with the differential between the two currencies' rates. The forward rate (driven by interest-rate differential) plays the role of spot in equity option pricing. Published 1983. Used industry-wide for vanilla FX option pricing; more sophisticated models (Heston, SABR, local vol) handle the smile. The textbook reference for FX vanilla pricing.
plain: A pricing formula for currency options — like the famous Black-Scholes recipe but adjusted to handle two countries' interest rates.

snappy: Broadest inflation measure — covers all goods and services in GDP.
detail: Calculated implicitly: nominal GDP divided by real GDP. Covers all output in the economy, not just consumption (like CPI). Differs from CPI in basket scope and weighting methodology. Typically closer to PCE than CPI in level. Used in academic and IMF cross-country inflation comparisons. Less timely than CPI/PCE (released quarterly with GDP, not monthly).
plain: A broad measure of inflation that covers every good and service a country produces, not just what shoppers buy.

snappy: Equivalent of ADR but listed outside the US — typically London or Luxembourg.
detail: Same mechanics as ADR: a depositary bank holds the underlying foreign shares and issues receipts that trade in another jurisdiction. London stock Exchange's International Order Book is the main GDR venue. Many Russian and Indian companies (back when they could) raised capital via London GDRs. Compliance and tax considerations drive the GDR/ADR choice for issuers.
plain: A way to buy shares of a foreign company through a local stock exchange without dealing with the foreign market directly.
US government agency that guarantees bonds made of mortgages backed by federal loan programmes — its guarantee is fully government-backed.
snappy: US government agency guaranteeing MBS backed by FHA and VA loans — full faith-and-credit backing.
detail: Unlike Fannie and Freddie, Ginnie is a wholly owned government agency — its guarantee is backed by the full faith and credit of the US Treasury, the same as Treasury bonds. Securitises pools of FHA-insured, VA-guaranteed, and other government-program mortgages. Roughly 2 trillion dollars outstanding. You'll hear Ginnie MBS yields cited slightly tighter than Fannie/Freddie because of the explicit government guarantee.

snappy: Depression-era US law separating commercial and investment banking — substantially repealed 1999.
detail: Forbade Federal Reserve member banks from underwriting securities or affiliating with securities firms. Repealed by Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act 1999, enabling commercial-investment banking mergers (Citi-Travelers/Salomon, JPMorgan-Chase). Sometimes blamed for setting the stage for 2008 crisis; counter-argument is that several pure investment banks (Bear, Lehman) and pure commercial banks (Washington Mutual) also failed. Periodic demands for revival.
plain: A 1933 US law that forced ordinary banks and Wall Street trading firms to be separate businesses — mostly scrapped in 1999.

snappy: Auditor's assessment that a company can continue operations for at least 12 months.
detail: Going-concern qualifications in audit reports signal financial distress. Trigger covenant breaches, accelerate debt, accelerate creditor enforcement. Major historical going-concern flags: Bear Stearns (March 2008), Lehman (September 2008), Hertz (2020 — eventually exited bankruptcy), Bed Bath & Beyond (2023). Modern accounting standards require management to assess and disclose substantial doubt about going-concern status.
plain: An accountant's verdict that a company has enough money and momentum to keep operating for at least another year.

snappy: Public company is acquired by an investor group and delisted from public markets.
detail: Typical structure: private-equity-led LBO. Notable take-privates: Dell (2013, returned public 2018), Hilton Worldwide (2007), Thomson Reuters' Refinitiv (2018), Sirius XM (under discussion 2024). Average premium 25-35 percent to undisturbed share price. Goes-private deals dropped sharply 2022-23 with higher financing costs; recovering in 2024 as rate expectations stabilised.
plain: When investors buy out all the shares of a public company and pull it off the stock exchange.

snappy: Yellow precious metal — monetary store of value across millennia, now also industrial.
detail: Priced in dollars per troy ounce. London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) sets the daily gold price fix. Central banks hold roughly 17 percent of all gold ever mined as reserves; private investors hold another 22 percent. Gold rallies in real-rate falls, USD weakness, and risk-off episodes. Crossed 2,000 dollars per ounce in 2020, 2,800 in 2024. Used as inflation hedge, currency hedge, and crisis insurance.
plain: The yellow precious metal — used for jewellery and electronics, but mostly bought as a safe place to park money during scary times.

snappy: Gold price divided by silver price — relative-value gauge between the two metals.
detail: Historically averages around 60. Above 80 typically marks silver as cheap relative to gold (silver underperforms in early metals bull markets, outperforms in late stages). Above 100 (2020) signals extreme dislocation. Below 50 signals silver-heavy bull market (1980s). Used by precious-metals traders for relative-value rotation between the two metals. Both gold and silver futures listed on COMEX.
plain: How many ounces of silver it takes to buy one ounce of gold — traders watch it to spot which metal looks cheap.

snappy: Bond issued by a national or regional government to fund operations.
detail: Includes US Treasury securities, UK Gilts, German Bunds, Japanese JGBs, French OATs — names vary by jurisdiction but mechanics are similar. National governments tap their own currency markets first; emerging-market sovereigns also issue in hard currency (USD or EUR) when needed. Local-currency sovereign bonds are the standard reference for that country's risk-free rate. Spreads between sovereigns measure relative credit and currency risk.
plain: A loan you make to a country's government — they pay you regular interest, then your money back on a set date.

snappy: Risk sensitivities of an option's price — delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho.
detail: Greek letters used (not all are actually Greek): Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega (not Greek — letter resembling V), Rho. Higher-order Greeks: Charm, Vanna, Volga, Zomma. Traders manage option books by Greeks rather than individual position P&Ls. Dealers hedge delta continuously (delta-neutral books), then manage gamma and vega exposures within risk limits. The Greeks aggregate across positions in a portfolio.
plain: Nicknames for the dials that measure how an option's price reacts to different changes — price, time, volatility, and so on.

snappy: Production-weighted commodity index — heavy in energy due to oil production scale.
detail: Originally Goldman Sachs Commodity Index. Energy is roughly 55 percent of the index — much higher than BCOM. Roll methodology can produce significant contango drag. Pioneered the era of commodity-index investing in the 2000s. Total return version critical to passive commodity investment strategies. Multiple sub-indexes available for sector-specific exposure.
plain: A basket measuring commodity prices, heavily weighted toward oil because the world produces so much of it.
A private US-chartered company that supports specific markets like home lending — and is treated by investors as having a government safety net.
snappy: Privately owned but government-chartered firm — Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae.
detail: Created by Congress to channel cheap funding into housing and agriculture. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy and guarantee residential mortgages; Ginnie Mae guarantees mortgages backed by federal agencies. Their debt has long traded at near-Treasury yields on the assumption of implicit government backing — confirmed when both were placed in conservatorship in 2008. You'll hear GSE in any conversation about US mortgage-backed securities or housing-policy reform.

snappy: Hong Kong's main equity index — large companies listed in Hong Kong.
detail: Approximately 80 constituents. Tencent, Alibaba, HSBC, AIA, China Construction Bank are heavy weights. Expanded recently to include more mainland Chinese tech companies via secondary listings. Operated by Hang Seng Indexes. Highly correlated with mainland Chinese equity sentiment. The 2021 Beijing tech crackdown caused dramatic underperformance versus global benchmarks.
plain: The main scoreboard for Hong Kong's stock market — tracks its biggest listed companies.

snappy: Major reserve currency — USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF — widely accepted for international payments.
detail: Distinguished from soft/local currencies in EM and frontier markets. Hard-currency sovereign debt (a Mexico USD bond, for example) carries different risk than local-currency debt (a Mexico MXN bond): hard-currency exposes the issuer to FX risk if revenues are local; local-currency exposes the investor to FX depreciation. Hard-currency EM debt is roughly 50 percent of the JPMorgan EMBI index.
plain: A currency the whole world trusts and accepts — the US dollar, euro, yen, pound, and Swiss franc.

snappy: Central bank tightening triggers a significant recession.
detail: Volcker's 1979-82 hard landing crushed inflation but cost massive unemployment (10.8 percent peak). The 1990-91 US recession after late-1980s tightening was milder. 2024 fears of a hard landing eased as employment held up despite Fed hikes. Hard landings can be unavoidable if inflation expectations are deeply embedded. Term is contested — defining when an outcome counts as hard versus soft involves judgment.
plain: When a central bank's effort to cool down inflation accidentally crashes the economy into a serious recession.

snappy: Investment strategy positioning for an economic downturn.
detail: Typical components: long long-duration Treasury securities (rally on rate cuts), long defensive equities (utilities, staples, healthcare), short cyclicals (consumer discretionary, banks), short oil, long USD or JPY (safe-haven). 2024 hard-landing-trade unwinds were sharp as US data kept beating recession expectations. Macro funds rotate between hard-landing and soft-landing trades as data flows.
plain: A bet that the economy is about to fall into recession — usually betting on safe bonds and against risky stocks.

snappy: Total inflation including all components — food, energy, and everything else.
detail: The number most often quoted in news headlines. Captures the cost-of-living impact most relevant to consumers. Subject to large fluctuations from food and energy price moves. The 9 percent US headline CPI peak in 2022 was driven heavily by post-Ukraine-invasion energy spikes. Central banks ultimately care about headline (it's what consumers experience) but focus on core for policy because core is the controllable underlying trend.
plain: The total cost-of-living number you see in the news, including all food, fuel, and everyday prices.

snappy: Diesel-grade fuel used for residential and commercial heating, mostly in the US Northeast.
detail: NYMEX-listed heating oil futures (/HO) are now ULSD (ultra-low sulphur diesel) post-2012, same as on-road diesel fuel. Quoted in dollars per gallon. Demand is heavily seasonal. The crack spread between WTI crude and heating oil futures is a refining margin indicator. Heating oil consumption has declined as households switch to natural gas and electric heat.
plain: The diesel-like fuel that heats houses in cold parts of the US — traded as a futures contract by energy traders.

snappy: Position taken to reduce exposure to a specific risk.
detail: Examples: oil company buying crude futures to lock in revenue; airline buying jet fuel futures; corporate borrower swapping floating-rate debt to fixed; portfolio manager buying VIX to hedge equity tail risk. Hedge effectiveness measured by reduction in P&L volatility. Imperfect hedges (basis risk) common — perfect hedges are rare. Distinct from speculation which seeks to profit from market moves.
plain: A protective move that offsets the risk of another position — like buying insurance on something you already own.

snappy: Lightly regulated investment fund — often uses leverage, derivatives, short selling.
detail: Limited to accredited investors. Charges performance fees (typically 20 percent of gains) plus management fees (1-2 percent). Strategies: long-short equity, global macro, event-driven, fixed-income arbitrage, multi-strategy. Industry AUM around 4 trillion dollars. Top funds: Citadel, Millennium, DE Shaw, Renaissance, Bridgewater. Performance varies enormously; average post-fee returns hardly beat S&P 500 in recent decades.
plain: An exclusive investment fund for wealthy clients that uses fancier tricks and borrowed money to try to beat the market.

snappy: Number of hedging instruments needed to offset a position's risk.
detail: For a single option: delta tells you how many units of underlying to hold to offset price risk. For a portfolio: gamma-vega ratios determine cross-hedges. Pension funds running LDI use duration-matching hedge ratios; commodity producers calculate barrels-hedged ratios. Imperfect hedging — basis risk between hedge instrument and underlying exposure — limits how much risk can be neutralised.
plain: The amount of protection you need to fully cancel out the risk of something you own — like how many umbrellas one rainstorm needs.

snappy: Direct central-bank transfer to citizens or government — money-financed fiscal stimulus.
detail: Coined by Milton Friedman (1969 essay). Hypothetical extreme policy — never actually deployed in pure form. Closest analogues: 2020 US stimulus checks (Fed-funded fiscally, not direct), Japan's deficit-funded stimulus financed by BoJ bond purchases. Distinct from QE (which buys assets, lends, doesn't gift). Permanently expands base money — irreversible. Theoretical guard against deflationary trap and ZLB-bound monetary policy.
plain: An emergency policy where a central bank effectively hands cash straight to citizens or government — never quite tried in pure form.

snappy: Pipeline interconnect in Erath, Louisiana — pricing reference for North American natural gas.
detail: NYMEX natural gas futures settle to Henry Hub delivery. Connects to a dozen pipelines crossing the Gulf Coast — the most-connected pricing point in the US gas system. Henry Hub prices diverge from regional prices (Permian, Marcellus, AECO in Alberta) when pipeline constraints bite. The 2022 European gas crisis pulled US LNG export demand, lifting Henry Hub prices via the international arbitrage.
plain: A pipeline junction in Louisiana that sets the benchmark price for natural gas across North America.

snappy: Stochastic-volatility option-pricing model — vol follows its own random process.
detail: Published 1993 by Steven Heston. Volatility mean-reverts and is correlated with the underlying. Better captures vol smile dynamics than Black-Scholes. Parameters: long-run vol, mean-reversion speed, vol of vol, correlation. Heston has a semi-closed-form solution via Fourier transform, making it tractable for calibration. Standard reference in derivatives quant interviews; widely used in production option-pricing engines.
plain: A pricing formula for options that lets a market's jumpiness change over time, instead of pretending it stays flat.

snappy: Algorithmic trading strategies relying on speed — typically holding positions for milliseconds to minutes.
detail: Roughly half of US equity volume. Strategies: market-making (Citadel Securities, Virtu), latency arbitrage (Hudson River Trading), statistical arbitrage (Two Sigma, Renaissance). Profitability has compressed as competition has scaled — HFT industry revenues fell from peaks of 7 billion in 2009 to roughly 1.5 billion in recent years. Maker-taker fee rebates and exchange data fees are substantial cost components.
plain: Computer trading at lightning speed, where profitable trades hinge on being a few millionths of a second faster than rivals.

snappy: Bonds rated BB+ or below — higher default risk, higher coupon.
detail: Pejoratively 'junk' bonds. Yields several percentage points above IG. Mike Milken pioneered the modern HY market at Drexel in the 1980s. Issued by leveraged buyouts, fallen-angel companies, and natural HY issuers (telecoms, energy, retailers). HY spreads gap dramatically in stress — over 1,000 bps in 2008, briefly there in March 2020. HY ETFs (HYG, JNK) democratised retail HY exposure post-2007.
plain: Bonds from companies seen as risky borrowers — they pay much more interest to compensate lenders for the chance of default.

snappy: VaR calculated by directly applying historical returns to current positions.
detail: Take the past 252 trading days of returns, apply to today's portfolio, find the 5th percentile. Captures actual market behaviour including non-normal distributions. Limitations: assumes the past is representative of the future. Crisis periods (2008, 2020) sit in or out of the rolling window depending on calculation date — sliding the window can produce dramatic VaR changes. Common in trading-book risk models.
plain: Estimating how bad tomorrow could be by replaying actual past price moves on today's investments.

snappy: Acquisition pursued against the target board's wishes — bypasses board via shareholder appeal.
detail: Tactics: tender offer (direct to shareholders), proxy fight (replace the board), public campaign. Carl Icahn (TWA 1985, Texaco 1988), KKR (RJR Nabisco 1988), Microsoft-Yahoo (2008, failed). Target defenses: poison pills, white knights, staggered boards. Increasingly rare since 2000s — most takeovers now negotiated. Activist investors use takeover threats as leverage for governance changes.
plain: An attempted purchase of a company that its board does not want — the bidder goes around them to shareholders instead.
Safe, easy-to-sell assets a bank must hold — like government bonds — to cover withdrawals during a financial panic.
snappy: Liquid assets that qualify under Basel III's LCR — easily converted to cash with little price loss.
detail: Three tiers: Level 1 (cash, central-bank reserves, sovereign bonds — no haircut), Level 2A (high-grade corporate bonds, certain sovereigns — 15 percent haircut), Level 2B (lower-rated corporates, equities in some jurisdictions — 25-50 percent haircut). Banks must hold enough HQLA to cover 30 days of stressed cash outflows under the Liquidity Coverage Ratio. You'll hear about HQLA whenever bank treasurers discuss balance-sheet composition or when Basel III implementation gets debated.

snappy: Extreme inflation, typically defined as 50 percent or more per month.
detail: Historical examples: Weimar Germany 1923, Hungary 1945-46 (highest recorded — prices doubled every 15 hours), Zimbabwe 2007-08, Venezuela 2017-19, Argentina recurring. Always rooted in massive monetary financing of fiscal deficits. Destroys savings, breaks contracts, ends in currency reform or dollarisation. Distinct from very high inflation (50-200 percent annual). Modern advanced economies don't experience it; remains an EM crisis-state phenomenon.
plain: Runaway price increases — when a loaf of bread can cost twice as much next week, and savings become worthless.

snappy: Banks' internal process for assessing risks and capital — fed into SREP/CCAR.
detail: Required under Basel II Pillar 2. Banks document risks not captured by Pillar 1 capital requirements (concentration risk, interest-rate-risk-in-banking-book, reputation risk). Annual submission to supervisors. Forms basis of supervisory dialogue. ILAAP (Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process) is the liquidity counterpart. Together, central to modern bank-supervisory framework.
plain: A bank's own annual report to regulators explaining every risk it faces and showing it has enough capital to survive them.
A global exchange operator that runs the New York stock Exchange, Brent oil Futures, US credit derivatives clearing, and many other markets.
snappy: US-based exchange group — owns NYSE, ICE Futures, ICE Clear Credit.
detail: Founded 2000 in Atlanta by Jeff Sprecher as an electronic energy-trading platform. Bought the New York stock Exchange in 2013 and the London-based International Petroleum Exchange in 2001, making Brent crude its flagship futures contract. Also runs the dominant CDS clearing house (ICE Clear Credit) and major European emissions and soft-commodity exchanges. You'll hear ICE quoted any time someone references Brent crude, NYSE-listed stocks, or US credit-derivatives clearing.

snappy: Broad US high-yield bond benchmark — formerly Merrill Lynch HY Master II.
detail: Includes most USD-denominated junk bonds. Total market value approximately 1.5 trillion dollars. Tracked by SPDR Bloomberg HY (JNK) and ishares Broad USD HY (USHY) ETFs. Effective yield, option-adjusted spread (OAS), and modified duration published daily. The standard reference for HY market commentary.
plain: The main scoreboard for risky US corporate bonds — tracks how junk-rated debt is performing overall.

snappy: Comprehensive US Treasury bond benchmark — alternative to Bloomberg Treasury Index.
detail: Operated by ICE. Multiple sub-indexes by maturity bucket (1-3y, 3-7y, 7-10y, 10-20y, 20+y). Used as benchmark for US Treasury portfolios. Total return versions include coupon reinvestment. Compete with Bloomberg US Treasury Index variants. Each fund chooses its preferred index based on construction methodology nuances.
plain: A scoreboard tracking how all US government bonds are performing as a group.

snappy: Algo that uses iceberg orders to gradually work a large order — only the tip visible.
detail: Reveals just a small slice of total intended quantity; replenishes as the visible tip fills. Conceals true order size to avoid market signalling. Used in equities (where iceberg orders are explicit order types) and adapted via algos in markets without native iceberg support. Distinct from broader liquidity-seeking algos that pull from multiple sources.
plain: A computer program that hides a big order by showing only a small slice at a time, refilling as each slice gets bought.

snappy: Large order that displays only a small portion of its size at any time — the rest is hidden.
detail: Common in equity and futures markets. Visible 'tip' replenishes when filled. Disguises large orders from front-runners and information leakage. Time priority is sometimes preserved at the same price for the hidden portion; varies by venue. Used by institutional investors and algos to work large orders without alarming the market.
plain: A large order that shows only a tiny tip on the public screen, hiding the bulk so it does not scare the market.
A US stock exchange that builds a tiny speed bump into every order — designed to neutralise high-frequency trading edges.
snappy: Stock exchange with a 350-microsecond speed bump — pitched against latency arbitrage.
detail: Founded 2012, became a registered exchange in 2016 after high-profile SEC approval. The 350-microsecond delay (the 'magic shoebox') gives the exchange time to update its book before HFTs can act on stale quotes. Roughly 2-3 percent of US equity volume. Featured prominently in Michael Lewis's 2014 book Flash Boys. Other exchanges have since experimented with similar speed-bump models.

plain: The global accounting rulebook that tells banks how to set aside money in advance for loans they expect might go bad.
snappy: Global accounting standard requiring banks to provision expected credit losses up front.
detail: Effective from 2018, replacing IAS 39. Forces banks to recognise loan losses based on lifetime expected losses rather than waiting for actual default — a forward-looking 'expected credit loss' (ECL) model. Pushed banks to build sophisticated default-probability and loss-given-default models. Adopted by most major banks outside the US (which uses CECL, a parallel standard). You'll see IFRS 9 cited in any non-US bank earnings release under 'credit provisioning'.

snappy: Multilateral institution providing balance-of-payments crisis financing — 191 members.
detail: Founded at Bretton Woods 1944. Originally to support fixed-exchange-rate system; now serves as global lender of last resort to countries in payments crises. Major facilities: Stand-By Arrangements, Extended Fund Facility, RFI (Rapid Financing). Loans come with conditionality (policy reforms). Recent large programs: Argentina 2018 (57 billion), Egypt 2020-24, Pakistan repeated, Ukraine post-2022. World Bank focuses on long-term development.
plain: A global agency that lends emergency money to countries facing financial crises — usually with strict conditions attached.

snappy: Difference between the price when the trade was decided and the average execution price.
detail: Captures total execution cost: market impact, opportunity cost from delayed fills, and spread paid. Coined by Andre Perold in 1988. The 'arrival price' benchmark for execution algos. IS algos try to minimise this gap by balancing impact (fill faster) against urgency (wait for liquidity). Distinct from VWAP/TWAP benchmarks which compare to participation-weighted prices, ignoring timing.
plain: The gap between the price you wanted when you decided to trade and the actual price you ended up paying.

snappy: The volatility the option market is pricing in — derived backwards from the option's premium.
detail: Black-Scholes (and successors) take inputs — spot, strike, time, rate, volatility — and output an option price. Invert the model on a traded option and the only unknown is volatility; that's IV, the market's forward-looking estimate. The VIX is a weighted IV reading off S&P 500 options. IV usually trades above realised volatility — the 'vol risk premium' that volatility sellers harvest.
plain: How jumpy the market expects a price to be in the future, reverse-engineered from what people are paying for options today.

snappy: Option that would have intrinsic value if exercised now.
detail: Call with strike below current price; put with strike above current price. Deep ITM options have high delta (close to 1.0 for calls, -1.0 for puts) and behave nearly like the underlying. Most option exercise activity concentrates on ITM options near expiry. Distinguished from ATM (near current price) and OTM (out-of-money).
plain: An option that would already make money if used right now — its Strike Price is favourable compared to today's market.
A measure that combines the prices of many assets into one number — like the S&P 500 tracking 500 big US stocks at once.
snappy: Statistical aggregate tracking a basket of securities — basis for benchmarks and passive funds.
detail: Major equity indexes: S&P 500, Dow Jones, Nasdaq Composite, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225. Bond indexes: Bloomberg US Aggregate, ICE BofA HY. Commodity indexes: S&P GSCI, Bloomberg Commodity. Indexes drive trillions in passive ETF and mutual-fund assets. Index providers (MSCI, FTSE Russell, S&P Dow Jones Indices) earn licensing fees. Index inclusion or exclusion events drive material trading volume.

plain: A fund that simply mirrors a market Index — buying the same stocks in the same proportions, so it tracks the Index very cheaply.
snappy: Mutual fund or ETF passively replicating a market index — low fees, broad exposure.
detail: Pioneered by Vanguard's First Index Investment Trust (1976). Now dominates retail and institutional flows: roughly half of US equity assets are passively managed (2024). Largest: Vanguard 500 Index, ishares Core S&P 500, SPDR S&P 500. Fees typically 0.03-0.10 percent versus 0.50-1.00 percent for active. Tracks index minus tiny tracking error. Index fund flows now drive material market structure dynamics.

snappy: Option on an equity index — cash-settled, European-style.
detail: SPX options (S&P 500) are the largest contract in the world by notional. Cash-settled because you can't deliver an index; the final settlement price comes from a special opening-rotation calculation. European-style (exercise only at expiry) avoids early-assignment risk. Used by institutional traders for portfolio hedging and macro positioning. Weekly, monthly, and quarterly expirations available; 0DTE (zero-days-to-expiry) options exploded in popularity post-2022.
plain: A bet on the whole stock market's direction rather than any single company — pays out in cash, not shares.

snappy: Sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services.
detail: Measured by various indexes: CPI (consumer prices, US BLS), PCE (Fed's preferred, US BEA), HICP (EU), RPI (UK). Drivers: demand pull (too much money chasing too few goods), cost push (rising input costs), expectations (self-fulfilling). The 2021-2022 US inflation surge took CPI to 9 percent; back near 3 percent by 2024. Hyperinflation is the extreme version; deflation is the negative version.
plain: When the same shopping basket costs more this year than last year. Higher inflation means each dollar buys less.
The inflation rate a central bank publicly aims for — usually 2 percent — and adjusts interest rates to try to hit.
snappy: Publicly stated inflation goal — anchors the central bank's policy framework.
detail: The Fed, ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, and most major central banks target 2 percent inflation. Pioneered by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand in 1990. The Fed adopted formal 2 percent targeting in 2012 and shifted to 'average inflation targeting' (FAIT) in 2020 — willing to overshoot temporarily after undershoots. Targets anchor expectations; credibility depends on long-run track record. Periodic academic debate about raising targets to 3-4 percent.

snappy: Monetary-policy framework where central bank explicitly commits to a numerical inflation target.
detail: New Zealand was the first (1990). Now standard across major central banks: Fed 2 percent (since 2012), ECB 2 percent (since 2003), Bank of England 2 percent (1997). The target anchors expectations and provides accountability. Hard targets (BoE — 'symmetric') versus 'within a band' (other approaches). Empirical evidence supports inflation targeting's success at anchoring expectations during the 2000s; tested by 2021-22 inflation surge.
plain: A central bank's public promise to keep inflation at a specific number, usually around 2 percent a year.

snappy: Bond whose principal adjusts with inflation — protects real purchasing power.
detail: US Treasury inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) are the largest market. Principal grows by CPI changes; coupons (set at a real rate) apply to the inflation-adjusted principal. UK index-linked Gilts and euro-area linkers (BTPei, OATei) work similarly. The break-even inflation rate — nominal Treasury yield minus TIPS yield — is the market's implied inflation expectation. Issued at 5-, 10-, and 30-year maturities; auctioned a handful of times each year.
plain: A bond whose payments grow with inflation, so its value keeps up with the cost of living.

snappy: Excess return over benchmark divided by tracking error — active-management skill metric.
detail: Tells you how much active risk a manager takes per unit of active return. High IR (1.0+) signals genuine alpha; low IR (below 0.3) suggests luck or expensive tracking. Compared with Sharpe Ratio (uses risk-free rate as benchmark). Active equity managers' IRs have been declining secularly as markets become more efficient. The 0.5 IR threshold separates institutional-grade active managers from average.
plain: A scorecard showing how much extra return a fund manager earns over their benchmark, adjusted for the risk they take.

snappy: Collateral posted at trade inception — covers potential future exposure.
detail: Required by clearing houses (CME, LCH, ICE) and bilateral counterparties (under post-2008 IM rules). Calculated using historical-simulation VaR or SIMM (the ISDA standard initial-margin model). Typically 5-10 percent of notional for swaps, higher for volatile or longer-dated trades. Held in the counterparty's name in segregated accounts. Returned at trade termination minus variation margin movements.
plain: Money or assets you must deposit upfront when entering a trade, as a safety cushion against future losses.

snappy: Trading securities while in possession of material non-public information (MNPI).
detail: Banned under SEC Rule 10b-5. Covers corporate insiders (officers, directors, employees), tippers and tippees who knowingly received MNPI. Section 16 of '34 Act requires disclosure of officer/director trades and bans short-swing profits. Federal prosecutions include Ivan Boesky (1986), Martha Stewart (2004), Raj Rajaratnam (2011). Recent SEC focus on cherry-picking, expert-network leaks, and political-intelligence trading.
plain: Buying or selling shares using secret company information that the public does not have — illegal in most countries.

snappy: Cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of principal per year.
detail: Different rates for different purposes and risks: federal funds rate (overnight bank lending), Treasury yields (risk-free for various maturities), mortgage rates (consumer borrowing), corporate bond yields (corporate borrowing). The 'risk-free rate' anchors all other rates plus credit spreads. Real rates strip out inflation expectations; nominal rates are what's quoted publicly. Drive valuations across asset classes.
plain: The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage you pay each year on what you owe.

snappy: Exchange of fixed coupon payments for floating, both on the same notional.
detail: The single largest derivatives market by notional — over 500 trillion globally. A standard swap exchanges fixed coupons for SOFR-linked floating (or EURIBOR/SONIA/TONAR), reset quarterly. Used by corporates to convert fixed-rate debt into floating exposure (or vice versa), by banks to hedge mortgage portfolios, and by hedge funds to express rate views. Centrally cleared at LCH and CME post-2012 Dodd-Frank reforms.
plain: A deal where two parties trade their loan payments — one swaps a fixed interest amount for the other's changing rate.

snappy: Broker matches client orders internally rather than routing to public venues.
detail: Large brokers (Citadel Securities for retail flow, banks for institutional flow) internalise extensively. Saves exchange fees and avoids leaking client intent. Critics argue internalisation reduces transparency and price discovery; supporters note many trades happen at NBBO midpoint or better. SEC's Best Execution rules and FINRA Rule 5310 require brokers to demonstrate internalisation produces favourable customer outcomes.
plain: When a broker matches your buy order against another client's sell order inside their own books, skipping the public exchange.

snappy: Amount an option would be worth if exercised immediately — current price minus strike (for calls).
detail: A call with strike 100 when the stock is at 110 has intrinsic value of 10 dollars per share, regardless of time to expiry. Puts: strike minus stock price (if positive). Out-of-money options have zero intrinsic value. Option premium equals intrinsic plus time value. As expiry approaches, time value decays to zero, leaving only intrinsic.
plain: The portion of an option's price that comes from being already in profit — the obvious, immediate value.

snappy: Maker-taker fee model with the signs flipped — takers get rebates, makers pay fees.
detail: Used by smaller exchanges (BATS BY, NYSE National) to attract aggressive order flow. Counterintuitive: liquidity-providers pay to post, liquidity-takers earn to lift quotes. Works when the venue can attract enough aggressive order flow to offset the rebates. Strategic role in capturing 'taker-heavy' segments of the market. Operates alongside standard maker-taker venues.
plain: An exchange fee setup that pays you to take prices and charges you to post them — the reverse of the usual model.

snappy: Yield curve where short rates exceed long rates — historically a recession signal.
detail: Most-watched inversion: 10-year Treasury yield below 2-year. Has preceded every US recession in the past 50 years with one false positive (1966). The 10y-3m spread also tracked. Inversions in 2022-23 were the deepest since the early 1980s. Mechanism: when investors expect future rate cuts, they bid up long bonds, pushing their yields below short rates anchored by current Fed policy.
plain: When short-term loans pay more interest than long-term ones — historically a warning sign of recession.

snappy: High-yield currency on the receiving end of a carry trade.
detail: Typical EM investment currencies: BRL, MXN, ZAR, TRY (when rates are high), IDR. G10 investment currencies: AUD, NZD, GBP, USD (during hiking cycles). The investment currency receives the carry but takes the credit/currency risk. When EM crises hit (Russia 1998, Turkey 2018), investment currencies depreciate sharply, often more than the accumulated carry.
plain: The higher-paying currency that investors borrow into when chasing extra yield in a Carry Trade.

snappy: Bonds rated BBB- or higher — institutional-portfolio eligible.
detail: Moody's: Aaa, Aa, A, Baa. S&P/Fitch: AAA, AA, A, BBB. The IG-HY boundary at BBB-/Baa3 is the most consequential threshold in credit — many institutional mandates and pension funds can hold only IG. Downgrades into HY (becoming 'fallen angels') trigger forced selling. IG corporates spread roughly 100-200 bps over Treasury securities in calm markets; widens to 300-500 in crises.
plain: Bonds from companies and governments rated safe enough that pension funds and other big conservative investors are allowed to buy them.

snappy: Rate the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed — sets the ceiling of the policy corridor.
detail: Introduced in 2008 (originally as IOER for excess reserves) to give the Fed control over short rates without draining reserves. Since 2021 it's the headline 'administered rate' the FOMC sets alongside the fed funds target range. With reserves abundant (over 3 trillion), banks won't lend below IORB in the interbank market — making IORB the effective ceiling. Currently the headline number watched at each FOMC meeting.
plain: The interest rate the Federal Reserve pays banks for parking their spare cash overnight at the Fed.

snappy: Company's first sale of stock to public investors — moves from private to public ownership.
detail: Underwriters (typically a syndicate of investment banks) price the offering, distribute to clients, and support trading post-listing. Standard 'IPO discount' 5-15 percent to first-day trading price. Issuer pays gross spread (typically 7 percent) and faces lock-up restrictions (6-month sales prohibition for insiders). The 2020-21 IPO boom (over 1,000 US IPOs raising hundreds of billions) collapsed to a multi-year low by 2023.
plain: A company's first public sale of shares, when it moves from being privately owned to trading on a stock exchange.

snappy: Steel-making raw material — China-dominated demand drives global prices.
detail: Priced in dollars per dry tonne of 62 percent iron content (Platts IODEX). China imports roughly two-thirds of global seaborne supply. Top exporters: Australia (Rio Tinto, BHP) and Brazil (Vale). The 2019 Vale tailings dam collapse triggered a price spike above 200 dollars per tonne; collapsed below 100 in 2022 as Chinese property slowdown crushed steel demand. SGX-listed iron ore futures are the benchmark.
plain: The rock dug out of mines and shipped to mills to make steel — China buys most of the world's supply.
A contract where two parties agree to swap interest payments on a notional amount — usually fixed for floating.
snappy: Common shorthand for Interest Rate Swap — fixed-for-floating rate exchange contract.
detail: The most-traded derivative globally — over 400 trillion dollars in notional outstanding. Standard structure: one party pays a fixed rate, the other pays a floating reference rate (SOFR in dollars, ESTR in euros), both on the same notional amount. Used by corporations to lock funding costs, by pension funds to match liabilities, and by traders to express rate views. You'll hear 'IRS' constantly on rates desks and in clearinghouse reports.

plain: The global trade body that writes the standard contracts used for almost every privately negotiated Derivative trade.
snappy: Industry body governing OTC derivatives documentation and credit-event determinations.
detail: Founded 1985. Publishes the ISDA Master Agreement — the contract template used by nearly every bank, hedge fund, and corporate counterparty for over-the-counter derivatives. Runs the Credit Derivatives Determinations Committee that decides whether a credit event has occurred and triggers CDS payouts. Also defines standard market conventions, runs auctions, and lobbies regulators globally. You'll hear ISDA invoked in any derivatives default discussion or master-agreement negotiation.

snappy: Industry-standard bilateral contract governing OTC derivatives between two parties.
detail: Includes the main agreement, schedule (with party-specific elections), CSA (collateral), and confirmations (for each trade). First version 1992; current 2002 form. Provides netting (close-out under default), events of default, and termination provisions. Without an ISDA, OTC derivatives would face vast counterparty risk and operational chaos. Roughly 250,000 active ISDA Master Agreements globally.
plain: A standard contract used worldwide that lays out the rules between two parties trading complex Derivatives.
An option whose Strike Price is set favourably relative to the current Underlying price — exercising it today would already make money.
snappy: Option with strike favourable relative to the current underlying price.
detail: An ITM call has strike below current spot; an ITM put has strike above. ITM options carry intrinsic value (the immediate exercise payoff) plus time value. Deep ITM options behave almost like the underlying itself (delta near 100). Tax timing of ITM option exercises matters for individual traders. Listed exchanges automatically exercise expiring ITM options unless instructed otherwise.

snappy: European/Asian equivalent of CDX — Markit-administered CDS index family.
detail: iTraxx Europe (125 European IG names), iTraxx Crossover (75 European HY names), iTraxx Asia ex-Japan, iTraxx SovX (sovereign CDS). Composition rolls semiannually. Most-traded European credit benchmarks. iTraxx Crossover spreads are the European equivalent of CDX HY — gap dramatically in stress. Operated by Markit under LSEG since the 2014 IHS Markit (then LSEG) acquisition.
plain: A family of indexes that track how expensive it is to insure European companies' bonds against default.
A bond issued by Japan's government — about half of all of them are owned by the Bank of Japan itself.
snappy: Sovereign debt of Japan — second-largest government bond market after US Treasury securities.
detail: Roughly 1,200 trillion yen outstanding (about 8.5 trillion dollars equivalent). Maturities range from short bills out to 40 years. The BoJ owns roughly half the market following decades of QE and Yield Curve Control — a level of central-bank ownership unmatched globally. Yields stayed near zero from 2016 to 2024 before normalising as the BoJ exited negative rates. You'll hear JGBs cited in any conversation about global yields, the carry trade, or Japanese monetary policy.

snappy: USD-denominated emerging-market sovereign bond benchmark.
detail: Operated by JPMorgan. EMBI Global Diversified (with country weight caps) is the most-followed version. Roughly 70 countries. Heavy weights: Mexico, Indonesia, Turkey, Brazil, Argentina. Tracked by ishares JPM EMB ETF, multiple EM debt funds. Long-running multi-trillion benchmark. Country additions and removals on issuance and credit-rating thresholds.
plain: A scoreboard tracking how dollar-denominated bonds from developing countries' governments are performing.

snappy: Local-currency emerging-market sovereign bond benchmark.
detail: Tracks local-currency sovereign debt (BRL, MXN, IDR, etc.). Different risk profile than hard-currency EMBI: FX exposure dominates, lower credit risk. GBI-EM Global Diversified has country weight caps. Roughly 20 countries. Tracked by VanEck JPM Local Currency EM (EMLC). Local-currency EM has grown substantially as EM governments build domestic capital markets.
plain: A scoreboard tracking how developing countries' government bonds perform when issued in their own local currency.

snappy: Model adding sudden price jumps to standard diffusion — captures fat-tail returns.
detail: Robert Merton's 1976 model. Stock price follows geometric Brownian motion plus a Poisson jump process. Captures crash risk that Black-Scholes misses. Out-of-the-Money option prices in jump-diffusion models are higher than Black-Scholes, matching observed market smiles. Popular in credit modelling (sudden defaults) and FX (currency crisis jumps). Calibration is also more involved than for pure diffusion — extra parameters control how often jumps happen and how large they are.
plain: A pricing model that adds sudden, unexpected price jumps to the usual smooth random walk — captures crash risk better.

snappy: Barrier feature — option only activates if the underlying touches a specified level.
detail: A down-and-in put activates only if the stock falls to a trigger level. Buyer pays less upfront because there's a chance the barrier is never hit and the option expires worthless. Common in retail structured notes ('memory autocallable with KI') — investor sells a knock-in put implicitly. The 2008 collapse triggered massive KI activations as equities plunged through barriers en masse.
plain: An option that only switches on if the price hits a chosen level — the buyer pays less for it because it might never become active.

snappy: Barrier feature — option terminates if the underlying touches a specified level.
detail: An up-and-out call extinguishes if the stock rallies above a ceiling. Holder gets normal call payoff up to the KO level, nothing if breached. Cheaper than vanilla calls because the upside is capped. Used in cost-reducing hedges and structured notes. The barrier creates pin risk and gap-risk near the level — Market Makers struggle to hedge KO options as the underlying approaches the trigger.
plain: A trigger feature that automatically extinguishes a derivative contract if the price hits a chosen level.

snappy: FX dealer's right to reject a quoted trade in the milliseconds before execution.
detail: Standard practice in OTC FX. Dealer commits to a quote, sees the incoming order, has milliseconds to decide whether to execute or reject (typically rejecting if market has moved against the quote). Controversial because it asymmetrically benefits dealers. Buy-side traders watch reject rates as an execution-quality metric. The FX Global Code (2017) imposed transparency rules but didn't ban last-look.
plain: An FX dealer's right to peek at an incoming trade for a few milliseconds and reject it if the market has moved against them.

snappy: Time delay between an event (price tick, news release) and a system's response.
detail: Measured in microseconds and nanoseconds in HFT. Sources of latency: physical distance (light-speed limit), network hops, processing time, exchange matching engines. Co-location facilities reduce latency by placing trader servers next to exchange match engines. Microwave radio links between major financial centres (NYC-Chicago, London-Frankfurt) are faster than fibre — significant infrastructure investment for HFT firms.
plain: The tiny time gap between something happening and a computer reacting — measured in millionths of a second for fast traders.

snappy: Profit strategy exploiting microsecond price differences across venues.
detail: Example: SPY ETF on NYSE Arca shows new price; the AMEX-listed alternative still has old price for 100 microseconds. Latency arbitrageurs trade the slow side at the obsolete price. IEX's 350-microsecond speedbump explicitly aims to neutralise latency-arb. Critics argue lat arb tax retail traders; defenders argue it tightens prices across venues. The Michael Lewis 'Flash Boys' book centred on lat-arb practices.
plain: A trading strategy that profits from being faster than rivals at spotting and exploiting tiny price gaps across exchanges.

snappy: Form of spoofing — placing multiple orders on one side of the book to create false depth.
detail: Trader places visible orders to make a stock look heavily bid (or offered), inducing other traders to react, then cancels and trades the opposite direction. The 2014 Coscia case was the first US criminal conviction for layering. Major banks have settled layering cases across spot FX, precious metals, Treasury securities. Surveillance algorithms now detect layering patterns automatically across asset classes.
plain: An illegal trick where someone places fake orders to mislead other traders about supply or demand, then cancels and trades the other way.
When investors buy a whole company mostly using borrowed money, then use the company's own cash flow to pay back the loan.
snappy: Acquisition financed mostly with borrowed money — debt secured against the target's assets and cash flow.
detail: Typical structure: 30 percent equity, 70 percent debt (term loans, high-yield bonds, mezzanine). Sponsor (private equity firm) provides the equity slice. Returns come from operational improvements, multiple expansion at exit, and debt paydown. Famous LBOs: KKR's RJR Nabisco (1988), Dell (2013), Twitter (2022). The 1980s LBO boom invented modern private equity. You'll hear about LBOs every time a PE firm announces a take-private deal.

snappy: Bank must hold high-quality liquid assets covering 30 days of net cash outflows in stress.
detail: Basel III minimum 100 percent. HQLA includes Treasury securities, central-bank reserves, and other government bonds. Stressed outflow assumptions: retail deposit run-offs (5-10 percent), wholesale funding rollovers, derivatives margin calls, contingent liabilities. Daily monitoring at most banks. Designed to prevent the 30-day liquidity crisis that contributed to 2008 failures (Lehman, Bear Stearns, Northern Rock).
plain: A rule forcing banks to hold enough safe, easy-to-sell assets to survive a month of customers pulling their money out.

snappy: Central bank's role providing emergency liquidity to solvent but illiquid institutions.
detail: Walter Bagehot's classic 1873 principle: lend freely at high rate against good collateral. Fed used LLR during 2008 (Bear Stearns rescue, Lehman didn't qualify), 2020 (PMCCF, MMLF), 2023 (Bank Term Funding Program). Includes Discount Window for routine emergencies. ECB's various refinancing operations serve similar role. The fundamental backstop preventing solvent-bank runs from collapsing the system.
plain: The central bank's role as emergency funder — lending to healthy banks when no one else will, to prevent panic.

snappy: Borrowed money used to amplify investment returns or business returns.
detail: Financial leverage (corporate debt to equity), operational leverage (fixed costs as percentage of total). 2x leverage doubles returns but also doubles losses. Banks operate at 10x leverage typical (Tier 1 ratio inverse). Hedge funds at 3-5x. The 2008 crisis exposed dangers of high financial leverage — Lehman ran at 30x. Modern Basel rules cap bank leverage explicitly.
plain: Borrowing money to make bigger bets — multiplies winnings if you are right but also multiplies losses if you are wrong.

snappy: Tier 1 capital divided by total bank assets (unrisk-weighted) — backstop to RWA-based ratios.
detail: Basel III minimum 3 percent. US Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) 5 percent for G-SIBs. Captures off-balance-sheet exposures (derivatives, lending commitments) at notional. Designed as a non-risk-sensitive backstop in case banks game RWA calculations. The 2021 SLR Treasury exemption expired, pressuring bank balance sheets and Treasury market intermediation capacity.
plain: A simple safety check on a bank — its safety capital as a fraction of all its assets, ignoring fancy risk weighting.

snappy: Percentage of exposure lost when an obligor defaults — equals 100 percent minus recovery rate.
detail: Bank credit-risk models combine three numbers: probability of default (PD), exposure at default (EAD), and LGD. Expected loss equals PD times LGD times EAD. Basel regulatory capital uses these inputs. LGD varies by seniority, collateral, jurisdiction, and economic cycle — recession LGD runs higher than normal. Senior secured LGD typically 30-40 percent; unsecured 50-70 percent.
plain: How much of a loan a lender actually loses when a borrower fails to pay back — usually expressed as a percentage.

snappy: Obligation a person or company owes to another party.
detail: Categories: current liabilities (due within 12 months), long-term liabilities (mortgages, multi-year debt). Bank liabilities are mostly deposits (customer money owed back). For corporates: accounts payable, accrued expenses, long-term debt, deferred tax liabilities. The balance-sheet identity: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Pension obligations are a major hidden liability for many corporates and governments.
plain: Money a person, company, or bank owes to someone else — the opposite side of the balance sheet from what they own.

snappy: Discontinued benchmark — once the world's most-used reference rate for trillions in contracts.
detail: Published in five currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CHF) and multiple tenors by the IBA. After the 2012 manipulation scandal exposed banks colluding on submissions, regulators forced replacement: most LIBOR settings ceased end-2021, and the final USD tenors stopped in June 2023. Legacy LIBOR contracts with no clear fallback got 'synthetic LIBOR' until 2024. Now historical only.
plain: An old worldwide reference interest rate that was retired in 2023 after a manipulation scandal — now replaced by newer benchmarks.

snappy: Order to buy at or below a specified price, or sell at or above — won't fill at worse prices.
detail: Adds liquidity to the order book. Won't execute if the limit price isn't reached. Used by patient traders, market-makers (passive quotes), and execution algos. Day-trader-popular for entry/exit at specific levels. The complement to market orders (which take liquidity). Most retail order types behind the scenes are limit orders, even when entered as 'market' (broker adds protective limits).
plain: An instruction to only buy below a set price, or only sell above one — protects you from paying more than you intended.

snappy: Ease with which an asset can be bought or sold without affecting its price.
detail: Highly liquid: cash, Treasury securities, large-cap stocks. Less liquid: corporate bonds, emerging-market equities, real estate, private equity stakes. Two flavours: market liquidity (can you trade now?) and funding liquidity (can you borrow against the asset?). Liquidity disappears in crises — 2008 commercial paper markets, March 2020 Treasury markets briefly. Bank Liquidity Coverage Ratio aims to ensure short-term funding resilience.
plain: How easily something can be sold for cash without dropping its price — a house is hard to sell quickly; Apple shares are not.

snappy: Risk that an institution cannot meet payment obligations as they fall due.
detail: Distinct from solvency risk (insufficient assets to cover liabilities). Liquidity risk caused multiple 2008 failures (Bear Stearns, Lehman) and 2023 SVB — institutions had assets but couldn't convert them to cash fast enough. Mitigations: LCR requirement, NSFR requirement, contingent funding plans. Market liquidity risk versus funding liquidity risk are related but distinct concepts. Treasury market liquidity stress periodic.
plain: The danger that you cannot raise cash fast enough to pay bills — even if you own valuable things that just cannot be sold quickly.

snappy: Algo that aggressively hunts for hidden liquidity across venues.
detail: Probes dark pools and reserve orders with small IOC orders to find blocks of latent demand. Used by traders confident in their direction who want to fill quickly with minimal market signalling. Less price-sensitive than VWAP/POV algos. Critics refer to them as 'sniper algos' for their predatory feel toward unsuspecting passive liquidity. Standard in modern algo toolkits — most major brokers offer some flavour.
plain: A computer program that hunts across multiple venues to fill a big order quickly without showing its hand to the market.

snappy: Trading venue with publicly displayed quotes — opposite of dark pool.
detail: NYSE, Nasdaq, NYSE Arca, BATS, IEX, CHX are the major US lit exchanges. Contribute to price discovery via visible order book. Required to publish quotes in real-time to SIPs. Make money from trading fees and market-data fees. Reg NMS protects displayed quotes at lit venues from trade-throughs by routing orders to the best price.
plain: A public stock exchange where everyone can see the buy and sell prices on offer — the opposite of a hidden Dark Pool.

snappy: Critical battery metal — boomed and busted with EV cycle.
detail: Two main sources: hard-rock spodumene (Australia) and brine evaporation (Chile, Argentina, China). Lithium carbonate prices peaked above 80,000 dollars per tonne in late 2022 as EV demand outran supply; collapsed below 12,000 by 2024 as new supply came online and EV growth slowed.
