Pricing increasingly transparent via Fastmarkets and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence indexes. Long-term demand outlook depends on EV adoption pace.
plain: The metal at the heart of every modern battery — prices boomed and busted with the rise of electric cars.

snappy: Beef-cattle futures — feedlot animals ready for slaughter.
detail: CME-listed live cattle futures (/LE). Companion contract: feeder cattle (younger animals headed to feedlots). US beef supply chain: cow-calf operations, feedlots, packers (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef control roughly 85 percent of US packing). Cyclical multi-year herd-rebuilding patterns. Lean Hogs (/HE) is the pork counterpart. African Swine Fever epidemic in China (2018-19) wiped out roughly half of Chinese hog herd, reshaping global protein trade.
plain: Beef cattle ready for slaughter, traded as futures contracts so ranchers and meatpackers can lock in prices ahead of time.

snappy: Bank's plan for how it could be resolved without disrupting financial stability or requiring bailout.
detail: Required by Dodd-Frank for largest US banks; EU equivalent under BRRD. Annual or biennial submission to regulators. Details: organisational structure, critical functions, resolution strategy (single-point-of-entry vs multi-point), contingency funding. Confidential to regulators but disclosed summaries public. Several US bank submissions deemed deficient by Fed and FDIC in recent years.
plain: A bank's written plan, filed with regulators, explaining how it could be safely wound down if it ran into trouble.

snappy: Global benchmark exchange for base metals — aluminium, copper, nickel, zinc, lead, tin.
detail: Founded 1877. Owned by Hong Kong Exchanges (HKEX) since 2012. Unique 'date structure' — contracts for every business day out to three months, then monthly out to multi-year tenors. Three-month rolling contracts are the standard benchmark. Physical delivery from LME-registered warehouses globally. Battered reputation post-2022 nickel cancellation; reforms ongoing.
plain: London's century-old exchange that sets benchmark prices for industrial metals like copper, aluminium, zinc, and nickel.

snappy: Natural gas chilled to liquid form for transport by sea — turned global the gas market.
detail: Cooled to minus 162 degrees Celsius, volume shrinks 600x for shipping. US went from net LNG importer in 2010 to largest LNG exporter by 2023. Cheniere's Sabine Pass led the US LNG export boom; QatarEnergy and Australia are major peers. Spot pricing benchmarks: JKM (Asia), TTF (Europe), Henry Hub (US). The 2022 European gas crisis drove TTF to 350 EUR/MWh, roughly 10x normal.
plain: Natural gas cooled into liquid form so it can be shipped across oceans — turned a regional gas market into a global one.

snappy: Sovereign debt issued in the issuer's own currency — investor takes FX risk.
detail: Brazil's BRL bonds, Mexico's MXN bonds, Indonesia's IDR bonds. The issuer faces no currency mismatch (revenues match debt). The international investor bears FX depreciation risk and gets paid higher yields for it. The JPMorgan GBI-EM index tracks local-currency EM sovereign debt. Increasingly the larger share of EM sovereign issuance as governments build local capital markets.
plain: A country's own money — the currency it spends and collects taxes in, and the one it usually borrows in domestically.

snappy: Vol model where instantaneous volatility is a deterministic function of underlying price and time.
detail: Published 1994 by Bruno Dupire. Calibrates exactly to any observed vol surface by construction — solves the inverse problem from market option prices. Used widely for pricing path-dependent derivatives (barriers, lookbacks) where exact vol-surface fit matters. Criticised for unrealistic forward vol dynamics — local vol typically forecasts the smile to flatten over time, which doesn't match real-world behaviour.
plain: A pricing model where market jumpiness depends on price and time, fitted to exactly match observed option prices.
A period after a company's IPO during which insiders and early investors aren't allowed to sell their stocks — usually 90 to 180 days.
snappy: Post-IPO restriction preventing insiders from selling shares for a set period.
detail: Typically 90 to 180 days, agreed between the company and its underwriters. Designed to prevent founders and pre-IPO investors from dumping shares on day-one buyers and crashing the price. Lock-up expiry dates are watched closely — the days when insiders can finally sell often produce noticeable selling pressure. Direct listings sometimes skip lock-ups entirely. You'll hear 'lock-up expiry' flagged in research notes around IPO three-month and six-month anniversaries.

snappy: Holding an asset with expectation of price appreciation.
detail: The opposite of short. 'Going long' means buying. Long-only funds (most mutual funds, pension funds) only take long positions. Long-short funds combine both. Long exposure determines economic interest — even via derivatives or synthetic positions. Net long exposure is total long minus total short across a portfolio.
plain: Owning something with the hope its price goes up — the everyday way of investing.

snappy: Option whose payoff depends on the most favourable price reached over the contract life.
detail: Fixed-strike lookback call pays the maximum stock price minus strike. Floating-strike lookback pays the final price minus the minimum observed. Eliminates regret — holder buys at the lowest and sells at the highest. Expensive premiums reflect that desirable feature. Rare in vanilla markets; common in structured notes targeting retail or wealth-management investors who like the 'no regret' narrative.
plain: An option that pays out based on the best possible price reached during its life, removing the regret of bad timing.

snappy: 1987 follow-up to the Plaza Accord — G7 agreed the dollar's decline had gone far enough.
detail: Signed February 1987 at the Louvre in Paris. Aimed to stabilise the dollar around levels reached after Plaza. Mostly unsuccessful: intervention couldn't fully counter capital flows, and the October 1987 stock crash followed (some commentators link the two via the Accord's restrictive interest-rate dynamics). Marked the high-water mark of post-Bretton Woods coordinated G7 FX management.
plain: A 1987 deal where the major rich countries agreed the US dollar had fallen far enough and tried to stabilise it.

snappy: US institutional leveraged-loan benchmark — covers most syndicated bank loans.
detail: Operated by Morningstar/PitchBook in partnership with the Loan Syndications and Trading Association. Roughly 1.4 trillion dollar market. Tracks performance, default rates, recovery rates. Distinct from HY bonds: loans are senior-secured (higher recovery), floating-rate (lower duration). CLO universe references the LSTA index. Default rates spiked to 6 percent in 2020, recovered to under 2 percent post-pandemic.
plain: A scoreboard tracking how loans to risky US companies perform — the loan-market cousin of the high-yield bond index.
Famous hedge fund that nearly collapsed the financial system in 1998 when its highly leveraged bond bets all moved against it at once.
snappy: 1998 hedge-fund collapse — Nobel-laureate-led firm with extreme leverage on convergence trades.
detail: Founded 1994 by John Meriwether with Nobel-winning economists Robert Merton and Myron Scholes on the team. Ran convergence trades (long off-the-run Treasury securities, short on-the-run, etc.) at leverage above 25-to-1. The August 1998 Russian default caused correlated losses across positions; the fund lost 4.6 billion in four months. Fed-orchestrated rescue by 14 banks. Standard case study in tail risk, leverage, and crowded trades.

plain: US rules that pause trading in a single stock for five minutes if its price swings too far too fast — a single-stock breather.
snappy: Single-stock circuit breaker — halts trading if price moves outside dynamic bands.
detail: Adopted by US equity markets in 2012 after the May 2010 Flash Crash. Sets price bands (typically 5-10 percent around a rolling reference price) above and below which trading pauses for 5-15 minutes. Distinct from market-wide circuit breakers, which halt all US trading on a big S&P 500 drop. Used heavily in volatile small-caps during meme-stock episodes and unexpected news. You'll see LULD halts mentioned on day-trading platforms and on CNBC's ticker.

snappy: Corporate transactions combining or acquiring companies.
detail: Strategic acquisitions (buyer absorbs target into operations), financial acquisitions (LBOs, private equity buyouts), mergers of equals. Global M&A volume varies dramatically with interest-rate and macro conditions: 2021 record 5 trillion, 2023 sub-3 trillion. Heavily regulated for antitrust (DOJ, FTC, European Commission) and securities laws. Activist investors increasingly drive M&A activity.
plain: Companies merging together or buying each other — common for growth, market entry, or eliminating competition.

snappy: Currency pair involving USD and one of the other most-traded currencies.
detail: The seven majors: EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD, NZD/USD. EUR/USD alone is roughly a quarter of global FX turnover. Majors have the tightest spreads, deepest liquidity, and 24-hour pricing during the trading week. Cross pairs and exotic pairs trade at wider spreads with thinner liquidity.
plain: A heavily-traded currency pairing involving the US dollar — like euro-dollar or dollar-yen. Tight spreads, deep liquidity, round-the-clock pricing.

snappy: Exchange fee structure where liquidity providers (makers) get rebates and takers pay fees.
detail: Standard in US equity, futures, and options. Typical: maker rebate 20-30 cents per 100 shares; taker fee 30 cents. Inverted-pricing venues (BATS Y, NYSE National) reverse this. The economics drive HFT market-making strategies. Critics argue maker-taker creates conflicts in broker order-routing decisions. SEC pilot programs have studied effects of fee changes on liquidity provision.
plain: Exchange fee plan that pays you a small rebate for posting prices and charges you a fee for taking someone else's.

snappy: Borrowed money used to buy securities; collateral posted against trading positions.
detail: Two contexts: margin loans (broker lends, security as collateral) and derivative margin (collateral posted with clearing house). Margin lending: Fed's Regulation T limits initial margin to 50 percent for equity. Variation margin: daily settlement of P&L on derivatives. Initial margin: prudential buffer at trade inception. Margin calls force position liquidation if collateral runs short.
plain: Money you deposit upfront when you borrow to invest or trade — collateral your broker can grab if your bets sour.

snappy: Daily revaluation of a position at current market prices — produces unrealised P&L.
detail: Standard for futures, cleared swaps, and most bilateral derivatives under CSAs. Daily MTM moves drive variation margin calls. Held-for-trading accounting (FAS 157, IFRS 13) requires MTM for derivative positions on balance sheets. Banks and broker-dealers MTM all trading-book derivatives daily. Distinct from mark-to-model, where complex products use modelled prices when market quotes don't exist.
plain: Updating the value of an investment to today's market price every day, so gains and losses are visible immediately.

snappy: Adverse price movement caused by a large trade's own activity.
detail: Empirically, impact scales roughly with the square root of order size relative to daily volume. Temporary impact reverses (price snaps back after the trade); permanent impact reflects information leakage. Pre-trade impact estimates inform algo selection and order sizing. Buy-side TCA (transaction cost analysis) measures realised impact versus pre-trade forecasts to evaluate algo and broker performance.
plain: When your own large order pushes the price against you — buying a lot drives the price up, selling a lot drives it down.

snappy: Firm continuously quoting two-way prices in a security — provides liquidity for a small spread.
detail: Citadel Securities, Virtu, Susquehanna, Jane Street are major equity market-makers. Bank desks make markets in fixed-income, FX, and OTC derivatives. Profitability: capture half-spread on trades, plus exchange rebates (maker rebates in maker-taker fee schedules). Risk: inventory accumulation, adverse selection (informed traders consistently pick off market-makers). Required liquidity providers in many designated-market-maker arrangements.
plain: A firm that constantly offers to buy or sell a security, earning a small margin on each trade and keeping markets liquid.

snappy: Order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price.
detail: Crosses the spread, takes liquidity. Fills at NBBO (or worse if the order is large enough to walk the book). Fast and certain execution but can produce surprising fills in thin markets — Knight Capital's 2012 algo bug placed billions in market orders, draining the book and bankrupting the firm. Modern brokers convert market orders into protected limit orders to prevent egregious fills.
plain: An instruction to buy or sell right now at whatever price is currently available — fast, but you can get a surprising price.

snappy: Stochastic process whose expected future value equals its current value.
detail: Foundational concept in derivative pricing. Under the right probability measure (risk-neutral measure), discounted asset prices are martingales — no arbitrage exists. Pricing a derivative reduces to computing the expected discounted payoff under the martingale measure. Martingale theory underpins the entire mathematical framework of modern finance, from Black-Scholes to forward measures used in interest-rate modelling.
plain: A mathematical idea where, on average, tomorrow's price is just today's price — the foundation for fair pricing of contracts.

snappy: Date a bond's principal is repaid — the end of the loan.
detail: Bonds are classified by time to maturity: bills (one year or less), notes (2-10 years), bonds (over 10 years), and perpetuals (no fixed maturity). Maturity drives a bond's sensitivity to rates — longer maturity, more duration, bigger price swings. 'Bullet maturity' means principal is repaid in one lump at the end; amortising bonds repay over the life. Maturities cluster around standard tenors for liquidity reasons.
plain: The end date of a loan or bond when the borrower must repay what they originally borrowed.

snappy: Worst peak-to-trough loss observed over a portfolio's history.
detail: Common headline risk metric for hedge funds and asset managers. S&P 500 maximum drawdown: 86 percent (Great Depression), 57 percent (2007-09), 34 percent (March 2020). Recovery time after maximum drawdown often longer than the drawdown itself. Used in performance evaluation: high Sharpe Ratio with low max DD is the holy grail. Calmar ratio = annualised return divided by max DD.
plain: The worst loss a portfolio ever suffered between its peak and the following low — a headline measure of pain.

snappy: Bond backed by a pool of residential or commercial mortgages.
detail: Holders receive monthly principal and interest from the underlying mortgages. Three sources of cash flow uncertainty: prepayments (homeowners refinancing or moving), defaults, and curtailments. The US MBS market is roughly 12 trillion outstanding — second only to Treasury securities in size. Agency MBS (guaranteed by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae) is most of it; private-label MBS shrank dramatically post-2008.
plain: An investment where thousands of home loans are bundled together, and investors earn the monthly mortgage payments homeowners make.

snappy: Tendency of prices to return to a long-run average — opposite of trend following.
detail: Persistent in short-term equity returns and FX. Long-term valuation metrics (P/E, P/B) mean revert over decades. Used in pairs trading, low-volatility strategies, contrarian investing. The 1990s convergence trades (LTCM, Salomon) bet on mean reversion of credit spreads — devastatingly when reversion took too long. Asymmetric: mean reversion in calm markets, momentum in stress.
plain: The idea that prices stretched far from their long-run average tend to snap back toward it eventually.

snappy: Combination of two companies into one — both entities cease to exist, new entity emerges.
detail: Distinguished from acquisitions where one company absorbs the other. Stock-for-stock mergers exchange shares; cash mergers buy out the target. Significant 21st-century mergers: ExxonMobil (1999), DaimlerChrysler (1998, failed), United-Continental Airlines (2010), Vodafone-Mannesmann (2000). Antitrust scrutiny intense — Microsoft-Activision deal took 18 months to close (2022-23).
plain: Two companies combining into one new company — neither survives on its own, a third name often emerges.

snappy: Middle-of-the-stack slice — pays after senior, before equity.
detail: Typically rated BBB to single-B depending on subordination. Yields the spread differential between AAA senior and equity. Hedge funds, insurance companies, and dedicated mezz funds buy it. The 2008 crisis taught that mezz tranches in mortgage CDOs could go from BBB to zero within months — credit ratings dramatically understated the tail risk. Modern CLO mezz holds up better due to tighter underwriting and less correlated underlying loans.
plain: A middle-risk slice of a bundled-loan deal — paid after the safest slice but before the riskiest equity slice.

full: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II
snappy: EU's sweeping 2018 markets regulation — investor protection, transparency, market structure.
detail: Together with sister regulation MiFIR. Key provisions: research-payment unbundling, broader best-execution rules, pre/post-trade transparency, trade reporting, OTF and SI trading-venue categories, position-limits regime, product-governance rules, inducement disclosures. Heavily reshaped European market structure. UK retained MiFID II after Brexit but is diverging on some details.
plain: Europe's sweeping 2018 markets rulebook — covers everything from research payments to trade transparency.

snappy: Sister regulation to MiFID II — directly applicable across EU without national transposition.
detail: Covers transaction-reporting requirements, trading-venue rules, post-trade transparency. Implemented same date as MiFID II (January 2018). The MiFIR Review proposed in 2021 aims to simplify the consolidated tape, transparency provisions, and pre-trade rules. Currently in legislative finalisation. UK MiFIR diverges post-Brexit on some details, including small-cap exemptions and bond-transparency rules.
plain: Sister rulebook to MiFID II — applies directly across the EU and handles reporting, transparency, and venue rules.

snappy: Information not yet public that a reasonable investor would consider important — basis of insider-trading rules.
detail: Trading on MNPI is insider trading under SEC Rule 10b-5. The 'mosaic theory' allows synthesis of public information into proprietary analysis without crossing the MNPI line. SEC and DOJ enforce aggressively — Galleon's Raj Rajaratnam (2011, convicted), Steven Cohen's SAC Capital (2013 settlement), and many smaller cases. Compliance walls, restricted lists, and trading-supervision systems are core MNPI controls at investment firms.
plain: Private company information important enough to move the stock price — trading on it is illegal insider trading.

snappy: Risk of loss from using inaccurate or inappropriate financial models.
detail: Models are simplifications. Black-Scholes assumes constant volatility — markets show vol smile. Copula models for mortgage CDOs missed correlation breakdowns. The 1998 LTCM crisis and 2008 mortgage debacle were partly model risk. Fed SR 11-7 letter (2011) mandates US bank model risk management: independent validation, ongoing performance monitoring, governance. CRO functions take model risk seriously post-crisis.
plain: Risk of losing money because the maths model you used to value or hedge something was wrong or oversimplified.

snappy: Strategy buying past winners and selling past losers — exploits persistent return patterns.
detail: Jegadeesh-Titman (1993) found momentum factor robust in equity markets. CTAs systematically trend-follow across futures markets. Long-run momentum returns: 8-10 percent annualised, low correlation to stocks/bonds. Spectacular drawdowns when trends reverse: 2009 momentum crash, 2020 March pandemic flip. Counterintuitive to value investors — but documented in 200+ academic papers across asset classes.
plain: Strategy that bets winners keep winning and losers keep losing — buy what's been going up, sell what's been going down.
A fund that pools cash and parks it in super-short safe investments like Treasury bills — the closest thing to a Bank account that pays Interest.
snappy: Mutual fund investing in very short-term debt — a near-cash parking spot for institutional and retail investors.
detail: Roughly 6 trillion dollars in US money fund assets (2024). Two types: government MMFs (T-bills, repo) and prime MMFs (commercial paper, bank CDs). Government MMFs ballooned after 2016 SEC reforms made prime funds less retail-friendly. Yield closely tracks the fed funds rate. The 2008 Reserve Primary Fund 'breaking the buck' (NAV below 1 dollar) prompted reforms. Critical plumbing for short-term funding markets.

snappy: Relationship between an option's strike and the underlying's current price.
detail: Categories: deep ITM, ITM, ATM, OTM, deep OTM. Quantitative moneyness: K/S (strike over spot) or ln(K/S). Vol surfaces are quoted by moneyness — at fixed-strike points (25-delta, 50-delta, etc.) rather than fixed prices, so the smile shape persists as the underlying moves. Important concept for any option-pricing or strategy discussion.
plain: How close an option's Strike Price is to where the underlying is trading right now — affects how much the option is worth.
A way of estimating an answer by simulating thousands of random scenarios and averaging the results.
snappy: Simulation method — generate many random paths, average their outcomes to price or measure risk.
detail: The workhorse for pricing exotic options where closed-form formulas don't exist — path-dependent payoffs, multi-asset baskets, basket Asians. Also used for VaR, counterparty credit risk, and stress testing. Quality depends on the random number generator, the number of paths (10k–1M typical), and variance-reduction techniques (antithetic, control variates, importance sampling). Named after the casino — gambling and probability.

snappy: Numerical method that prices derivatives by simulating thousands of possible underlying paths.
detail: Generate many random paths consistent with the model dynamics, calculate the derivative's payoff on each, average to get the price. Indispensable for path-dependent options (Asians, barriers, lookbacks) where no closed form exists. Variance-reduction techniques (antithetic variates, control variates, importance sampling) speed up convergence. GPUs and quasi-random sequences (Sobol) make Monte Carlo tractable for production pricing.
plain: Pricing method that runs thousands of random paths for a price, then averages the payoffs to estimate fair value.

full: Minimum Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities
snappy: EU resolution-funding requirement — equivalent of TLAC but extends beyond G-SIBs.
detail: Single Resolution Board sets MREL targets bank-by-bank. Loss-absorbing layer above operating-company senior debt. Substantial issuance forecast across EU banks 2025-2030. Combined with EU bail-in tool, designed to make resolution credible without state aid. Notable test in 2023 Credit Suisse case — though Switzerland used a state-supported merger rather than full MREL resolution.
plain: EU rule that forces banks to keep enough loss-absorbing capital and debt to be wound down without taxpayer money.

snappy: Developed markets ex-US and Canada — Europe, Australasia, Far East.
detail: 21 developed countries. Japan, UK, France, Germany top weights. Heavily used as international-equity benchmark for US pension funds and asset managers. Tracked by ishares MSCI EAFE ETF (EFA). Persistent EAFE-US performance gap since 2010 reflects US tech dominance — EAFE returns roughly half those of US equities over the past decade.
plain: Stock-market benchmark covering developed countries outside the US and Canada — Europe, Australia, Japan, and similar.

snappy: 24 emerging-market countries — the global EM equity benchmark.
detail: 1,400-plus constituents. China, India, Taiwan, Korea, Brazil top weights — China's weight has grown then shrunk in recent years. South Korea and Taiwan technically developed by World Bank standards but classed as EM by MSCI for years (relatively unique classification). Tracked by ishares MSCI EM ETF (EEM), Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets (VWO). Multi-trillion in indexed flows.
plain: Benchmark tracking large companies across 24 emerging economies — China, India, Brazil, Taiwan, and Korea dominate.

snappy: 23 developed-market countries, large- and mid-cap stocks — the global DM equity benchmark.
detail: 1,500-plus constituents. US makes up over 70 percent (its share has grown over the decade). Japan, UK, France, Germany next largest. Methodology: free-float-adjusted market-cap weighting. Underlies trillions in passive and benchmark-linked assets. MSCI ACWI adds EM countries; MSCI EAFE excludes US/Canada (heavy in pension benchmarks).
plain: Benchmark covering large companies across 23 wealthy developed countries — the global blue-chip index.

snappy: European equivalent of US Alternative Trading Systems — non-exchange trading venues.
detail: Cboe Europe, Aquis Exchange, Turquoise are major MTFs. Same regulatory category as RM (regulated market, i.e. exchange) under MiFID II but with lighter listing requirements. MTFs handle roughly 35 percent of European equity trading volume. The post-Brexit split between EU MTFs and UK MTFs fragmented liquidity further — many securities now trade in multiple jurisdictions.
plain: European trading venue that competes with traditional exchanges — like the EU equivalent of Nasdaq versus NYSE in the US.

snappy: Pooled investment vehicle collecting money from many investors to buy a diversified portfolio.
detail: Two main types: open-end (issue/redeem shares at NAV daily) and closed-end (fixed share count, trades on exchange). US mutual fund industry: 25-plus trillion in assets. Vanguard, Fidelity, BlackRock are largest managers. Subject to Investment Company Act of 1940 disclosure and conduct rules. ETFs (1990s onward) have stolen market share from mutual funds for cost and tax-efficiency reasons.
plain: An investment pool where many people invest money together, and a manager buys a mix of stocks or bonds on everyone's behalf.

snappy: Theoretical unemployment rate below which inflation accelerates.
detail: Pre-2010 estimates place US NAIRU around 5-6 percent. The 2014-2019 period of falling unemployment to 3.5 percent without inflation pressure forced economists to revise NAIRU downward dramatically — to 4 percent or lower. The 2021-22 inflation episode revived debates about how reliable NAIRU estimates are. Central banks use NAIRU implicitly in reaction functions; estimates are policy-dependent.
plain: The lowest unemployment rate economists think the economy can run at before wages and prices start rising too fast.

snappy: Market-cap-weighted index of all 3,000+ Nasdaq-listed stocks.
detail: Heavy tech tilt — Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Nvidia together comprise over 30 percent. Launched 1971. Survived massive 78 percent decline in 2000-2002 dot-com crash. Crossed 20,000 for the first time December 2024. Tracked by Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ ETF, technically tracks Nasdaq-100, not Composite). Distinct from Nasdaq stock exchange itself.
plain: A US stock-market index covering every company listed on Nasdaq — heavily weighted toward big tech names.

snappy: Largest 100 non-financial Nasdaq-listed stocks by market cap.
detail: Subset of Nasdaq Composite excluding financials. Highly tech-heavy: top six tech names approach 40 percent weight. Tracked by Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ ETF), one of the most-traded ETFs globally. Quarterly rebalances; annual reconstitution. Underlies Nasdaq-100 futures (/NQ) on CME and Nasdaq-100 options. The S&P 500's tech-heavy alternative.
plain: Index of the 100 largest non-bank Nasdaq companies — extremely tech-heavy. Tracked by the popular QQQ fund.

snappy: Hydrocarbon fuel used for power generation, heating, industry, and as petrochemical feedstock.
detail: Priced in dollars per million BTU (MMBtu). US natural gas peaked around 13 dollars per MMBtu in 2008, crashed below 2 dollars in 2020, surged above 9 in 2022, sat around 2 in 2024. Heavily seasonal demand drives winter price spikes. The US shale boom turned the US from net importer to net exporter (via LNG). Storage levels reported weekly by EIA.
plain: Fossil fuel used to generate electricity, heat homes, and feed chemical plants — prices swing hard with winter weather.
The per-share value of a fund — its assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding. Mutual funds price at NAV daily.
snappy: Per-share value of a fund's assets minus liabilities — the price at which open-end funds transact.
detail: Mutual funds strike NAV once per day at 4 PM Eastern using closing prices; ETFs trade throughout the day at prices that bob around NAV. Closed-end funds trade at significant premiums or discounts to NAV. Hedge funds calculate NAV monthly or quarterly with fair-value adjustments. NAV is the official accounting value — what investors get when they subscribe or redeem. You'll hear it in every fund report and capital flows discussion.

snappy: Highest bid and lowest offer across all US equity venues — the consolidated 'top of book'.
detail: Established under Reg NMS. SIPs (Securities Information Processors) consolidate quotes from all venues into the NBBO. Broker-dealers must execute customer orders at NBBO or better — the trade-through rule. Direct exchange data feeds are faster than SIPs, giving HFT firms a milliseconds-level edge that retail traders don't see. The 2010 Flash Crash exposed weaknesses in NBBO during stress.
plain: The best price to buy and the best price to sell a US stock right now, combined from every exchange into one quote.

snappy: FX forward settled in cash on the difference between agreed and realised spot — no currency change hands.
detail: Used for currencies with capital controls or thin onshore markets: BRL, CNY, INR, KRW, TWD. Settled in USD (or the convertible currency) based on the gap between the contract rate and a fixing rate on settlement day. London is the dominant NDF trading centre. Volumes have grown as EM hedging demand has scaled and onshore access remains restricted.
plain: A currency forward that settles in cash on the price gap, used for currencies you can't freely move in and out of the country.
An unfortunate property of certain bonds — they go up less when rates fall than they go down when rates rise. Common in MBS.
snappy: Price-yield curve bends the wrong way — gains lag losses on equal-sized rate moves.
detail: Standard bonds have positive convexity: prices rise faster than they fall for equal yield moves. Bonds with embedded prepayment or call options (MBS, callable corporates) have negative convexity — when rates fall, prepayments and calls cap upside, but when rates rise, extension risk amplifies downside. MBS portfolio managers manage convexity hedging carefully. The 2003, 2013, and 2022 convexity flushes were big sources of cross-asset volatility.

snappy: Interest rates below zero — depositors pay the bank to hold money.
detail: Adopted by the ECB (2014-2022), Bank of Japan (2016-2024), SNB (2015-2022), Riksbank, and Danish Nationalbank to fight deflation and stimulate lending. Pass-through to retail depositors was rare; banks ate the cost or charged corporates and large savers. Bond yields went negative across multi-trillion notional. Departed once inflation returned. Mechanically unusual: cash holding (zero rate) imposes a soft floor.
plain: When you pay the bank to hold your money instead of earning interest — a tool central banks tried to fight deflation.

snappy: Combining multiple offsetting payment obligations into a single net settlement.
detail: Bilateral netting: two parties net amounts they owe each other. Multilateral netting (via a CCP) consolidates across all members. Hugely reduces gross settlement volumes and required liquidity. The 'novation' to a CCP enables multilateral netting. ISDA Master Agreement provides netting upon default for bilateral derivatives. Netting reduces credit risk and operational burden.
plain: Combining many amounts owed in both directions into a single net payment, so only the difference actually moves.

snappy: Base metal — stainless steel and EV battery cathode demand.
detail: Stainless steel is roughly 70 percent of demand; battery demand is the fast-growing 15 percent. Indonesia dominates production (40 percent). The March 2022 LME nickel short squeeze (price 4x in two days, triggered by a Chinese tycoon's massive short position) forced the LME to halt trading and cancel trades — controversial episode that damaged LME's reputation. Battery-grade nickel sulfate commands premium over LME contract.
plain: Industrial metal used to make stainless steel and, increasingly, batteries for electric vehicles.

snappy: 225 large Japanese stocks, price-weighted — the headline Japanese equity index.
detail: Launched 1950, the post-war Japanese benchmark. Price-weighted methodology (like DJIA) gives Fast Retailing (Uniqlo) and SoftBank outsized weights. Hit historic 38,915 in December 1989 — wasn't surpassed until 2024. Tracked by Nikkei 225 futures (/NK), Nikkei ETFs. TOPIX (broader market-cap-weighted index of TSE Prime stocks) is the alternative Japanese benchmark.
plain: Japan's headline stock-market index — 225 large Tokyo-listed companies.

snappy: GDP in current-dollar terms — without inflation adjustment.
detail: Difference between nominal and real GDP is the GDP deflator. Nominal GDP is what's used for debt-to-GDP ratios, fiscal-policy comparisons, currency-area size rankings. China and India have higher real GDP growth than the US; on nominal-dollar terms (with FX effects) the rankings shift. Nominal GDP growth roughly equals real GDP plus inflation in the simple identity.
plain: A country's total output measured at today's prices, before adjusting for the fact prices keep rising.

snappy: The headline interest rate quoted in the market — includes both real return and expected inflation.
detail: Every yield in the financial press is nominal unless explicitly labelled 'real'. The Federal Reserve's policy target, mortgage rates, corporate bond yields, deposit rates — all nominal. Used in cash-flow calculations where the cash flows themselves are nominal (most bond coupons). Compare to real rates for purchasing-power analysis. The nominal-versus-real distinction matters most in high-inflation environments.
plain: The interest rate you see quoted — includes both real return and what people expect inflation to eat away.

snappy: MBS without a government guarantee — credit risk priced separately.
detail: Underlying loans typically don't meet conforming-loan criteria (jumbo mortgages, alt-A, subprime). Investors take both rate/prepayment and credit risk. The 2008 crisis was largely a private-label MBS event — issuance went from 1.2 trillion in 2006 to near-zero in 2008. Slowly recovering since but a fraction of pre-crisis size. Modern non-agency deals include detailed loan-level disclosure.
plain: A bond made of home loans with no government guarantee — investors take on the risk that homeowners default.

snappy: Reference quantity in a derivatives contract — not money that changes hands.
detail: A 100-million IRS doesn't involve 100 million dollars moving; the notional just determines coupon and payment sizes. Total notional outstanding in global derivatives is approximately 600 trillion dollars (BIS data) — far larger than actual market value (roughly 20 trillion). Headline notional figures can dramatically overstate counterparty risk. Net market value and credit exposure are the meaningful risk metrics.
plain: The headline reference number in a derivatives contract — used to size payments, but no one actually exchanges that amount.

snappy: Transfer of a derivative trade to a new counterparty — replaces the original contract.
detail: Used in bilateral derivative compression cycles to reduce gross exposures, and to migrate trades to central clearing post-Dodd-Frank. Original counterparty needs consent to novate. The new counterparty steps fully into the trade's economics. ISDA published novation protocols to standardise the process. Each clearing-eligible OTC swap that came on after 2014 was effectively novated to a clearing house.
plain: Swapping one party in a contract for another — the new party fully takes over the old party's role.

snappy: Bank must have stable funding sources covering at least 100 percent of its required stable funding.
detail: Basel III long-run liquidity ratio — complement to LCR's 30-day focus. Stable funding sources: long-term debt, retail deposits, Tier 1 capital. Required stable funding: long-term loans, illiquid assets, derivatives positions. Implemented later than LCR (2018-21 in major jurisdictions). Forces banks toward longer-tenor funding mixes.
plain: Bank rule requiring stable, long-term funding to cover long-term loans — stops banks relying too heavily on flighty short-term cash.

snappy: Reference asset against which other assets are priced — usually a risk-free bond or money-market account.
detail: Change-of-numeraire technique lets quants switch the reference asset to simplify pricing problems. Forward-measure pricing uses a zero-coupon bond as numeraire — handy for interest-rate options. Risk-neutral pricing uses the money-market account. Choosing the right numeraire can turn a hard pricing problem into a manageable one. Standard tool in advanced derivatives quant work.
plain: The reference asset you measure other prices against — like quoting everything in dollars, or in units of a bond.

snappy: CME-owned exchange listing the world's most-traded energy futures — crude, gas, gasoline, heating oil.
detail: Acquired by CME Group in 2008. Listed contracts (codes in parentheses): WTI Crude (/CL), Henry Hub Natural Gas (/NG), RBOB Gasoline (/RB), NY Harbor ULSD heating oil (/HO). All physically deliverable in principle, mostly financially settled or rolled before expiry. Floor trading ended in 2016; all electronic via CME Globex. Margin requirements managed via CME Clearing.
plain: New York exchange where the world's most-traded energy futures live — crude oil, natural gas, gasoline, heating oil.

snappy: Z-spread minus the embedded option value — true credit spread for callable bonds.
detail: Critical for MBS and callable corporates where prepayment or call options shift cash flows. Calculated via Monte Carlo simulation over interest-rate paths. MBS OAS is the standard credit measure for mortgage portfolios — wide OAS in 2007-08 and again 2022 signalled MBS stress. Lower OAS means richer pricing relative to underlying optionality.
plain: A credit-risk spread that strips out the value of any early-redemption feature embedded in the bond.

snappy: Swap where the floating leg is the compounded overnight rate — minimal credit risk.
detail: The floating leg averages the daily overnight rate (SOFR in USD, ESTR in EUR, SONIA in GBP) over the period. Because overnight rates are collateralised, OIS contains almost no credit component — making the OIS curve the cleanest discount curve for derivative valuation. Post-2008, dealers price collateralised derivatives off OIS rather than LIBOR. Standard tenors run from one week to 30 years.
plain: A swap where the floating side pays the average overnight interest rate — almost no credit risk, used as the cleanest discount curve.
A Fed facility that lets eligible firms park overnight cash with the Fed at a set rate — puts a floor under short-term interest rates.
snappy: Fed facility lending Treasury securities overnight in exchange for cash — sets a floor under short rates.
detail: Counterparts (money funds, GSEs, primary dealers) lend cash to the Fed overnight in exchange for Treasury securities. Set at IORB minus a small margin. ON RRP usage ballooned to 2.5 trillion in 2022-23 as money funds parked excess cash; has shrunk steadily through 2024 as the Fed runs off the balance sheet. The 'reverse' from the Fed's perspective: the Fed is borrowing cash and lending Treasury securities. Counterpart to the standing repo facility.

snappy: Rate the Fed pays counterparties on cash deposited at its overnight reverse repo facility.
detail: Sits below IORB by a few basis points. The floor of the policy corridor: non-bank cash holders (money funds, GSEs) won't accept lower rates in private markets when they can park cash at the Fed. Counterparties include the major money funds, GSEs like Fannie and Freddie, and primary dealers. Daily balances published by the New York Fed.
plain: Rate the US central bank pays money funds and similar firms to park overnight cash — acts as the floor under short-term rates.

snappy: 13-member oil cartel coordinating production to support prices.
detail: Founded 1960 in Baghdad. Members: Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Venezuela, Nigeria, Algeria, Libya, Angola (exited 2023), Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Republic of Congo. Holds roughly 40 percent of global production and 80 percent of proven reserves. Quarterly meetings set production quotas. Saudi Arabia, with the largest spare capacity, plays swing-producer role. OPEC discipline has wavered over decades.
plain: Cartel of 13 oil-producing countries — Saudi Arabia is the biggest — that coordinates output to influence global oil prices.

snappy: OPEC plus 10 non-OPEC producers (notably Russia) coordinating supply — formed 2016.
detail: Saudi Arabia and Russia anchor OPEC+, with combined production around 20 million barrels per day. Production-cut deal triggered by the 2014-16 oil price crash. The April 2020 OPEC+ price war (Saudi-Russia disagreement) triggered the WTI negative-price event; resolved with the largest-ever production cut. OPEC+ post-2022 has cut production several times to defend prices around 80 dollars per barrel.
plain: OPEC plus ten allied oil producers including Russia — they meet to coordinate production and defend prices.

snappy: Total number of open futures or options contracts at the end of each day.
detail: Differs from volume: volume counts daily trades, open interest counts unsettled contracts. Increases when new positions are opened; decreases when positions are closed. Rising open interest plus rising prices signals new long money entering; rising OI with falling prices signals short build-up. CME and ICE publish OI daily by contract. Crucial gauge of trader positioning.
plain: Number of futures or options contracts currently outstanding — tells you how many bets are still on the table.

snappy: Day-to-day Fed activity buying or selling Treasury securities to manage reserves and short rates.
detail: Distinct from large-scale QE/QT. Permanent OMOs (POMO) for outright purchases; temporary OMOs (TOMO) via repo and reverse repo. Conducted by the New York Fed's Open Market Desk. Pre-2008, OMOs were the primary tool — Fed kept reserves scarce and moved short rates by adjusting supply. Post-2008 abundant-reserves regime, OMOs play smaller role; IORB and ON RRP are the primary tools.
plain: Day-to-day buying and selling of government bonds by a central bank to nudge short-term interest rates.

snappy: Risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, systems, or external events.
detail: Examples: rogue traders (Barings 1995, SocGen 2008 Kerviel), settlement failures, IT outages, cyber attacks, fraud, natural disasters. Basel II/III imposes operational-risk capital — banks can use Standardised approach (income-based) or AMA (modelled). Multi-billion losses from operational risk are sadly routine: BNP Paribas 9-billion sanctions penalty 2014, JPMorgan whale 6-billion loss 2012. Hard to model.
plain: Risk of losing money from internal mistakes — IT outages, fraud, rogue traders, broken processes, or natural disasters.
A contract giving you the right — not the obligation — to buy or sell an Asset at a fixed price by a chosen date.
snappy: Right (not obligation) to buy or sell an asset at a set price by a set date — for a fee.
detail: Buyer pays a premium for that right; the seller (writer) collects the premium and takes the obligation. Two flavours — call (right to buy) and put (right to sell). The fixed price is the strike; the cutoff is the expiry. Listed options trade on CBOE, Eurex, OCC; OTC options (FX, rates) trade dealer-to-client. Black-Scholes is the canonical pricing model for the vanilla case.

snappy: Real-time list of all outstanding buy and sell orders at each price level.
detail: Continuous double auction: limit orders rest at their prices, market orders cross immediately. Top of book is the best bid and best offer (NBBO in US equities). Depth measures resting orders at and behind the top — thinner book means more impact for large trades. Order-book data is the raw material for HFT, market-making, and execution algos. Most exchanges publish via direct feeds and consolidated feeds.
plain: A live list of every buy and sell order waiting at each price level — what makes modern electronic markets tick.

snappy: Trading directly between two parties, off-exchange.
detail: Most fixed-income, FX, and complex derivatives trade OTC. Negotiated bilaterally rather than via centralised order book. Pricing varies by counterparty creditworthiness, size, market conditions. Less transparent than exchange trading. Post-2008 regulatory push moved standardised OTC derivatives onto central clearing and electronic trading platforms (SEFs, MTFs). Bespoke and complex products remain OTC.
plain: Trading done directly between two parties — privately negotiated, not run through a public exchange.
An option whose Strike Price is set so it would currently be worthless to exercise — the price has to move first before it pays.
snappy: Option where the strike is unfavourable relative to the current underlying price.
detail: An OTM call has strike above the current spot; an OTM put has strike below. OTM options trade cheaply because they're pure time value — no intrinsic value yet. The wings of the vol smile sit at OTM strikes; far-OTM puts price in crash risk. Retail options speculation often focuses on OTM calls (cheap, leveraged). Theta decays OTM options faster than ATM ones near expiry.

snappy: Option with no intrinsic value — all premium is time value.
detail: Call with strike above current price; put with strike below. Cheapest options but low probability of profit. Lottery-ticket appeal drives heavy retail trading of OTM options, especially short-dated calls in meme stocks. Far OTM options are sometimes called 'tail-risk hedges' — small premium for large payoff in extreme moves. Probability-weighted expected value of OTM options is typically negative.
plain: An option that would be worthless if you tried to use it right now — its Strike Price is far from where the market is.
A rule capping how much a bank can shrink its safety-capital requirement using its own internal computer models.
snappy: Basel rule capping internal-model capital savings at 72.5 percent of standardised approach.
detail: Introduced in the final Basel III package (2017, often called Basel IV). Banks using internal risk models cannot drop their risk-weighted assets below 72.5 percent of what they'd calculate using the regulator-set standardised approach. Designed to limit aggressive model manipulation and ensure cross-bank comparability. EU implementation began 2025; US follows in phases. You'll hear the output floor cited whenever European banks complain about capital headwinds from the Basel Endgame.

snappy: Difference between actual economic output and the economy's potential output.
detail: Positive gap (output above potential) signals overheating and inflation pressure; negative gap (slack) suggests room for non-inflationary growth. Estimated by CBO, IMF, OECD with significant uncertainty — potential output is unobservable. Negative output gap reached -5 percent during 2008-10 (large slack); recently closed and slightly positive (overheating). Used in Taylor Rule and central-bank reaction functions to assess policy stance.
plain: The difference between what an economy is actually producing and what it could produce at full capacity.

snappy: Single FX trade settling later than spot — locks in the rate today.
detail: Used by corporates to hedge known future cash flows: a UK importer expecting to pay 10 million dollars in three months sells GBP for USD forward today, fixing the conversion rate. Pricing comes from spot plus forward points (driven by the interest-rate differential). Distinct from an FX swap (which combines spot and forward legs) and from non-deliverable forwards (cash-settled).
plain: A simple deal to swap one currency for another at a fixed rate on a future date — locks in today's price for later.

snappy: Total number of shares the company has issued and that are currently held by investors.
detail: Includes shares held by insiders, institutional investors, retail, and employee plans. Excludes treasury stock (shares the company has bought back and not retired). 'Diluted shares outstanding' adds shares from in-the-money options, warrants, and convertibles. Market cap equals share price times shares outstanding. Companies disclose monthly via 10-Q and 10-K filings.
plain: The total number of shares a company has issued and that investors currently hold.

snappy: Share price divided by earnings per share — most common valuation multiple.
detail: A stock at 50 dollars with 5 dollars EPS trades at a 10 P/E — investors pay 10 dollars for every dollar of current earnings. Trailing P/E uses the past four quarters; forward P/E uses analyst forecasts. The S&P 500 has averaged a forward P/E around 17 over the past 30 years; tech stocks command higher multiples. High P/E suggests either expected growth or overvaluation; context required.
plain: Share price divided by earnings per share — tells you how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of company profit.

snappy: Long one security, short a correlated one — profit from mean reversion of the spread.
detail: Classic stat arb strategy. Identify pairs that historically move together (Coke-Pepsi, Ford-GM, gold-gold miners). When the ratio diverges from historical mean, bet on convergence. Equity neutral by construction. Modern algos systematically scan thousands of potential pairs. Variants: index pairs (long index, short component basket), commodity pairs (corn-soybeans, Brent-WTI). Drawdowns when historical relationships break.
plain: Buying one stock and shorting a similar one — betting their prices drift apart and then snap back together.

snappy: Precious metal heavily used in gasoline-engine catalytic converters.
detail: Roughly 80 percent of demand is auto-catalyst. Russia and South Africa produce most supply. Prices surged to over 3,000 dollars per ounce in 2022 as Russia sanctions hit supply; collapsed to under 1,000 by 2024 as EV adoption reduced demand for ICE catalysts. The 2018-2022 palladium bull market was one of the most dramatic commodity runs of the century.
plain: A precious metal used mostly in gasoline-car exhaust filters — supply heavily concentrated in Russia and South Africa.

snappy: Bond priced at exactly 100 percent of face value — neither at a premium nor a discount.
detail: Bonds issued at par sell at face value with a coupon equal to the prevailing yield. As market rates change, the bond trades to a premium (above par) if its coupon is now generous, or to a discount (below par) if it's stingy. 'Par swap' rates are the swap fixed leg that would make the swap value zero at inception.
plain: A bond price equal to its original face value — neither premium nor discount, often where new bonds first launch.

snappy: VaR calculated by assuming returns follow a normal (or other parametric) distribution.
detail: Uses current portfolio sensitivities (delta, gamma) and historical volatility/correlation estimates. Fast to compute, good for large portfolios. Major flaw: assumes normal distribution while financial returns have fat tails. Underestimates tail risk. The 1998 LTCM blow-up and 2008 bank losses repeatedly exceeded parametric VaR. Useful as baseline calculation, not as sole risk measure.
plain: A quick way to estimate worst-case losses by assuming returns follow a tidy bell-curve shape — underestimates real-world tail risk.

snappy: Derivative whose payoff depends on the underlying's price history, not just the final value.
detail: Asian options (averaging), lookbacks (extreme values), barriers (touching levels), autocallables (intermediate observations) all path-dependent. Cannot be priced with simple Black-Scholes; needs Monte Carlo, finite-difference, or tree methods. Path-dependent payoffs are central to structured-product engineering — they let issuers create payoff profiles that can't be replicated with vanilla options.
plain: When a derivative's payoff depends on the journey the price took, not just where it ends up.

snappy: Dividends as a percentage of earnings — how much profit is returned to shareholders.
detail: A 50 percent payout ratio means half of earnings go to dividends. Mature companies (utilities, consumer staples) run 50-70 percent; growth companies 0-20 percent. Above 100 percent is unsustainable — dividends are exceeding earnings. The flip side is reinvestment: low payout ratios mean retained earnings to fund growth. Tracked alongside buyback yield for total shareholder return analysis.
plain: Share of a company's profits paid out as dividends rather than reinvested — high means generous, above 100% is unsustainable.

snappy: China's central bank — manages renminbi exchange rate and key domestic financial conditions.
detail: Less independent than developed-market peers; coordinates closely with State Council. Active reserve-requirement adjustments, multiple policy rates (LPR, MLF), targeted lending tools. Manages CNY against trade-weighted basket with significant intervention. PBoC reforms reflect China's evolving monetary framework — gradual marketisation alongside continued state guidance. CNY-CNH spread reflects offshore-onshore dynamics.
plain: China's central bank — manages the yuan, sets domestic interest rates, and coordinates with the Chinese government.

snappy: Statistical technique decomposing data into uncorrelated factors ranked by explained variance.
detail: In fixed income: first three PCs of yield-curve moves capture level (parallel shift), slope (steepening/flattening), curvature (butterfly) — explain ~99 percent of curve variance. In equity: PCs identify dominant industry or factor exposures. Used in factor model construction, dimensionality reduction for ML models, scenario design. The mathematical foundation for many risk-modelling and stat-arb approaches.
plain: A statistical trick that boils down a tangled dataset into a handful of independent factors that capture most of the variation.

snappy: BEA's measure of consumer prices — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
detail: Calculated from BEA's national income accounts data. Differs from CPI in scope (includes employer-paid healthcare), weights (chain-weighted), and methodology. Core PCE (ex food and energy) is the FOMC's explicit 2 percent target. Typically runs 0.3-0.5 percentage points below CPI. Released after CPI with a 2-week delay, so CPI captures more immediate market attention even though PCE is the policy target.
plain: The US Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge — measures what households actually spent, including healthcare paid by employers.

snappy: P/E divided by earnings growth rate — adjusts valuation for growth.
detail: A stock with 30 P/E and 30 percent earnings growth has PEG of 1.0; a 30 P/E with 10 percent growth has PEG of 3.0. PEG below 1.0 suggested undervalued (Peter Lynch's heuristic). Highly sensitive to growth assumptions — small forecast errors swing PEG materially. Useful for comparing companies at different growth stages within a sector; less useful across vastly different business types.
plain: P/E Ratio divided by expected growth — a way of judging whether a high price tag is justified by fast growth.
A pool of money set aside by employers or governments to pay workers' retirement income — invested across stocks and bonds for decades.
snappy: Investment pool managing retirement assets on behalf of workers and retirees.
detail: US public pensions hold roughly 5 trillion dollars (state and local). Private corporate pensions plus 401(k)-style defined-contribution plans add trillions more. Largest: California's CalPERS, the Dutch ABP, Japan's GPIF. Pension funds are big buyers of long-dated bonds and equities, providing stable demand. Defined-benefit pensions face funding-ratio pressures when rates fall or stocks weaken. You'll hear on every earnings announcement for major asset managers (BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street).

snappy: Maximum expected counterparty credit exposure over a future horizon, at a confidence level.
detail: Critical input for derivatives counterparty risk and Basel regulatory capital. Calculated by simulating portfolio evolution and taking the high-quantile (typically 97.5 percent) at each future time. PFE profile grows with derivative tenor — peaks somewhere in the middle for swap-like products. Used in setting trading-line credit limits and as the basis for SA-CCR regulatory capital calculations.
plain: Worst-case forecast of how much a counterparty could end up owing you on a derivative trade over its life.

snappy: Broker receives compensation from market-makers for routing retail orders to them.
detail: Standard practice in US retail equity and options trading. Robinhood made it famous (and controversial). Critics argue it conflicts with best-execution duties; supporters note it enables zero-commission trading. UK's FCA banned PFOF in 2012; EU restrictions tightened in 2024. SEC adopted Reg NMS updates in 2023 to improve disclosure but didn't ban PFOF. Annual PFOF revenue across US brokers approached 4 billion dollars in peak years.
plain: Your broker is paid a small fee by a market-maker for sending them your trade — controversial, but funds zero-commission trading.

snappy: Empirical relationship between unemployment and inflation — typically inverse.
detail: Documented 1958 by A.W. Phillips. Forms basis of much central-bank thinking. Has shown remarkable instability over decades: appeared flat during 2010s (low unemployment without inflation), then sharply steep in 2021-22 (inflation surge). Augmented Phillips curve includes inflation expectations. Death of the Phillips curve has been repeatedly proclaimed; some version of it always seems to come back.
plain: Old idea that low unemployment pushes prices up and high unemployment cools them down — wobbly but persistent.

snappy: Risk near expiry that the underlying closes exactly at the strike — uncertain exercise.
detail: If a stock closes at exactly $50 on Friday and you're short a $50 call, you don't know if it'll be exercised — depends on each holder's discretion. Creates an unwanted long or short position Monday morning. Dealers manage pin risk by adjusting hedges close to expiry. The 'magnet effect' near round numbers ('pinning to strike') is real and tied to gamma hedging at the strike with highest open interest.
plain: Near an option's expiry, the underlying closes exactly at the Strike Price — leaving holders unsure whether to exercise.

snappy: Smallest standard increment of an FX quote — usually the fourth decimal place.
detail: EUR/USD moving from 1.0850 to 1.0851 is one pip up. Most pairs use four decimal places, making one pip 0.0001 of the quote currency. JPY pairs use two decimal places, so one pip is 0.01. 'Pipettes' (fifth decimal) are sub-pip resolution offered by some dealers. P&L on FX positions is naturally measured in pips times position size.
plain: The smallest standard step in a currency quote — usually the fourth decimal place, like a one-cent move in dollar pricing.

snappy: Private placement of public-company stock — typically to institutional investors at a discount.
detail: Used by companies needing capital without going through a full secondary offering — faster, less regulatory friction. Common in SPAC deals: PIPEs anchor the merger by committing capital alongside SPAC trust. Standard 10-20 percent discount to market. Often comes with anti-dilution protections, registration rights, and lock-up provisions. PIPE volume tracks broader risk-on cycles.
plain: Public company sells new shares quickly to a few big private investors, usually at a discount — faster than a public offering.

snappy: Precious metal — catalytic converter feedstock, jewellery, industrial.
detail: Priced in dollars per ounce. Roughly 70 percent of supply comes from South Africa. Diesel-engine catalytic converter demand collapsed post-Dieselgate (2015) as gasoline cars (using palladium instead) took share. Platinum has traded below gold since 2015 — historically rare inversion. Hydrogen-economy demand could revive platinum prices over the next decade as fuel cells scale.
plain: Precious metal used in diesel-car filters, jewellery, and some industrial processes — supply concentrated in South Africa.

snappy: 1985 G5 agreement to weaken the US dollar through coordinated FX intervention.
detail: Signed September 22 1985 at the Plaza Hotel in New York. The dollar had appreciated 50 percent against the yen and Deutsche mark over 1980-85, hurting US manufacturers. The five (US, Japan, West Germany, UK, France) agreed to sell dollars; USD fell roughly 50 percent against JPY over the next two years. Sometimes blamed for triggering Japan's late-1980s asset bubble.
plain: 1985 deal where five rich countries agreed to coordinate selling US dollars to weaken the dollar against the yen and mark.

snappy: Anti-takeover defence allowing existing shareholders to buy discounted stock if acquirer crosses ownership threshold.
detail: Standard threshold 10-15 percent. When triggered, existing shareholders (except the acquirer) can buy new shares at half price, severely diluting the acquirer's stake. Twitter adopted poison pill in 2022 in response to Elon Musk's initial stake — later withdrawn when Musk agreed to acquire the company. Delaware law generally upholds poison pills if independently approved.
plain: Defensive trick where a company lets existing shareholders buy cheap new shares if a hostile buyer crosses a threshold.

snappy: Collection of investments owned by a person or institution.
detail: Sized by total market value, characterised by asset allocation, risk metrics, and benchmark. Institutional portfolios: pension funds (15-30 trillion globally), sovereign wealth funds (10-trillion), endowments, foundations. Retail portfolios: brokerage accounts, retirement accounts, real estate. Portfolio construction balances return objectives, risk tolerance, liquidity needs, and time horizon. Rebalancing maintains target weights as markets move.
plain: The whole collection of investments someone owns — stocks, bonds, cash, property, all measured together.

snappy: Maximum number of futures or options contracts an entity may hold in a single security.
detail: Set by CFTC for US commodity futures, by exchanges for equity and rate futures. Designed to prevent market manipulation and excessive speculation. Spot-month limits typically tighter than aggregate limits. The 2011 Dodd-Frank position-limits rule went through extensive revisions and litigation; finalised 2021. Exemptions exist for hedging by commercial users.
plain: Caps on how many futures or options contracts in one product any single trader can hold — stops anyone cornering a market.

snappy: Algo that targets a percentage of market volume — adapts to changing trading activity.
detail: Trader specifies, say, 10 percent participation. Algo trades 10 percent of each minute's volume — accelerates when others trade, slows when they don't. Different to VWAP (volume profile assumed in advance) and TWAP (constant pace). Used by traders confident in their direction but unwilling to drive prices. POV-targeting algos can hit excessive impact if market volume surges and the algo can't keep up.
plain: Trading algorithm that tracks a fixed percentage of the day's trading volume — speeds up when others trade, slows when they don't.

snappy: Inflation measure from the producer's perspective — wholesale prices of goods and services.
detail: BLS-published. Captures pricing pressure upstream — manufacturers, processors, wholesalers. Often a leading indicator of CPI: rising input costs eventually feed through to consumer prices. PPI surged in 2021-22 as supply-chain disruptions pushed up commodity and goods prices. Core PPI (ex food and energy) more stable. Less retail-visible than CPI but watched by economists and the Fed.
plain: Inflation measure for the prices factories and wholesalers charge — often an early warning for shop-price inflation.

snappy: Theory that exchange rates should equalise the cost of a basket of goods across countries.
detail: Long-run anchor for fair-value FX models. The Economist's 'Big Mac Index' is the popular illustration: a Big Mac costing $5 in the US and 4 pounds in the UK implies GBP/USD around 1.25 if PPP holds. In practice, PPP holds poorly over short and medium horizons because of trade frictions, non-tradeable goods, and capital flows. Useful as a long-run reversion benchmark, not a trading signal.
plain: Theory that exchange rates should make a basket of goods cost the same in every country — popular as a long-run anchor.

snappy: Equity with bond-like features — fixed dividend, priority over common, usually non-voting.
detail: Sits between debt and common equity in the capital structure. Pays a fixed dividend (sometimes cumulative, meaning missed payments accumulate). Senior to common stock for dividends and liquidation; junior to all debt. Common in bank capital stacks (Tier 1 capital). Convertible preferreds can convert to common stock on certain triggers. Liquidity is thinner than common; most retail investors only encounter them via preferred ETFs.
plain: Hybrid investment that pays a fixed dividend like a bond but ranks behind debt and ahead of common stock if the company fails.

snappy: Bond trading above par — usually because its coupon beats current market rates.
detail: A 5 percent coupon bond in a 3 percent yield environment trades at a premium — the high coupon makes the bond more valuable than face value. Holders pay extra upfront but recover it through the bigger coupon stream. Mathematically, the premium amortises down to zero by maturity. Most callable bonds trade close to par because issuers redeem early when premiums build up.
plain: A bond trading above its original face value — usually because its coupon is more generous than today's market interest rates.

snappy: Risk that MBS holders get their principal back early — usually when rates fall and homeowners refinance.
detail: Forces reinvestment at lower yields. Higher-coupon MBS (originated when rates were high) are most exposed: as soon as rates fall, refinancing surges. MBS modellers estimate Conditional Prepayment Rates (CPR) and Public Securities Association (PSA) speeds. The 2003 refi wave produced extreme prepayment shocks; the 2020 wave was deepest. Negative convexity follows directly from prepayment risk.
plain: Risk that homeowners refinance their mortgages early when rates fall, leaving bond investors to reinvest at lower yields.

snappy: Process by which markets determine fair prices through order flow.
detail: Driven by the aggregate of buying and selling decisions reflecting traders' information and expectations. Lit venues (exchanges) contribute more to price discovery than dark pools (which don't display quotes). Periods of stressed price discovery — when prices move on thin volume — produce wider spreads and bigger price gaps. The 2020 March pandemic week saw extreme price-discovery stress across asset classes.
plain: How a market figures out the right price for something — through the constant tug-of-war of buy and sell orders.

full: Packaged Retail and Insurance-based Investment Products
snappy: EU rule requiring standardised disclosure documents for retail investment products.
detail: Effective 2018. Issuers must produce a Key Information Document (KID) for any complex retail product — structured notes, ETFs (under contested interpretation), insurance products, mutual funds (post-UCITS-to-PRIIPs transition completed 2023). Standardised format includes performance scenarios, risk indicator, costs. UK-specific PRIIPs amendments diverge post-Brexit.
plain: EU rule requiring a short standard fact-sheet — the Key Information Document — for any complex retail investment product.
A Bank designated by the Fed to buy directly at US Treasury auctions and make markets in Treasury securities — wholesale plumbing of the bond market.
snappy: Bank designated to bid at Treasury auctions and trade directly with the Fed.
detail: Around 25 firms currently, including JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, BofA, BNP Paribas, Nomura. Required to bid in every Treasury auction in proportion to their dealer designation, provide market data to the New York Fed, and trade with the Fed's open-market desk. Critical to monetary-policy implementation. Lost primary dealer status is a meaningful blow to a bank's fixed-income franchise.

snappy: Investment in private companies, often via leveraged buyouts.
detail: Major firms: Blackstone, KKR, Carlyle, Apollo, Bain Capital. Charge 2-and-20 fee structure (2 percent management, 20 percent carry). 10-year fund vehicles typical. AUM industry-wide approaches 8 trillion globally. Returns: roughly 11-12 percent net annualised long-run, with significant dispersion. Currently focused on continuation vehicles, secondaries, and special situations as exits have slowed since 2022.
plain: Funds that buy whole companies, usually private ones, run them for years, then sell at a profit.

snappy: Estimated likelihood that a borrower will default over a given horizon.
detail: Drawn from rating agency data, internal bank models, or market-implied (CDS-derived) probabilities. One-year PD for IG averages well under 1 percent; HY runs 3-5 percent in normal times, spiking in stress. Banks use through-the-cycle versus point-in-time PD distinctions for capital adequacy. Critical input to expected loss calculations and IFRS 9 forward-looking provisioning.
plain: Estimated chance a borrower won't be able to repay over a given period — a core input to credit pricing and bank capital.

snappy: Oil, gas, or mining company selling forward production to lock in revenue.
detail: Standard risk management: an oil producer with 100,000 bpd output sells WTI futures or buys put options to lock in prices for the next 1-3 years. Reduces revenue volatility; sacrifices upside if prices rally. Major producers (Pioneer, Devon, Hess) disclose hedge books in 10-Ks. Mexico's sovereign hedge program (Hacienda Hedge) is the largest single oil hedging program — billions in coverage annually.
plain: An oil company, miner, or farmer selling their future output today to lock in a known price — sacrifices upside for certainty.
A contract that pays off if a stock or other Underlying falls below an agreed price — used to insure against drops or bet on declines.
snappy: Option giving the holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price before expiry.
detail: The mirror image of a call. Buyers of puts profit when prices fall — used for downside hedging by long-only investors and for outright bearish speculation by traders. Protective puts on index ETFs (SPY, QQQ) are a standard portfolio-hedge tool. Selling puts ('cash-secured puts') generates income if the buyer thinks the underlying won't fall. You'll hear it daily on options desks: 'I need to buy the 4,500 puts'.

snappy: Option giving the right to sell the underlying at a strike price by expiry.
detail: Long put: holder profits if underlying falls below strike minus premium. Protective puts hedge long positions (limit downside while keeping upside). Naked short puts: writer collects premium, takes downside risk (limited to strike minus premium). Cash-secured puts: collateralised by cash, common in income strategies. Tail-risk hedging often uses far out-of-money puts. The 1987 crash drove the persistent equity skew toward put premium.
plain: A contract giving you the right to sell something at a fixed price by a chosen date — pays off if the price falls.

snappy: FX settlement mechanism where both currency legs settle simultaneously.
detail: Implemented globally via CLS (Continuous Linked Settlement). Eliminates Herstatt risk where one party pays out before receiving. Roughly two-thirds of global FX settlement now goes via CLS or equivalent PvP arrangements. Remaining settlement (mostly EM currencies outside CLS) still bears principal risk. Continuous push to expand PvP coverage to additional currencies and counterparties.
plain: FX settlement where both currencies move at exactly the same moment — eliminates the risk one side pays and the other doesn't.
When a central bank prints money to buy huge piles of government bonds — pushing down longer-term interest rates and pumping cash into the system.
snappy: Central-bank large-scale asset purchases — drives down long-end yields and expands the balance sheet.
detail: Pioneered by the Bank of Japan in the early 2000s; the Fed adopted it after 2008. Three Fed rounds (QE1, QE2, QE3) plus the 2020 COVID expansion brought the Fed balance sheet from under 1 trillion to nearly 9 trillion dollars. ECB and Bank of England ran their own programs. Aims to lower long rates, support asset prices, and stimulate borrowing once short rates hit zero. Reversed via QT (quantitative tightening) as central banks shrink balance sheets.

plain: A central bank shrinking the pile of bonds it bought during emergency support — pulling money back out of the financial system.
snappy: Common shorthand for Quantitative Tightening — central-bank balance-sheet runoff.
detail: The reverse of Quantitative Easing. Started by the Fed in 2017-2019 (first attempt, ended after market stress) and again from June 2022 onwards (more aggressive, hundreds of billions per year). The Fed lets maturing Treasury securities and agency MBS run off rather than reinvesting proceeds, shrinking its balance sheet. Other major central banks (Bank of England, ECB) followed suit. You'll hear 'QT' cited in any conversation about Fed policy stance or Treasury market liquidity.

snappy: August 2007 systematic strategy crash — many market-neutral funds lost 10-20 percent in a week.
detail: Crowded positions in similar quant signals unwound simultaneously. Likely triggered by initial fund liquidations tied to Subprime exposure, forcing wider deleveraging. Affected stat arb, market-neutral, factor strategies. Recovered by year-end but many funds had taken structural losses. Highlighted concentration risk in seemingly diversified quant strategies — many models had similar inputs and similar trades.
plain: August 2007 crash when many computer-driven hedge funds lost a tenth of their money in a week as their bets unwound at once.

snappy: Central bank buys government bonds and other assets — expands balance sheet, lowers long rates.
detail: Used when policy rates are near zero (the ZLB). Fed bought trillions in Treasury securities and agency MBS through QE1 (2008-10), QE2 (2010-11), QE3 (2012-14), and pandemic QE (2020-22). Peak Fed balance sheet 9 trillion dollars (April 2022). ECB, BoE, BoJ ran parallel programs. Mechanism: increases reserves, lowers long-term yields, eases financial conditions. Now winding down via QT.
plain: Central bank creates new money to buy government bonds — pushes long-term interest rates down to stimulate the economy.

snappy: Central bank shrinks balance sheet — typically by letting bonds mature without reinvesting.
detail: Reverse of QE. Fed's current QT runs at roughly 60 billion dollars per month of Treasury runoff and 35 billion in agency MBS runoff (slowed from peak pace in 2024). Drains reserves from the banking system. Different from rate hikes — affects different parts of the yield curve. Banks of England and Canada are also reducing balance sheets. ECB QT progressing slower. Long-term effects still being studied.
plain: Reverse of Quantitative Easing — central bank shrinks its balance sheet by letting bonds mature without replacing them.

snappy: Option on a foreign-currency asset that pays in a different currency at a fixed exchange rate.
detail: A USD-paying option on the Nikkei 225 is a quanto — Japanese-yen index, dollar payoff. Investor gets index exposure without yen exposure. Pricing accounts for the correlation between the underlying and the FX rate — a parameter that's harder to estimate than vol alone. Common in structured notes sold to retail investors wanting foreign-equity exposure without FX risk.
plain: A derivative on a foreign Asset that pays out in your own currency at a fixed exchange rate — strips out currency risk.

snappy: Pre-IPO and pre-offering window during which company communications are restricted.
detail: From IPO filing through effectiveness, companies and underwriters can't engage in marketing speech outside the prospectus. Reg M extends quiet-period-like restrictions on share repurchases and analyst recommendations. Google's 2004 Playboy interview violated quiet period; Salesforce and others have had similar issues. Has been modernised to allow certain communications (testing-the-waters) under JOBS Act 2012.
plain: Window around a company's share offering when bosses and bankers must avoid public marketing speech beyond official documents.

snappy: Stated price at which a security is bid or offered.
detail: Two-sided quote: bid and offer. One-sided quote: bid only or offer only. Firm quote: commitment to trade at that price. Indicative quote: suggestion subject to confirmation. Quote currency: the currency expressing the price (USD in EUR/USD). Quote-driven markets (FX, OTC bonds): dealers quote prices. Order-driven markets (equities): order book aggregates limit orders into quotes.
plain: The price someone offers to buy or sell a security at — markets are built from a constant stream of these prices.

snappy: Second currency in a pair — the unit the price is denominated in.
detail: In EUR/USD at 1.0850, USD is the quote currency: the price says 1.0850 USD per 1 EUR. The quote currency is what you pay (when buying the base) or receive (when selling the base). Profits and losses on a position accrue in the quote currency unless explicitly converted. Some quote-currency conventions are surprising: GBP/JPY is GBP-base/JPY-quote, with prices like 195.50.
plain: The second currency in a pairing — the one the price is denominated in. For euro-dollar, the dollar is the quote currency.

snappy: Real interest rate consistent with stable inflation and full employment in the long run.
