detail: Unobservable; estimated via macroeconomic models (Laubach-Williams, Holston-Laubach-Williams). Pre-2008 estimates around 2-2.5 percent real; collapsed to roughly 0.5 percent by 2010s. Most recent FOMC longer-run rate dots imply a nominal r-star around 2.9 percent (2-percent inflation plus 0.9 real). Critical input to monetary-policy stance — current rates above r-star imply restrictive policy.
plain: The hypothetical interest rate that keeps inflation steady and the economy at full employment — never directly seen, only estimated.

snappy: Structured product that accrues coupon for each day the underlying stays within a range.
detail: If the reference rate (often LIBOR replacement) stays between a floor and ceiling on a given day, the coupon accrues; otherwise the day's coupon is zero. Embedded short option on volatility — investor profits if the rate stays inside the range. Popular as yield-enhancement during low-rate periods. Risk: rate gaps outside the range during volatility spikes, coupon accrual goes to zero, principal can be at risk.
plain: Structured product that pays a daily coupon only on days the underlying stays inside a chosen price band.

snappy: Specification gasoline traded on NYMEX — proxy for US wholesale gasoline price.
detail: Quoted in dollars per gallon. Standard contract is 42,000 gallons. RBOB is the unfinished gasoline before retail-grade ethanol blending. Crack spreads (RBOB minus WTI) measure refining profitability; widened sharply post-2022 amid global refining capacity tightness. Retail gasoline prices typically lag RBOB futures by 1-2 weeks. The EIA publishes weekly inventory and demand data.
plain: Standard US wholesale gasoline traded on the futures market — what refineries sell before retail stations add ethanol.

snappy: Gross Domestic Product adjusted for inflation — measures real economic output growth.
detail: Reported as annualised quarterly growth in the US (BEA), quarter-on-quarter in Europe (Eurostat). Real GDP growth roughly equals labour-force growth plus productivity growth in steady state. US trend growth around 1.8-2 percent post-2010; emerging economies higher. Quarter-to-quarter swings dominated by inventory changes, trade, and government spending. The output gap measures real GDP versus potential.
plain: Total economic output adjusted for inflation — tells you whether the economy is actually growing or just prices are.

snappy: Interest rate after stripping out expected inflation — the rate that grows purchasing power.
detail: Equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation (the Fisher equation). Negative real rates — a feature of 2020-21 — mean savers lose purchasing power even at positive nominal yields. TIPS (Treasury inflation-Protected Securities) trade explicit real yields; the gap to nominal Treasury securities is the breakeven inflation rate. Central banks track real rates closely because they're what actually constrains or stimulates economic activity.
plain: Interest rate minus expected inflation — what your savings actually grow by in real purchasing power.

snappy: Actual past volatility of the underlying — what 'really happened'.
detail: Computed from daily log returns, annualised by multiplying by the square root of 252 (trading days). Compare with implied vol to gauge the vol risk premium — the gap usually favours implied (sellers profit). Realised vol around earnings days, FOMC meetings, and macro shocks spikes far above its trend. High realised vol with stable implied vol means systematic options sellers are getting hurt.
plain: How bumpy a price has actually been over a past window — the historical reality you compare against forecasts.

snappy: Significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months.
detail: Officially dated by the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee in the US (typically with a lag). Commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (informal rule of thumb). The pandemic recession (Feb-Apr 2020) was the shortest ever — two months. The 2007-09 'Great Recession' was the longest post-WWII at 18 months. NBER uses broader factors: employment, real income, sales, industrial production.
plain: A broad and sustained downturn in the economy — typically falling output, rising unemployment, and weaker spending.

snappy: Date on which a shareholder must own shares to be eligible for a dividend or corporate action.
detail: Distinct from ex-date (typically two business days before record date) when the stock starts trading without the dividend. Settlement-cycle change to T+1 in 2024 shortened the gap — ex-date is now one business day before record date. Payable date is when the dividend hits accounts. Sequence: declaration date → ex-date → record date → payable date.
plain: The cutoff date for owning a stock to qualify for a dividend — own it before this date, you get paid.

snappy: Percentage of bond face value recovered by creditors after default.
detail: Senior secured: 60-80 percent average. Senior unsecured: 30-50. Subordinated: 10-30. Determined post-default through bankruptcy court (Chapter 11) or auction (for CDS settlement). Recovery rates fall during recessions when liquidation values shrink and many defaults happen simultaneously. Moody's, S&P, and the Loan Pricing Corporation publish recovery datasets. Crucial input to credit-spread analysis (CDS pricing assumes 40 percent default-recovery convention).
plain: Cents on the dollar that bond investors get back after a borrower defaults — depends on what the lender ranks against.

snappy: Trade-weighted exchange rate adjusted for inflation differentials.
detail: Published monthly by the BIS for 60-plus countries. Adjusts the nominal effective rate (basket of currencies weighted by trade) for relative price levels. Tracks competitiveness: a rising REER means the country's exports are getting pricier relative to peers. REER deviations from long-term averages flag potential currency mis-valuation. Central banks watch REER closely; it's a better fair-value gauge than nominal bilateral rates.
plain: Trade-weighted exchange rate adjusted for inflation — shows whether a country's exports are getting expensive or cheap versus rivals.
A widely published interest rate that other contracts use as a baseline — like SOFR for dollars or ESTR for euros.
snappy: Benchmark rate used to set floating payments on loans, swaps, and securities.
detail: The foundation of trillions in floating-rate contracts. Dominant USD reference rates: SOFR (Treasury repo, secured) and pre-2023 LIBOR (interbank unsecured, since retired). Euro reference rates: ESTR (overnight) and EURIBOR (1-12 month tenors). Reference rates must be representative, transparent, and resistant to manipulation — the post-2012 LIBOR scandal forced a global overhaul. You'll hear 'reference rate' in any floating-rate bond prospectus or swap term sheet.

snappy: Profit per barrel a refiner earns turning crude into products — broader than the crack spread.
detail: Includes the cost of operating, financing, and maintaining the refinery — beyond just the crude-versus-product spread. Refineries with complex configurations (cokers, hydrocrackers) earn higher margins on heavier crude grades. The 2022 European refining margins on diesel exceeded 60 dollars per barrel, historically unheard-of, before settling to 15-25 in 2024. Captured in EIA's gross product margin data.
plain: Profit per barrel a refinery makes by turning crude oil into gasoline, diesel, and other products — wider than the crack spread.

snappy: Period of rising prices and economic activity — often after deflation or disinflation.
detail: 1933-35 New Deal reflation under FDR. Post-2020 pandemic reflation drove the historic 2021-2022 inflation surge as monetary and fiscal stimulus collided with supply constraints. 'Reflation trade' typically: long cyclicals, commodities, value over growth, short bonds. The 2016-2017 reflation expectation following Trump's election produced a major rally in cyclical assets.
plain: Period when prices and economic activity start rising again — often follows a deflationary slump and is welcomed by policymakers.

snappy: SEC rule requiring research analysts to certify their reports reflect personal views.
detail: Adopted 2003 post-Wall Street research scandals. Analysts must certify (in each report) that views accurately reflect personal opinions and disclose any compensation tied to specific recommendations. Together with the 2002 Global Research Settlement, reshaped sell-side research independence from investment banking. MiFID II's research-unbundling rules in Europe achieve similar separation through different mechanism.
plain: US rule forcing equity research analysts to certify their published views genuinely reflect their personal opinion.

snappy: SEC rule requiring broker-dealers to act in retail customers' best interest when recommending securities.
detail: Adopted 2019, effective June 2020. Imposes Care, Disclosure, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance obligations. Doesn't require pure fiduciary duty — explicitly preserves the broker-dealer/IA distinction. Critics argue Reg BI is weaker than DOL's earlier proposed fiduciary rule (vacated by court). Influences broker compensation, product recommendations, and disclosure forms (Form CRS).
plain: US rule requiring brokers to act in their retail customers' best interest when recommending investments.

snappy: SEC anti-manipulation rules governing securities offerings.
detail: Adopted 1997. Prohibits issuers, distribution participants, and affiliates from engaging in market activities that could artificially influence the price during a 'restricted period' around an offering. Three components: Rules 100 (definitions), 101-102 (distribution participants), 103 (Nasdaq market-makers), 104 (stabilising bids), 105 (short sales). Tightens during IPOs and secondary offerings.
plain: US anti-manipulation rules that restrict trading activity by people involved in a new share offering during a quiet window.

snappy: SEC framework that ties together US equity venues into a single national market.
detail: Adopted 2005, implemented 2007. Core rules: Order Protection Rule (trade-throughs banned at protected prices), Access Rule (fair access to quotes), Sub-Penny Rule, Market Data Rules. Created the patchwork of competing exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, BATS, IEX, etc.) connected by SIPs. Now under SEC review — proposals to update market-data infrastructure and tick sizes for 2024-25.
plain: US framework that stitches together every stock exchange into a single national market — guarantees customers get the best price.

snappy: SEC rule requiring critical market infrastructure entities to maintain technology resilience.
detail: Adopted 2014 in response to flash crashes and exchange technology failures. Applies to SCI entities: exchanges, SIPs, clearing agencies, large ATSs. Requires policies for systems, business continuity, disaster recovery, cyber resilience. Annual senior-management reviews and 24-hour outage reporting. Several high-profile SCI events (Nasdaq 2013 outage, BATS 2012 IPO failure) drove its creation.
plain: US rule requiring exchanges and clearing houses to maintain solid, resilient technology and report outages quickly.

snappy: SEC rule governing short selling — locate requirement, close-out, mark-and-hold.
detail: Adopted 2005. Short-sellers must 'locate' shares available to borrow before selling. Threshold securities (chronic FTDs) face stricter close-out requirements. The 2008 emergency SEC short-selling restrictions and the 2021 GameStop-era discussions reignited Reg SHO scrutiny. Naked short selling (selling without proper locate) is prohibited but persists in some forms. SEC modernised some provisions in 2023.
plain: US rule governing short selling — you have to locate borrowable shares before selling them short.

snappy: Statistical model where the data-generating process changes between distinct states.
detail: Markov regime switching models (Hamilton 1989) capture market state transitions: low-vol versus high-vol regimes, bull versus bear regimes. Useful for capturing structural breaks (1990s low-vol period, 2008-09 stress, 2020 COVID). Forecasting regime changes ex ante is hard; identifying current regime usually easier. Used in dynamic asset allocation, volatility forecasting, signal generation.
plain: Statistical model that lets data behave one way in calm periods and a different way in stressed periods.

snappy: SEC rule requiring public companies to disclose material information broadly, not selectively.
detail: Adopted 2000. Banned the practice of companies feeding earnings tips or guidance to select analysts. Material disclosures must be simultaneous and public (via 8-K, press release, or webcast). Modernised in 2008 to include social media disclosure. Reshaped sell-side analyst access to management — analyst-day events, broad investor meetings, conference appearances are now the standard channel.
plain: US rule banning public companies from leaking earnings tips to favoured analysts — material news must be released to everyone at once.

snappy: Risk that future coupon income earns less than the original yield — falling-rate problem.
detail: When a bond pays a coupon, the holder needs somewhere to reinvest it. If rates have fallen since purchase, the new investment earns less than the original yield-to-maturity assumed. Longer coupon-paying bonds carry more reinvestment risk than zero-coupon bonds (which have none). Pension funds use immunisation strategies — matching asset duration to liability duration — partly to neutralise reinvestment risk.
plain: Risk that the coupon payments you collect have to be reinvested at lower interest rates than your original bond paid.
A company that owns income-producing buildings — offices, apartments, shopping malls — and must pay most of its profits out as Dividends.
snappy: Listed property vehicle — must distribute 90 percent of taxable income as dividends.
detail: Created by US Congress in 1960 to give small investors access to commercial real estate. Pays no corporate tax provided it distributes at least 90 percent of taxable income to shareholders — so REIT Dividend yields run high, typically 3-6 percent. Major US REIT sectors: residential, office, retail, healthcare, industrial, and data centres. The 2020-22 office crisis hammered office REITs. You'll hear REITs cited in income-portfolio conversations and any commercial-property discussion.

snappy: Borrowing cash overnight against collateral — usually Treasury securities.
detail: A repo is a sale with an agreement to buy back next day at a slightly higher price; the difference is the repo rate. The plumbing of short-term funding: dealers fund inventories, money funds park cash. Tri-party repo at BNY Mellon clears trillions daily. The September 2019 repo spike — rates briefly hit ten percent — forced the Fed to launch standing facilities. SOFR is calculated from repo activity.
plain: Short-term borrowing arranged like a sale-and-buyback — you sell a bond today, buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price.

snappy: Currency that other central banks hold in their FX reserves — primarily the US dollar.
detail: USD makes up roughly 58 percent of allocated global reserves (IMF COFER, late 2024), down from 70 percent in 2000. EUR around 20 percent, JPY 6, GBP 5, CNY 2, plus smaller shares of CAD, AUD, CHF. Reserve status confers 'exorbitant privilege' — global demand for the currency keeps borrowing costs lower than economic fundamentals alone would suggest. Sanctions and de-dollarisation discussions are a recurring theme.
plain: A currency that central banks around the world hold as savings — primarily the US dollar.

snappy: Fraction of customer deposits banks must hold as reserves at the central bank.
detail: Traditional monetary-policy tool. Fed eliminated reserve requirements in March 2020 (set to zero), reflecting the abundant-reserves regime where reserves are no longer the binding constraint. ECB still has a 1 percent reserve requirement. China's PBOC actively uses reserve requirements as a policy tool (10-15 percent range in recent years). The Fed's elimination signals fundamental shift in monetary plumbing.
plain: Minimum cash banks must keep at the central bank — once a key policy tool, now barely used in the US.

snappy: Government agency with power to resolve failing banks — restructure or wind down without bankruptcy.
detail: US: FDIC plus Fed under Title II of Dodd-Frank (orderly liquidation authority). EU: Single Resolution Board for euro-area banks. UK: Bank of England. Powers include bail-in, asset transfers to bridge banks, sale to acquirers. The 2023 SVB and Signature resolutions used FDIC's regular receivership powers; First Republic was sold to JPMorgan in a similar mechanism.
plain: Government body with power to take over a failing bank and wind it down without a chaotic bankruptcy.
Changing the terms of a bond or loan — extending the deadline or accepting partial repayment — when the borrower can't pay as agreed.
snappy: Modification of debt terms to reduce burden — often counts as a credit event for CDS.
detail: Triggered when a borrower is in financial distress but parties want to avoid outright Default. Forms include maturity extension, coupon reduction, principal write-down, or debt-for-equity swaps. Counts as a credit event for CDS in European contracts (less commonly in US post-2009). Famous cases: Greek sovereign restructuring 2012 (53.5 percent haircut), Argentine 2005 and 2020 restructurings, US municipal Detroit 2014. You'll hear restructuring cited in any distressed-debt discussion.

snappy: Mirror of a repo — the cash lender's side of the transaction.
detail: Same trade as a repo, named from the other side: the party temporarily lending cash and receiving collateral 'does a reverse repo'. The Fed's Overnight Reverse Repo Facility (ON RRP) lets money funds and GSEs deposit cash at the Fed against Treasury securities; balances peaked above 2.5 trillion in 2022-23 as excess liquidity sought a floor. ON RRP rate acts as the floor of the policy corridor.
plain: Mirror of a Repo from the lender's side — you lend cash overnight and receive a bond as collateral.

snappy: Company reduces shares outstanding while proportionally increasing per-share price.
detail: Used to lift a low stock price above exchange listing minima (1 dollar typical NYSE threshold) or to remove penny-stock stigma. One-for-ten reverse split: 10 dollars stock at 1 dollar becomes 1 share at 10 dollars. Often signals weakness. AIG (2009), Citigroup (2011), and many SPACs in 2023-24 used reverse splits to maintain listings.
plain: Company shrinks its share count and proportionally lifts the price — often used to get a low-priced stock back above listing thresholds.

snappy: Identifies scenarios that would cause a specific level of loss — works backward from outcome to inputs.
detail: Required by Basel III. Question: 'What scenario would cost us 10 percent of capital?' rather than 'What loss in the standard scenario?'. Useful for tail-risk identification — surfaces scenarios that internal models might not naturally generate. Difficult to operationalise; results sensitive to model assumptions. Increasingly required in regulatory capital plans.
plain: Asks what scenario would cause a specific bad outcome — works backwards from disaster to identify dangerous risks.

snappy: Buyer requests prices from multiple dealers; dealers respond competitively.
detail: Standard execution protocol in fixed-income, FX, and OTC derivatives. Dealer-to-customer (D2C) RFQ platforms: MarketAxess (bonds), Tradeweb (rates, bonds), Bloomberg (multi-asset). Quotes are firm for a brief window (often 30-60 seconds). RFQ-IS (RFQ Implementation Shortfall) execution lets traders compare quoted prices to internal valuations. EU MiFID II requires RFQ disclosure for transparency.
plain: Trader asks several dealers for a price at the same time, then picks the best one — standard for bonds, FX, and OTC trades.

snappy: Option's sensitivity to a one-percent change in interest rates.
detail: The least-watched Greek. Matters most for long-dated options where the discount rate has time to compound. Calls have positive rho (higher rates increase forward price, helping calls); puts have negative rho. Long-dated equity LEAPS see meaningful rho exposure; short-dated options have almost none. FX options and rate options have their own rho sensitivities to the two underlying rate environments.
plain: How much an option's value changes when interest rates move — the least-watched of the option sensitivity measures.

snappy: Counterparty credit exposure declines just when their credit deteriorates — favourable case.
detail: Opposite of wrong-way risk. Example: bank lends to oil producer collateralised by oil reserves — if oil prices crash (hurting producer credit), collateral value falls together but bank's claim becomes less valuable when most needed. Less common than WWR in practice. Some collateralised lending structures inherently produce right-way risk (loans collateralised by counterparty-correlated assets).
plain: Lucky case where exposure to a counterparty shrinks just as their credit weakens — opposite of the dangerous wrong-way kind.

snappy: Existing shareholders given priority to buy new shares — usually at a discount.
detail: Common in Europe and Asia for capital raises. Each rights holder can subscribe pro-rata for new shares; non-subscribers can sell their rights in the market. UK banking sector used massive rights issues post-2008 (RBS's 12 billion pound rights issue famously failed). Less common in the US, where secondary offerings to institutional investors dominate capital-raising. Heavily discounted (20-50 percent to market) to ensure full subscription.
plain: Capital raise where existing shareholders get first dibs to buy new shares at a discount — common in Europe and Asia.

snappy: HY bond upgraded to IG — gains pricing premium as IG buyers enter.
detail: Opposite of fallen angel. Companies typically work toward rising-star upgrades through deleveraging, business improvement, or M&A by IG acquirers. Bonds usually trade up before the formal upgrade as the market prices in the expectation. Spreads tighten on the upgrade announcement. Tracked in dedicated indexes by ICE and Bloomberg. Common in post-LBO refinancing stories.
plain: A bond once rated junk that gets upgraded to investment quality — usually rallies as new, safer-minded buyers move in.

snappy: Portfolio allocation method that equalises risk contributions across asset classes.
detail: Pioneered by Bridgewater's All Weather Fund (Ray Dalio). Traditional 60/40 portfolios have most risk from equities; risk parity adds significant fixed-income exposure scaled up via leverage to equalise risk contributions. Performed well 2008-2020 (rates falling, equity/bond negative correlation). Hit hard in 2022 as both equities and bonds fell together. AQR's risk-parity strategies have been industry leaders alongside Bridgewater.
plain: Portfolio approach that gives each asset class the same share of risk, not the same share of dollars — usually leverages up bonds.

snappy: Difference in implied vol between out-of-money calls and puts — measures FX skew.
detail: A 25-delta risk reversal quotes vol of the 25-delta call minus vol of the 25-delta put. Positive RR means calls more expensive than puts — the market expects upside skew. EUR/USD RRs tend toward zero in calm markets; USD/JPY skew is famously persistent (puts more expensive — yen rallies in risk-off). Tracked by macro funds as a sentiment gauge.
plain: Difference in price between an upside option and a downside option — measures which way the market is leaning.

snappy: Theoretical rate of return with zero default risk — the foundation of every valuation model.
detail: Used as the discount rate floor in DCF analysis, the baseline for CAPM, and the input to option-pricing models. In practice, US Treasury yields proxy for the dollar risk-free rate; German Bunds for euro; Japanese government bonds for yen. Post-LIBOR transition, swap rates referenced to SOFR play this role for derivatives. 'Risk-free' is shorthand — no asset is fully default-free, but Treasury securities are as close as it gets.
plain: The interest rate on a truly safe investment — usually US Treasury securities — forms the floor for valuing everything else.

snappy: Adjusted probability under which all assets earn the risk-free rate — used for option pricing.
detail: Not the actual probability of events — it's the probability that makes derivative prices consistent with no-arbitrage. The risk-neutral expected discounted payoff equals today's option price. Implied probabilities can be back-solved from option market prices to get the 'risk-neutral density' of future prices. Used in event-trading (binary outcomes) and as a market-implied probability gauge.
plain: Mathematical probabilities used in pricing — not the real chance of an event, but the ones that make derivative prices add up correctly.
Market mood label — when investors crowd into riskier bets it's risk-on, when they flee to safety it's risk-off.
snappy: Market regime label — investors collectively buying or selling risky assets in correlation.
detail: In risk-on episodes, equities and high-yield credit rally while government bonds, dollar, yen, gold, and Swiss franc weaken. Risk-off reverses it: equities sell off, safe-haven currencies and Treasury securities rally. The pattern intensified post-2008 as cross-asset correlations rose. Macro hedge funds construct portfolios with explicit risk-on or risk-off tilts. You'll hear traders describe a session as 'pure risk-off' on days of synchronised flight to safety.

plain: An influential 1996 risk-measurement framework released by JPMorgan — taught a generation of traders how to estimate portfolio risk.
snappy: JPMorgan 1996 risk methodology — popularised VaR and EWMA volatility modelling.
detail: Released free by JPMorgan in 1994 (technical document), expanded 1996. Brought parametric Value-at-Risk and EWMA volatility to a wide audience and became the industry default for years. Spun off as a standalone company (RiskMetrics Group, eventually acquired by MSCI in 2010). Most modern bank risk systems still trace their lineage to its conventions — daily horizon, 95 or 99 percent confidence, exponential weighting with lambda 0.94. You'll hear RiskMetrics referenced in any historical discussion of bank risk management.

snappy: MBS backed by residential mortgages — the bulk of the global MBS market.
detail: Cash flows come from millions of individual homeowner payments. Agency RMBS (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie) dominates US issuance; non-agency RMBS issuance remains a fraction of pre-2008 levels. Prepayment risk is the central modelling challenge — homeowners refinance freely when rates fall, hurting MBS holders. RMBS deals tranched into pass-throughs, CMOs, and IO/PO strips for different risk appetites.
plain: An investment bond made of bundled home mortgages — investors collect the monthly payments homeowners make on their houses.

snappy: Net income divided by shareholders' equity — profitability per dollar of book value.
detail: DuPont decomposition breaks ROE into net margin times asset turnover times leverage — three drivers managers control differently. Sustained high ROE (over 15 percent) signals competitive advantage. Tech companies routinely exceed 25 percent; commodity businesses sit in single digits. Excessive leverage can inflate ROE without underlying improvement — why analysts compare ROE alongside ROIC and balance-sheet quality.
plain: Annual profit a company makes as a percentage of what shareholders have invested — higher is better, but high leverage can inflate it.

snappy: After-tax operating profit divided by capital employed — ROE without the leverage distortion.
detail: Strips out the financing decision: ROIC measures the business's return on its asset base regardless of how it's funded. Compared with weighted average cost of capital (WACC) — ROIC above WACC creates value, below destroys it. Favoured by long-horizon investors (Buffett, Munger) over ROE because it's harder to game with leverage. Best-in-class businesses sustain 20-percent-plus ROIC for decades.
plain: Annual profit as a percentage of all the money invested in the business — measures how well managers turn capital into earnings.

snappy: Gain or loss from rolling expiring futures contracts into the next month.
detail: Positive in backwardated markets (selling expiring contract at higher price than rolling into cheaper next month); negative in contango. Long-only commodity ETFs (USO, UNG, DBC) systematically pay roll yield in contango — explains why USO underperforms WTI spot over time. Optimised commodity indexes (Goldman, Bloomberg) try to smartly time rolls or weight curve points to minimise contango drag.
plain: Profit or loss from rolling expiring futures into the next month — depends on whether further-out contracts are cheaper or pricier.

snappy: Payment system where transfers settle individually and immediately — no netting.
detail: Used for high-value wholesale payments to eliminate settlement risk. Fedwire (USD), TARGET2 (EUR, ECB-operated), CHAPS (GBP, BoE-operated), BOJ-NET (JPY). Differs from net settlement (FedNet, CHIPS, Bacs) where payments are batched and netted. RTGS prevents systemic risk from a payment-system participant failure but requires participants to fund every gross outflow with liquidity.
plain: Payment system where each transfer settles immediately and individually — no batching, no netting. Used for big, time-critical payments.

snappy: Small-cap US stock index — 2,000 smallest of the Russell 3000.
detail: Benchmark for US small-cap performance. Total market cap around 3 trillion dollars. Heavy regional-bank, biotech, and consumer-cyclical exposure. ishares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) is the largest tracker. Annual reconstitution in late June causes significant index trading. Distinct from S&P 600 (S&P's competing small-cap index). Underperformed large-caps significantly 2014-2023.
plain: US small-company stock index — tracks the 2,000 smaller names just below the giants of the S&P 500.

snappy: Bank assets adjusted for their credit, market, and operational risk profiles.
detail: Foundation of regulatory capital ratios — capital divided by RWA gives the headline ratios. Different asset types get different risk weights: sovereign bonds 0 percent, retail mortgages 35 percent, unsecured corporate loans 100 percent, junk bonds 150 percent. Banks can use Standardised approach (regulator-set weights) or Internal Models approach (their own estimates). Basel III Endgame restricts internal-model use.
plain: A bank's assets scaled up or down by how risky each one is — used to size the cushion of capital regulators demand.

snappy: Top 500 US large-cap stocks weighted by market cap — the dominant US equity benchmark.
detail: Maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices. Selection criteria: market cap, liquidity, sector representation. Constituents reviewed quarterly; rebalances drive significant trading volume. Total market value approaches 50 trillion dollars (2024). Tracked by 7+ trillion in Index Funds and ETFs — SPY, VOO, and IVV are the three biggest. Total return version (with dividends reinvested) is the standard benchmark for US equity performance comparisons.
plain: An Index tracking the share prices of the 500 biggest US listed companies — the headline gauge of the US stock market.

snappy: Stochastic Alpha-Beta-Rho model — industry standard for interest-rate vol smile fitting.
detail: Published 2002 by Hagan, Kumar, Lesniewski, Woodward. Four parameters — α, β, ρ, and ν — fit the smile shape. β controls the underlying dynamics (between normal and lognormal); ρ is the correlation between underlying and vol; ν is vol of vol. Approximate closed-form solution makes calibration fast. The de facto standard for interest-rate-derivative vol modelling, especially swaptions and caps/floors.
plain: A maths formula traders use to estimate how option prices change across different Strike Prices for interest-rate bets.

snappy: 2002 US legislation enhancing corporate governance and financial-reporting accountability.
detail: Enacted post-Enron, WorldCom, Tyco accounting scandals. Required CEO/CFO certification of financial reports (Section 302), independent audit committees, internal-controls reporting (Section 404), and CEO/CFO clawbacks for misstatements. Created PCAOB to oversee auditing. Section 404 compliance is famously costly. Whistleblower protections embedded. Reshaped public-company financial-reporting culture.
plain: A US law passed after the Enron scandal forcing public-company bosses to personally sign off on the truthfulness of their financial reports.

snappy: Bank-specific capital buffer derived from CCAR stress-test results.
detail: Replaced the fixed 2.5 percent conservation buffer for largest US banks in 2020. Calculated from peak-to-trough capital decline in CCAR adverse scenario plus four quarters of planned dividends. Buffer floor 2.5 percent. Banks must maintain capital above the buffer; constraint on dividends and buybacks if it dips. Personalises capital requirements to each bank's risk profile.
plain: A bank-specific cushion of extra Capital, sized by how badly the bank would fare in the Fed's annual stress test.

snappy: Evaluating portfolio performance under specific hypothetical conditions.
detail: Distinct from Stress Tests (which focus on extreme conditions). Scenario analysis examines moderate to severe but plausible scenarios. Macro scenarios: 'soft landing', 'hard landing', 'no landing', 'reaccelerating inflation'. Geopolitical: 'Russia-Ukraine resolution', 'Taiwan crisis'. Used in portfolio construction, capital allocation, business planning. Multi-scenario discounting in DCF models — running cash-flow projections under several scenarios and probability-weighting them — applies the same idea.
plain: Running a portfolio through several made-up futures — say a recession or a war — to see how it would hold up under each one.

snappy: Algo executing a pre-defined trading schedule — VWAP, TWAP, POV.
detail: Trader specifies parameters (start/end time, target rate, etc.) and the algo executes according to schedule without real-time decisioning. Predictable behaviour; easy to model. Critics note schedule-based algos can be gamed by predatory traders detecting the regular slicing pattern. Most institutional flow uses adaptive algos that adjust to real-time market conditions rather than fixed schedules.
plain: An automated trading program that breaks a big order into small pieces and feeds them into the market on a fixed timetable.

snappy: IMF-created reserve asset — basket of USD, EUR, CNY, JPY, GBP.
detail: Allocated to IMF members in proportion to quotas; can be exchanged for hard currency among central banks. SDR weights (effective Aug 2022): USD 43.4, EUR 29.3, CNY 12.3, JPY 7.6, GBP 7.4. The SDR rate is calculated daily from a basket of short-term yields. Limited use outside official sector — periodic proposals to expand SDR for development finance haven't gained traction.
plain: A reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund — a basket of major currencies that member governments can swap among themselves.

snappy: Top US securities regulator — oversees exchanges, brokers, listed companies, and investment funds.
detail: Created 1934 after the 1929 crash. Five commissioners appointed by the President. Writes and enforces federal securities law: registration of public companies, disclosure (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), insider-trading rules (Reg FD), market structure (Reg NMS), and money managers (Investment Advisers Act). Operates the EDGAR filing system. Delegates day-to-day broker-dealer supervision to FINRA. Distinct from the CFTC, which oversees derivatives, futures, and swaps.
plain: The main US watchdog for public companies and stock markets — sets what firms must disclose to investors and goes after fraud.

snappy: Sale of additional shares by an already-public company.
detail: Two flavours: primary (new shares issued, dilutes existing holders) and secondary (insiders sell existing shares, no dilution). Often announced after-hours with overnight bookbuild — pricing the next morning. Hurts short-term stock price (1-5 percent typical drop) due to dilution and signalling. Required for capital needs, deleveraging, insider liquidity events.
plain: When a company that's already public issues fresh shares to raise more cash — usually nudges the existing share price down a bit.
Packaging up thousands of loans — mortgages, car loans, credit cards — and selling slices of the bundle to investors as new bonds.
snappy: Process bundling loans or receivables into tradable securities — backbone of ABS and MBS.
detail: Mechanics: an originating lender sells a pool of loans to a bankruptcy-remote SPV (SPV), which issues bonds backed by the cash flows. Tranches at different seniority levels — Senior Tranche, Mezzanine Tranche, Equity Tranche — appeal to different investors. Securitisation channels capital from bond markets into consumer and commercial lending. Pre-2008 mortgage securitisation collapsed under poor underwriting; post-crisis reforms (Reg AB II in the US, Securitisation Regulation in EU) tightened disclosure. You'll hear securitisation in any conversation about ABS, MBS, or CLO markets.

snappy: EU framework for securitisation issuance — STS label, transparency, retention.
detail: Effective 2019. Established the 'Simple, Transparent, Standardised' (STS) label for high-quality securitisations qualifying for preferential capital treatment. Mandatory risk retention (5 percent skin-in-the-game) for originators. Investor due-diligence rules. Aimed at reviving European securitisation post-2008 (which has lagged US recovery). Currently under review for further loosening to support EU capital-markets union.
plain: The EU rulebook for bundling loans into bonds — gives 'high-quality' deals lighter regulatory treatment and forces lenders to keep Skin in the Game.

snappy: Dodd-Frank trading-venue category for standardised swaps — alternative to RFQ on platforms.
detail: Required for clearable swaps after 2013. Two execution methods: order book (auction-style) and RFQ (request for quote to multiple dealers). Bloomberg's SEF and Tradeweb's are the largest. EU equivalent is MTF/OTF under MiFID II. Roughly half of US cleared swap volume goes through SEFs. CFTC adopted significant updates in 2024 to modernise SEF rules.
plain: An online venue where banks and traders are required to execute standardised Swap contracts so deals are visible to regulators.

snappy: Highest-priority slice of a structured product — paid first from cash flows.
detail: Usually AAA-rated, lowest yield. In a typical CLO, the senior tranche makes up 60-70 percent of the capital stack and absorbs losses only after all subordinated tranches are wiped out. Senior CLO tranches survived even the 2008 crisis with full principal recovery. Banks, insurance companies, and money funds are the typical buyers. Sized so that the rating-agency stress scenario doesn't penetrate it.
plain: The safest slice of a bundled-loan deal — gets paid first from incoming cash and only takes losses after every junior slice is wiped out.

snappy: Standard corporate bond — claim ranks behind secured debt but ahead of subordinated.
detail: Default ladder: secured (collateralised) → senior unsecured → subordinated → preferred → common equity. Most investment-grade corporate issuance is senior unsecured. Recovery rates in default historically average 40 percent for senior unsecured (compared to 60-80 for secured, 10-30 for subordinated). The cushion of subordinated debt below it determines recovery prospects.
plain: A standard corporate bond with no specific collateral — sits ahead of junior debt but behind any loans secured against the company's assets.

snappy: When ownership and cash actually change hands — distinct from the trade date.
detail: US equities moved to T+1 (one business day after trade) in May 2024, joining India and Canada. US Treasury bonds and notes also settle T+1. Most government bonds settle T+1 or T+2. FX spot is T+2 for most pairs (T+1 for USD/CAD). Fails to settle attract penalties under SEC Rule 204 and CSDR in Europe. The shorter cycle reduces counterparty risk but compresses post-trade processing time.
plain: The day money and securities actually change hands — usually one or two business days after the trade itself is agreed.

snappy: Risk-adjusted return — excess return over risk-free rate divided by return volatility.
detail: Bill Sharpe Ratio's 1966 ratio: (return minus risk-free rate) divided by standard deviation. Higher is better. S&P 500 long-run Sharpe Ratio roughly 0.4. Hedge funds claim 1.0+ Sharpe Ratio — often inflated by smoothed returns, selection bias. The 0.5-1.0 Sharpe Ratio range covers legitimate institutional managers. Doesn't distinguish upside from downside volatility (see Sortino Ratio). Returns that aren't normally distributed (think hedge funds with rare big losses) make the score less reliable for some strategies.
plain: A score measuring how much extra return an investment earns per unit of risk — higher means better reward for the same price swings.

snappy: Selling borrowed shares with intent to buy back later at a lower price.
detail: Borrower pays a fee to the share lender; profits if the stock falls. Open-ended risk on the upside (no cap on how high a stock can go). Used for speculation, hedging long positions, statistical arbitrage. Famous short squeezes: Volkswagen (2008), GameStop (2021). Regulators have temporarily banned shorting in specific stocks during crises (banking sector 2008). Reg SHO mandates locate before shorting in the US.
plain: Borrowing shares you don't own, selling them straight away, and hoping to buy them back cheaper later — a bet that the price will fall.

snappy: Rapid price spike forces short-sellers to cover, accelerating the rally.
detail: Mechanism: high short interest plus a positive catalyst forces those who have been Short Selling to buy back shares to cover, pushing the price higher and forcing more covering. The 2008 Volkswagen squeeze (briefly the most valuable company in the world), the 2021 GameStop episode (driven by retail coordination on Reddit's WallStreetBets), and the AMC and Bed Bath & Beyond run-ups are the famous examples. Hedge funds approach Short Selling of heavily-shorted names with caution.
plain: A rapid price spike that forces traders who bet against a stock to scramble and buy it back, pushing the price up even faster.

snappy: Bank or non-bank whose failure would threaten financial stability.
detail: FSOC designates US SIFIs; FSB designates G-SIFIs internationally. Subject to enhanced supervision, higher capital requirements, recovery and resolution planning. Non-bank SIFI designation contentious: AIG (2014), MetLife (2014, vacated 2018 by court), Prudential (2013, de-designated 2018). FSOC under Biden re-tightened SIFI designation procedures in 2024.
plain: A bank or financial firm so big that its failure could shake the whole system — supervisors apply extra-tight rules to it.

snappy: Precious metal — half monetary store of value, half industrial input.
detail: Roughly 50 percent of demand is industrial (solar panels, electronics, medical), 50 percent investment/jewellery. More volatile than gold because the industrial demand swings with the economy. The 1980 Hunt brothers attempt to corner silver took it from 6 to 50 dollars per ounce before crashing. Gold-silver ratio (gold price / silver price) hovers historically 60-80; spikes to 100+ in stress, collapses in metals bull markets.
plain: A precious metal that's part store of value, part industrial material — used in everything from jewellery and coins to solar panels and electronics.

snappy: Futures contract on an individual stock — small market in the US, larger in Europe and Asia.
detail: Eurex and the Indian exchanges trade actively. The US OneChicago exchange shut in 2020 — single-stock futures never gained traction here, partly due to regulatory complexity (jointly overseen by SEC and CFTC). Offer leveraged single-name exposure without traditional Margin borrowing. CFDs and synthetic prime brokerage substitute in markets where SSFs lack Liquidity.
plain: A futures-style contract tied to one individual company's share price — lets traders take leveraged bets without borrowing the actual shares.

snappy: Asymmetry of the implied vol smile — equities skew left (puts pricier than calls).
detail: Single-stock equity skew widens around earnings (left-tail fear). Index skew widens in selloffs as protective put demand surges. Quoted as the vol differential between 25-delta puts and 25-delta calls, or as a slope of the smile. Skew tracking is core to vol arbitrage strategies. The post-1987 'permanent skew' in S&P options is a market-microstructure landmark.
plain: The pattern in option prices where bets on a stock falling cost more than bets on it rising — markets pay up for crash protection.

snappy: CCP's own equity capital that absorbs losses before tapping the default fund.
detail: Typically 5-25 percent of the smallest tier of the default fund — modest relative to total mutualised resources. Designed to align CCP incentives with risk management. Critics argue it's too small to materially incentivise CCPs to manage risk prudently; supporters note it sits in the right position in the waterfall. EMIR 3.0 in Europe is increasing skin-in-the-game requirements 2024-25.
plain: The CCP's own money, sitting between member contributions and bigger backstops, that absorbs losses when a member defaults — so the CCP has something to lose.

snappy: Difference between expected execution price and actual fill price.
detail: Positive slippage = better than expected; negative = worse. Causes: bid-ask spread, market impact from large orders, latency between decision and execution. Quantified in basis points or cents per share. Implementation Shortfall captures total slippage versus the decision-time price. Algo execution aims to minimise expected slippage; risk management caps maximum acceptable slippage on individual orders.
plain: The gap between the price you expected to trade at and the price you actually got — often worse for larger or rushed orders.

snappy: US-specific leverage ratio for G-SIBs — 5 percent of total exposure.
detail: More stringent than Basel III's 3 percent. The 2020-2021 Fed Treasury exemption (temporarily excluded Treasury securities and reserves from the denominator) helped banks support Treasury markets during COVID stress. Expired April 2021. Critics argue SLR constraint limits bank capacity to intermediate Treasury markets, contributing to volatility episodes. Ongoing debate about adjustment.
plain: A rule forcing the biggest US Banks to back their entire balance sheet with at least 5 percent Capital, regardless of asset risk.

snappy: ETFs and indexes weighting by factors rather than market cap.
detail: Equal-weighted, fundamentally weighted (revenue, earnings), low-vol, dividend-weighted, multi-factor. Roughly 1.5 trillion in US smart-beta ETFs. Largest sponsors: BlackRock ishares, Invesco, Vanguard, WisdomTree. Performance depends on factor exposure — value-tilted versions underperformed cap-weighted 2014-2022, then partially recovered. Cheaper than active funds but more expensive than vanilla cap-weighted.
plain: An ETF that picks and weights stocks by rules other than size — like dividends or low volatility — sitting between passive and active.

snappy: System that decides where to route each child order across available venues to optimise execution.
detail: Considers visible quotes (NBBO), hidden liquidity at dark pools, exchange fees, latency, and routing logic from broker preferences. Routes parent orders to the venue most likely to fill at the best price. Smart routers represent decades of evolution from simple 'route to NYSE' systems to multi-venue optimisation. Quality varies by broker; sophisticated buy-side institutions evaluate SOR performance via TCA.
plain: Software that splits a buy or sell order and sends pieces to whichever exchanges or trading venues offer the best price and speed.

snappy: UK individual-accountability framework for financial-services firms.
detail: Effective 2016 for banks, 2018 for insurers, 2019 for solo-regulated firms (those supervised by the FCA alone, not jointly with the PRA). Senior managers face explicit responsibilities and personal liability for misconduct. Annual certifications for staff in significant roles. Replaced the discredited Approved Persons Regime after the LIBOR scandals. EU's Senior Managers requirements under CRD have similar effect. Has reshaped UK bank governance culture.
plain: A UK regime that names individual senior bankers as personally responsible for what happens on their watch — and can fine or ban them.

snappy: Overnight rate based on Treasury repo trades — the LIBOR replacement.
detail: Published daily by the New York Fed using actual transaction volume (roughly 1.5 trillion dollars daily), making it manipulation-resistant. Replaced USD LIBOR after the 2012 manipulation scandals; the formal cessation was June 2023. SOFR is risk-free (collateralised), so the spread between SOFR and credit-sensitive benchmarks (historically Eurodollar Futures) matters when pricing interest rate Swaps. Term SOFR (CME-published forward-looking rate) is used in business loans, and the Fed's Standing Repo Facility — an emergency lending tool — helps keep SOFR from spiking by lending against Treasury collateral at a fixed ceiling rate.
plain: An interest rate based on what it costs banks to borrow overnight using US Treasury bonds — the modern replacement for LIBOR.

snappy: CME-listed futures on average SOFR over a future period.
detail: Two main contracts: 1-month SOFR futures (average daily SOFR over the contract month) and 3-month SOFR futures (compounded SOFR over a quarter). Replaced Eurodollar Futures as the benchmark short-rate hedging tool after LIBOR was phased out. Quarterly serial expiries out to 10 years. Used by banks to hedge Floating Rate exposure, by traders to express Fed-policy views, and as inputs to forward-rate curves.
plain: Exchange-traded contracts that lock in a future SOFR rate — banks and traders use them to bet on or hedge against where US rates head next.

snappy: Gap between term SOFR rates and the compounded overnight SOFR — measures rate-volatility expectations.
detail: Term SOFR (CME-published) is a forward-looking estimate; OIS averages realised overnight SOFR. When markets expect significant policy moves or volatility, term SOFR includes a premium over OIS. Tracked by traders to gauge the market's anticipation of Fed action between meetings. Spreads compressed in 2024 as Fed policy stabilised.
plain: The gap between interest rates traders lock in for coming months and the overnight rate — widens when markets expect the Fed to shift policy.

snappy: Central bank successfully reduces inflation without triggering a recession.
detail: Historically rare — only the 1994-95 Greenspan tightening cycle is the textbook US example. The 2022-2024 US disinflation from 9 to 3 percent without recession is the second clearest case. Requires policy precision: tight enough to slow demand and break inflation but not so tight as to crash labour markets. Often debated whether achieved — 2024 narratives shifted from soft-landing skepticism to acceptance.
plain: When a central bank tames inflation by raising rates just enough to cool the economy without tipping it into a Recession — historically rare.

snappy: Bank of England's overnight benchmark — sterling LIBOR replacement.
detail: Volume-weighted median of unsecured overnight sterling deposits at major banks. Replaced GBP LIBOR by end-2021. Underlies sterling OIS contracts and most new sterling Floating Rate instruments. Backward-looking (rate known only after the day ends), so compounded-in-arrears methodology is used for term coupon calculations. Compare with Term SONIA, which is forward-looking and used in business loans.
plain: The Bank of England's daily benchmark interest rate, based on actual overnight lending between UK banks — replaced sterling LIBOR.

snappy: Risk-adjusted return measure using downside deviation rather than total volatility.
detail: Sharpe Ratio ratio penalises both upside and downside volatility equally; Sortino Ratio only counts downside. Calculation: excess return over downside standard deviation. Favoured by alternative-asset managers who argue upside volatility is good. Higher Sortino Ratio values better. Limitations: less data robust than the Sharpe Ratio (only counts negative returns), more sensitive to sample size. Tracked alongside the Sharpe Ratio in modern performance reporting.
plain: A scoring formula like the Sharpe Ratio but only counting downside risk — judging investments by their losses rather than their total ups and downs.

snappy: Debt issued by a national government — typically the safest credit in its own currency.
detail: US Treasury securities, UK Gilts, German Bunds, Japanese JGBs sit at the top of the sovereign credit hierarchy. Emerging-market sovereigns (Brazil, Turkey, South Africa) pay credit-spread premia reflecting default risk. Sovereign debt in a country's own currency is theoretically default-free (the government prints the currency) — but the 1998 Russia default and 2012 Greece restructuring proved exceptions. Hard-currency sovereign issuance carries higher risk than local-currency.
plain: Money lent to a national government — usually the safest kind of borrowing in that country, with US Treasury securities the global gold standard.

snappy: Government failing to meet its debt obligations on time and in full.
detail: Russia 1998 (rouble bonds), Argentina 2001 (USD bonds), Greece 2012 (private creditor exchange, technically default), Lebanon 2020, Sri Lanka 2022, Ghana 2022, Zambia 2020. Hard-currency defaults more common than local-currency (the government can print local currency). Resolution: IMF programs, Paris Club restructurings for official creditors, London Club / private negotiations for bonds. Long market-access exclusion typically follows.
plain: When a government fails to pay back the money it borrowed on time — rare for big economies, more common in emerging markets.

snappy: Spread between soybean futures and the value of resulting soybean meal and oil.
detail: Processor margin: buy beans, crush into meal and oil, sell the products. Standard crush ratio: one bushel of soybeans yields roughly 44 pounds of meal and 11 pounds of oil. CBOT-traded crush spread futures simplify hedging for processors (ADM, Bunge, Cargill). Wider crush spreads incentivise more processing; narrower spreads slow processing and tighten product markets.
plain: The gap between raw soybean prices and the combined value of the meal and oil they produce — measures soybean processor margins.

snappy: High-protein oilseed — meal for animal feed, oil for food and biodiesel.
detail: Soybean futures listed at CME (/ZS) are the benchmark. US and Brazil dominate global production. Soybean complex: bean, meal (animal feed), oil (cooking oil, biodiesel). Crush spread (bean price minus meal and oil prices) measures processor margins. Chinese hog herd cycle drives global soybean demand. Trade-war dynamics around the 2018 US-China tariffs reshaped global soybean trade flows.
plain: A high-protein crop traded heavily on exchanges — crushed into meal for animal feed and oil for cooking and biodiesel.

snappy: Shell company that IPOs with the intent to merge with a private target — backdoor public listing.
detail: Investors hold cash in trust until a deal closes; can redeem if they don't like the chosen target. Massive 2020-21 boom: 600+ SPACs raising 160 billion in 2021. Most underperformed dramatically post-merger. SEC tightened SPAC rules 2024 — required underwriter liability, enhanced disclosures, hindering future deal flow. Most 2021-vintage SPACs that completed mergers (de-SPACs) traded well below 10-dollar redemption.
plain: A shell company that lists on an exchange to raise cash, then hunts for a private firm to merge with — a back-door listing.

snappy: One-off dividend payment outside the company's regular dividend schedule.
detail: Used when companies have excess cash but don't want to commit to a higher regular dividend (which would imply ongoing capability). Microsoft's 3-dollar special dividend in 2004 (32 billion total) was one of the largest. Costco regularly pays special dividends. Tax treatment generally same as regular dividends in the US. Sometimes used to return capital without buyback excise tax implications.
plain: A one-off cash payout to Shareholders, separate from the regular Dividend — usually when a company has spare cash to distribute.

snappy: Company separates a subsidiary into a standalone public entity — existing shareholders receive new shares.
detail: Standard tax-free reorganisation in the US. Notable spin-offs: GE's healthcare (GE HealthCare, 2023), GE Vernova (energy, 2024), Kellanova/WK Kellogg, ADT split. Often creates value when the spin-off has different growth or capital-allocation characteristics than the parent. Spin-off shares typically underperform initially as Index Funds and ETFs are forced to sell the new shares (the spin isn't yet in indexes).
plain: When a company separates one of its business units into a brand-new standalone listed company — existing shareholders get free shares of the new firm.

snappy: Illegal practice of placing orders with no intent to execute — to mislead other traders about supply or demand.
detail: Banned under Dodd-Frank. The 2010 Flash Crash trader Navinder Sarao was convicted of spoofing E-mini S&P futures. JPMorgan paid 920 million in 2020 to settle CFTC and SEC spoofing charges related to its precious metals desk. Detection algorithms (cancelled orders relative to executed orders, patterns of one-sided pressure followed by reversal) identify suspicious behaviour for regulators.
plain: Illegally placing fake buy or sell orders with no intention of executing them, just to fool other traders about real demand — banned and prosecuted.

snappy: ETF holding physical gold — gives investors gold exposure without bars.
detail: SPDR Gold shares (GLD), launched 2004, was the first major spot gold ETF — now holds roughly 27 million ounces (worth 80 billion dollars). ishares Gold Trust (IAU) is the largest competitor. The shares represent a fractional ownership stake in actual gold held in vaults (HSBC London for GLD). The 2024 launch of US spot Bitcoin ETFs explicitly modelled the GLD structure.
plain: An exchange-traded fund holding actual gold bars in a vault — letting investors track the gold price without storing metal themselves.

snappy: Spot market is the physical commodity delivered now; futures are contracts for later delivery.
detail: Spot oil prices reflect the cargo available at the delivery point today; futures reflect expected price plus storage, financing, and convenience yield. Spot markets are usually thinner and more locally driven; futures are highly liquid global benchmarks. The basis (spot minus futures) varies with local supply, demand, transport constraints. Refiners and traders arbitrage the basis when it strays from fundamentals.
plain: Buying a commodity for delivery today (spot) versus locking in a price for delivery later (Futures) — two related but distinct markets.

snappy: Bond price sensitivity to a one-basis-point change in credit spread.
detail: Credit equivalent of interest-rate duration. A bond with 7-year spread duration loses 0.07 percent per bp of spread widening. Long-duration HY bonds get hammered when spreads widen in stress. Portfolio managers manage spread duration separately from rate duration — IG bond funds tend to be high spread duration and high rate duration; HY funds high spread duration, lower rate duration.
plain: A measure of how much a bond's price moves if its credit risk premium widens by a tiny amount — sister concept to interest-rate Duration.

snappy: Bankruptcy-remote legal entity created solely to hold assets and issue securities.
detail: The legal shell behind every CLO, CDO, MBS, and ABS. Structured to be isolated from the originator's bankruptcy — if the bank or originator fails, the SPV's assets remain available to its bondholders. SPVs are typically Delaware or Cayman entities with limited purposes set in the trust agreement. The 'orphan' SPV variant (owned by a charity, not the originator) provides extra bankruptcy isolation.
plain: A standalone legal company set up purely to hold assets and issue bonds against them — protected from the parent firm's bankruptcy.

snappy: ECB's annual review setting bank-specific capital and qualitative requirements.
detail: Single Supervisory Mechanism conducts SREP for major euro-area banks. Outputs: Pillar 2 Requirement (binding capital surcharge), Pillar 2 Guidance (non-binding capital guidance), qualitative supervisory measures. Bank-by-bank assessment of business model, governance, capital adequacy, liquidity. Results not fully public — but ratings categories disclosed.
plain: The European Central Bank's yearly health check on each big eurozone Bank, which sets bespoke Capital and risk-management requirements.

snappy: High inflation combined with high unemployment and stagnant growth.
detail: Classic 1970s phenomenon: 1973-1981 saw the US suffer through repeated stagflation episodes triggered by oil shocks. Confounds standard Phillips Curve thinking — both inflation and unemployment rising. Volcker's tight monetary policy 1979-82 broke it at huge employment cost. 2022's surge of inflation amid solid employment was widely feared to be a stagflation precursor but the US navigated to disinflation without major job losses. UK 2022-24 came closer to mild stagflation.
plain: The miserable combination of rising prices, high unemployment, and a stalled economy — what 1970s economies suffered through after oil shocks.

snappy: Fed facility that lends cash overnight against Treasury collateral at a pre-set rate.
detail: Launched July 2021 after the September 2019 repo spike. Lets primary dealers (and some banks) borrow from the Fed against Treasury securities at a rate slightly above IORB, capping how high repo rates can spike. Counterparts to ON RRP: SRF caps the upside, ON RRP caps the downside. Combined, they form a tighter corridor for short rates.
plain: A Fed desk swapping cash for US Treasury securities overnight at a set rate — caps how high overnight borrowing costs can spike.

snappy: Quantitative strategy exploiting short-term price deviations from statistical patterns.
detail: Pioneered by Morgan Stanley's APT desk (1980s) and David Shaw's DE Shaw (1988). Two main flavours: pairs trading (mean reversion between related instruments) and broader equity stat arb (industry-neutral factor exposures). Modern stat arb is dominated by Two Sigma, Renaissance, AQR, Citadel. Annual returns have compressed as the field has grown but still significant for top performers.
plain: A computer-driven strategy that bets on small, short-lived patterns in how related stocks tend to move relative to each other.

snappy: Mathematical model for systems evolving randomly over time.
detail: Foundational to derivative pricing and quant modelling. Common examples: Brownian motion (continuous random walk — Black-Scholes), Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (mean-reverting), Poisson process (jumps), Levy processes (broader fat-tailed class). The choice of stochastic process shapes pricing models. Calibration to historical data and option prices selects the process and parameters that fit best.
plain: A maths recipe for how something moves when randomness is baked in — the building block for pricing options and other random-payoff contracts.

snappy: Class of models where volatility follows its own random process, separate from the underlying.
detail: Heston, SABR, and others are stochastic-vol models. Capture vol smile and term-structure dynamics that local-vol models miss. Trade-off: more parameters to calibrate, more computational cost. Hybrid local-stochastic vol (LSV) models combine the calibration-fit of local vol with the realistic dynamics of stochastic vol. Standard in modern exotic-options desks.
plain: A pricing technique where the amount of price wobble is itself wobbly — gives more realistic option values than assuming volatility stays constant.

snappy: Unit of ownership in a corporation — a tradable slice of equity.
detail: Stocks (or 'shares') are issued by corporations to raise capital. Holders are shareholders, entitled to a share of profits (via dividends), votes on corporate matters, and residual value on liquidation. Common stock is the default flavour; preferred stock has bond-like priority. Stocks trade on exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, LSE) or OTC, with prices set continuously by buy and sell orders.
plain: A small piece of ownership in a public company that you can buy and sell — its price changes daily based on demand.

snappy: Temporary transfer of shares from a long-holder to a short-seller — a fee is paid.
detail: Custodian banks (State Street, BNY Mellon) and prime brokers run the lending. Long holders (pension funds, mutual funds, ETFs) lend their shares for extra income — typically 5-50 bps annualised, much higher for 'hard-to-borrow' names. The borrower (typically a short-seller or arbitrageur) returns the shares on demand. Stock-loan markets are opaque but essential plumbing for short-selling.
plain: When a long-term Shareholder temporarily rents their shares to someone else — usually a Short Seller — in exchange for a small fee.

snappy: Company increases shares outstanding while proportionally reducing per-share price.
detail: Two-for-one split halves the price, doubles the share count — total market cap unchanged. Often used by companies whose share prices have grown to levels (1,000+ dollars) that limit retail accessibility. Tesla's 5:1 split (2020), Apple's 4:1 split (2020), Nvidia's 10:1 split (2024). Mechanical effect on price; theoretical equivalence to a stock dividend with similar reverse-purpose effect.
plain: When a company swaps each share for several smaller ones — total value is unchanged, but each share now trades at a lower price.

snappy: Order that becomes a market order once a trigger price is touched.
detail: Stop-buy triggers above the current price; stop-sell (stop-loss) triggers below. Used to enter on breakouts or exit losing positions automatically. Stop orders aren't visible in the order book — they convert to market orders only on trigger. The May 2010 Flash Crash was amplified by stop-loss cascades — once prices started falling, stops triggered into thin liquidity, accelerating the rout.
plain: A dormant instruction that only triggers a buy or sell once the price crosses a level you set — often used to cap losses automatically.

snappy: 600 large- and mid-cap stocks across 17 European countries — the broad European equity benchmark.
detail: More comprehensive than the headline national indexes (FTSE 100, DAX, CAC 40, IBEX). Heavy in financials, consumer staples, healthcare. Operated by STOXX (Deutsche Börse subsidiary). Tracked by ishares STOXX Europe 600 (EXSA), large European ETFs. Eurostoxx 50 (50 large euro-area stocks) is the narrower derivatives-focused alternative.
plain: A broad Index tracking 600 large and mid-sized European companies — the standard yardstick for European stock performance.

snappy: US government's emergency oil stockpile — held in salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana.
detail: Established 1975 post-Arab embargo. Capacity 714 million barrels; held roughly 350 million as of late 2024 after massive 2022 releases (180 million barrels) aimed at cushioning post-Ukraine prices. SPR releases require presidential authorisation; the 2022 release was the largest in history. Refilling the SPR at lower prices is a Biden-administration objective. Other countries maintain analogous reserves.
plain: A vast US government stockpile of crude oil held in underground salt caverns — tapped in emergencies to ease shortages or cool prices.

snappy: Risk calculation applying hypothetical or historical extreme scenarios to current portfolios.
detail: Standard scenarios: 1987 crash repeat, 2008 financial crisis, 1998 LTCM crisis, 2020 COVID crash. Forward-looking scenarios: 25 percent equity drop, 200 bp rate move, 30 percent FX move. Banks and asset managers run stress tests routinely. Regulatory stress tests (CCAR, EBA tests) prescribe specific scenarios. The 2023 SVB collapse highlighted gaps between internal stress tests and actual rate-rise scenarios.
plain: Running a portfolio or Bank through fake disasters — like a 2008-style crash — to see how big the losses get and whether the cushion holds.

snappy: Price at which an option holder can buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
detail: Set at trade inception. Determines moneyness: a call with strike below current price is in-the-money; above is out-of-the-money. Listed options trade at standardised strikes — typically integer dollar increments for cheap stocks, larger gaps for expensive ones. Index options strike in 5- or 25-point increments. OTC options can use any strike negotiated between counterparties.
plain: The fixed price agreed in advance at which the buyer of a contract can buy or sell the Underlying.

full: Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal
plain: A Treasury bond chopped into its individual Coupon and principal payments — each piece trades separately as its own Zero-Coupon bond.
snappy: Treasury notes and bonds split into individual zero-coupon pieces for separate trading.
detail: Created in 1985 to allow dealers to strip Treasury coupons and principal into single-payment securities. A 30-year T-bond becomes 60 coupon strips plus 1 principal strip. Each strip trades as a zero-coupon bond. Used heavily by pension funds and insurance companies for liability matching — long-dated strips have the highest duration of any liquid US fixed-income instrument. Reconstitution (rebuilding the bond from strips) is allowed.

plain: A custom-built investment that bundles a bond with an option payoff — sold mostly to wealthier individuals.
snappy: Bundled bond-and-derivative instrument with a custom payoff — typically issued by an investment bank for retail or private-bank clients.
detail: Common shapes: principal-protected notes, autocallables, range accruals, equity-linked notes with knock-in puts. Issuer (a bank) embeds the option in a debt instrument that pays the investor a tailored payoff at maturity. Marketed heavily to wealth-management clients seeking yield or specific market views. Roughly 100 billion dollars annual US issuance. Criticised for opaque pricing and embedded dealer margins. You'll hear about structured notes from private banks and wealth advisers pitching yield enhancement.

snappy: Local custodian appointed by a global custodian to hold securities in a specific jurisdiction.
detail: Global custodian (State Street) appoints local sub-custodians (a local bank in each market) to access the local CSD. The 2008 Madoff fraud highlighted sub-custody risks; subsequent rules tightened due-diligence requirements. Cross-border investing depends on robust sub-custody networks. Sub-custodian risk includes country risk, operational risk, and legal/regulatory risk.
plain: A local Bank that physically holds foreign securities for a bigger international custodian — the local link in a global custody chain.

snappy: Bond ranking junior to senior debt — paid after seniors in default.
detail: Banks issue subordinated debt as part of regulatory capital structures (Tier 2 capital). Holders receive higher coupons in exchange for taking deeper-in-the-capital-stack risk. Recovery rates historically 10-30 percent. In bank resolution scenarios under the BRRD (Europe), sub debt is fair game for bail-in before senior debt — confirmed in the March 2023 Credit Suisse rescue where 17 billion of AT1 was wiped out.
plain: A bond that ranks below regular bonds in default — holders get paid only after everyone senior is made whole.

snappy: Junior tranches absorbing losses below a senior tranche — creates the senior's credit cushion.
detail: If a CLO senior tranche is 70 percent of the deal, it has 30 percent subordination — losses can hit 30 percent of the pool before the senior tranche takes any loss. Rating agencies set subordination levels to achieve target ratings: AAA seniors typically require 30-40 percent subordination in CLOs. Other forms of credit enhancement: overcollateralisation, reserve accounts, and excess spread.
plain: The way junior slices of a bundled-loan deal take losses first — building a cushion so the senior slices stay safe.
Borrowers with weak credit histories — they pay higher interest because lenders see a bigger risk of default.
snappy: Borrowers with damaged credit — pay higher rates to compensate lenders for the elevated default risk.
detail: FICO scores below 620 typically qualify as subprime. Subprime mortgage loans drove the 2003-07 housing boom and the 2008 collapse — Countrywide, New Century, and similar lenders pushed adjustable-rate subprime mortgages to borrowers who couldn't sustain payments. Subprime auto lending grew aggressively post-2010 and faces its own stress periodically. You'll still hear 'subprime' as shorthand for any credit segment of dubious quality.

snappy: Mortgage to a borrower with poor credit history or other adverse underwriting features.
detail: FICO scores below 620, no income verification, high loan-to-value ratios, or option-ARM payment features. Subprime origination peaked around 600 billion annually in 2005-06, then collapsed. The wave of subprime defaults in 2007 triggered the 2008 financial crisis. Modern definitions and underwriting standards have tightened; what's called 'non-prime' or 'non-QM' today is far better-underwritten than pre-crisis subprime.
plain: A home loan given to borrowers with weak credit — common before the 2008 crisis, when mass defaults helped trigger the meltdown.

snappy: Abrupt reversal of capital inflows to an emerging economy — typically triggers currency crisis.
detail: Coined by economist Guillermo Calvo. Mechanism: foreign investors lose confidence (whether for local reasons or global risk-off), pull capital out simultaneously, currency plunges, financing dries up for the country's banks and corporates. The 2013 Fed Taper Tantrum was a partial sudden stop for the 'Fragile Five' (Brazil, India, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey). Reserves cushion the blow; debt structure determines damage.
plain: When foreign investors abruptly pull their money out of an emerging country — the currency tumbles and local Banks struggle to refinance.

snappy: Sweetener and ethanol feedstock — concentrated production in Brazil and India.
detail: Two ICE-listed contracts: Sugar No 11 (raw, world price) and No 16 (refined, US domestic). Brazil produces roughly 40 percent of global supply. Brazilian sugar/ethanol mills swap between products based on price ratios — drives sugar supply elasticity. India is the second-largest producer; government policy and monsoon weather drive Indian sugar dynamics. EU sugar reform in 2017 removed quotas and shifted European pricing.
plain: A sweetener crop traded on global exchanges — mostly grown in Brazil and India, also a feedstock for ethanol fuel.
The mistake of judging an investment strategy by looking only at survivors — and forgetting the ones that went bust and quietly disappeared.
snappy: Statistical bias from studying only the survivors of a process — overstates historical returns.
detail: A pervasive trap in finance research. Backtesting a strategy on today's S&P 500 constituents ignores companies that delisted, went bankrupt, or got acquired — they're gone from the database. Hedge-fund index returns are systematically inflated because failed funds stop reporting. Mutual-fund category averages similarly skew upward as poor performers get merged out of existence. Academic research adjusts for survivorship using point-in-time databases like CRSP. You'll hear it cited in any rigorous strategy-backtest critique.

snappy: Gap between the swap rate and the Treasury yield at the same maturity.
detail: Quoted in basis points. A 10-year swap rate of 4.50 percent versus a 10-year Treasury at 4.30 percent gives a 20 bp swap spread. Negative swap spreads (common since 2015) reflect dealer balance-sheet costs from holding Treasury inventory, regulatory capital pressure, and net duration demand. Once seen as a credit signal, now a plumbing indicator.
plain: The gap between a Swap rate and the matching Treasury yield — once read as a credit signal, now mostly a plumbing indicator.

snappy: Option to enter into an Interest Rate Swap at a future date — pays fixed (payer) or receives fixed (receiver).
detail: Two flavours: European (one exercise date) and Bermudan (several). A payer swaption protects against rates rising; a receiver swaption protects against rates falling. Quoted by tenor of the swap (e.g. '5 into 10' = a 5-year option into a 10-year swap). Used by corporates locking in funding costs and by banks hedging callable bonds and mortgage pipelines. Vol surface fit with the SABR Model.
plain: An option that lets the buyer enter into a future Interest Rate Swap on agreed terms — used to hedge before rates move against you.

full: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
snappy: Global banking messaging network — handles payment, securities, FX messages.
detail: Belgium-based cooperative owned by member banks. Roughly 11,000 institutions across 200-plus countries. Sends 50 million-plus messages daily. Cut off Russian banks in 2022 in response to Ukraine invasion — significantly limited Russian cross-border banking. Replaced by competing systems (SPFS in Russia, CIPS in China) as geopolitical sanctions concerns grow.
plain: A worldwide messaging network Banks use to send each other payment and trading instructions — the plumbing behind most cross-border transfers.

snappy: CLO using CDS rather than physical loans for credit exposure.
detail: References a basket of loans via CDS contracts rather than owning the loans outright. Issuer (typically a bank) buys protection on its loan portfolio; investors sell protection and earn premiums. Lets banks transfer credit risk off-balance-sheet without selling the loans. Synthetic CLO issuance has grown post-2018 as banks face higher regulatory capital requirements on retained credit risk. SRT (Significant Risk Transfer) trades fall in this space.
plain: A bundle that mimics owning loans by selling protection on them via CDS contracts — lets Banks shift risk without selling the loans outright.

snappy: Long call plus short put at the same strike — same payoff as owning the stock.
detail: Put-call parity in action: long call plus short put equals long stock minus PV of strike. Used to replicate equity exposure without borrowing, to manage tax timing, or to circumvent shareholding limits. The reverse — synthetic short — combines long put and short call. Conversion and reversal trades exploit small mispricings between cash and synthetic positions, mostly arbitraged away.
plain: Combining a bought Call and a sold Put at the same Strike Price to mimic owning the stock — same payoff, no actual shares.
