snappy: Settlement one business day after trade — US equities adopted T+1 in May 2024.
detail: Replaced the long-running T+2 cycle. Shorter settlement reduces counterparty risk between trade and final ownership transfer but compresses post-trade processing time. India was the first major market on T+1; Canada and Mexico moved simultaneously with the US. UK and EU equities remain on T+2 as of late 2024. T+0 (same-day) settlement studies ongoing.
plain: A rule that finalises a stock trade one business day after it's agreed — US markets moved to this faster cycle in May 2024.

snappy: Standard equity settlement cycle in most markets outside the US — two business days post-trade.
detail: EU and UK equities, Asian markets, most government bonds outside the US. Long-standing standard before the US T+1 transition. Most international FX spot also settles T+2 (except USD/CAD and USD/MXN at T+1). The transition costs of shortening settlement cycles are significant — affects collateral pipelines, fail rates, and cross-border timing. EU consulting on potential T+1 move 2027+.
plain: The longer settlement cycle still used in Europe and most other markets — stock trades take two business days to fully complete.

snappy: Short-term US government debt — matures in one year or less, issued at discount.
detail: Sold at auction by the Treasury weekly in 4-, 8-, 13-, 17-, 26-, and 52-week maturities. Pay no coupon — return is the gap between purchase price and face value at maturity. The three-month T-bill rate is the most common proxy for the risk-free rate in academic finance. Money funds hold trillions in T-bills as the safest dollar parking spot.
plain: A super-short-term US government IOU that matures in a year or less — bought below face value and pays the difference when it matures.

snappy: Long-term US government debt — 20 or 30-year maturity, fixed coupon.
detail: Issued by the Treasury monthly via auction. Pays semiannual coupon, returns principal at maturity. The 30-year T-bond ('the long bond') is the longest standard Treasury maturity — its yield reflects inflation expectations and term premium far out the curve. Used by pension funds and insurance companies to match long-duration liabilities. Liquidity is thinner than the 10-year, so price moves can be sharper.
plain: A long-term US government bond, usually 20 or 30 years — pays a fixed Coupon twice a year until it matures.

snappy: Medium-term US government debt — 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10-year maturity, fixed coupon.
detail: Pays semiannual coupon. Auctioned monthly. The 10-year T-note is the most watched maturity in global markets — its yield benchmarks mortgage rates, swap spreads, and equity valuations. Sold in increments of a hundred dollars face value. Quoted in thirty-seconds: '100-08' means 100 and 8/32 of par. Total US Treasury Notes outstanding: roughly fourteen trillion in 2024.
plain: A medium-term US government bond — matures in 2 to 10 years and pays a fixed Coupon every six months.

snappy: Risk of extreme outcomes — events in the tails of return distributions.
detail: Financial markets have fatter tails than Gaussian models suggest. Examples: 1987 crash (22 percent in one day, a 20-sigma event under Gaussian assumptions), 2008 Lehman week, March 2020 COVID crash, 2022 Russia-Ukraine equity vol. Standard portfolios underestimate tail risk; portfolios benefit from explicit tail hedges (long-vol, long Treasury securities, gold). Nassim Taleb's 'Black Swan' framework popularised tail-risk thinking.
plain: The danger of rare but devastating losses — events markets treat as nearly impossible until they happen, like the 1987 crash.

snappy: May 2013 EM rout triggered by Bernanke's hint that the Fed would taper QE.
detail: Fed Chair Ben Bernanke testified May 22 2013 that the Fed might begin reducing asset purchases. EM currencies, bonds, and equities sold off sharply over the following months. The 'Fragile Five' (Brazil, India, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey) saw the worst depreciation due to current-account vulnerabilities. The episode became a cautionary tale for Fed communication and shaped how central banks now signal policy changes.
plain: The 2013 emerging-market sell-off triggered when the Fed first hinted it would slow its post-crisis bond buying — investors fled risky assets.

snappy: Monetary-policy rule prescribing the fed funds rate based on inflation gap and output gap.
detail: Published 1993 by John Taylor. Rule: rate equals r-star plus inflation plus 0.5 times (inflation minus target) plus 0.5 times output gap. Used as benchmark for evaluating Fed policy — Taylor Rule estimates often deviate from actual Fed policy in interesting ways. Numerous variants and modifications (inertial Taylor, balanced approach). Fed itself doesn't follow any specific rule but considers Taylor-Rule prescriptions in policy discussions.
plain: A formula suggesting where a central bank should set interest rates based on how far inflation and employment are from target.

snappy: Post-trade analysis measuring execution quality against benchmarks.
detail: Standard benchmarks: arrival price (IS), VWAP, TWAP, opening/closing prices, reverse-VWAP. Buy-side institutions use TCA to evaluate brokers, algos, and traders. Pre-trade TCA forecasts expected costs to guide execution choices. Regulatory frameworks (MiFID II, Reg BI) increasingly require TCA disclosure to investors. Vendors: Abel Noser, ITG, IHS Markit (LSEG), Trade Informatics.
plain: A post-trade health check that measures how good a price you actually got compared to typical benchmarks like the day's average.

snappy: Direct offer to buy shares from existing shareholders at a stated price.
detail: Used in hostile takeovers (bypass target's board), going-private transactions, and accelerated share repurchases. Standard premium 20-40 percent over market price. Subject to SEC Reg 14D-9. Famous tender offers: Microsoft's failed 2008 Yahoo bid, Cooper Tire's 2014 tender, frequent activist-investor tenders. Distinct from open-market purchases which don't require formal offer documentation.
plain: A formal public offer to buy shares directly from existing Shareholders at a stated price — often used in takeover bids.

snappy: Mexican peso devaluation in December 1994 that triggered EM-wide capital flight.
detail: Mexico had been running a current account deficit funded by short-term USD-denominated debt (tesobonos). When the political environment soured and capital flowed out, reserves drained. The government devalued, then floated. Peso fell 50 percent in days. Argentina, Brazil hit by contagion. US-led 50-billion-dollar rescue package (Clinton, Rubin, Greenspan). Lasting effect: established the modern IMF crisis-response playbook.
plain: Mexico's 1994 currency collapse — the peso lost half its value in days, dragging other emerging markets down with it.

snappy: Extra yield long-dated bonds pay over rolling short bonds — compensation for locking up money.
detail: If investors only demanded expected average short rates over the bond's life, long yields would equal those expected averages. They don't — they include a term premium that compensates for inflation surprise, default risk, and inconvenience. The Federal Reserve's ACM model decomposes long yields into expected rates and term premium. Term premium turned negative after 2014 QE — unprecedented in modern history.
plain: Extra yield long-dated bonds pay over short ones — compensation investors demand for locking their money up for years.

snappy: CME-published forward-looking version of SOFR — used in business loans.
detail: Calculated from SOFR derivatives (SOFR futures and OIS) to produce 1-, 3-, 6-, and 12-month rates known at the start of each period. Solves the practical problem that compounded-in-arrears SOFR isn't usable for business loans where borrowers need to know the rate upfront. Strict use restrictions: ARRC limits Term SOFR to specific cash-product use cases, not derivatives.
plain: A version of SOFR set at the start of each period rather than averaged in arrears — useful for loans where borrowers want certainty.

snappy: Implied vol across different option maturities — usually upward-sloping in calm markets.
detail: Short-dated vol typically prices lower than long-dated because the long maturity has more time for vol surprises. Inverts during stress — short vol spikes above long vol when crisis is acute. Tracked by VIX futures curve, which sometimes inverts ahead of recessions or events. Vol-arbitrage strategies trade calendar spreads (long one tenor, short another) to capture term-structure mispricings.
plain: The pattern of option volatility across different expiries — usually higher for longer-dated contracts, but flips during a crisis.

snappy: Option's price decay per day — how much premium is lost to time passing.
detail: Negative for long options (option-buyers lose to theta), positive for short options. Accelerates as expiry approaches — particularly the last 30 days, and especially the last week. Short-premium strategies (iron condors, naked options) live or die on theta versus realised vol. Quoted as dollars per day for a position. Watched closely by retail options sellers who write covered calls for income.
plain: How much an option loses in value each day just because time is passing — accelerates sharply as expiry approaches.

snappy: Minimum price increment a security can trade at.
detail: Most US stocks above 1 dollar trade in penny ticks (0.01 dollar). Sub-penny tick proposals (0.005, 0.001) periodically debated. Smaller ticks tighten spreads but reduce displayed liquidity (incentive to post resting orders shrinks). Futures and options have venue-specific tick sizes — SPX options in 0.05 dollar, ES in 0.25 index points. SEC's 2024 tick-size reforms reduce some pilot stocks to half-penny ticks.
plain: The smallest amount a stock or other security's price can move — usually a penny for US shares, but varies by venue and product.

snappy: CET1 plus Additional Tier 1 — going-concern capital that absorbs losses while bank operates.
detail: Includes CET1 (highest-quality) plus AT1 instruments (CoCo bonds with conversion triggers). Basel III minimum 6 percent of RWA. Distinct from Tier 2 (gone-concern, subordinated debt) which absorbs losses only at resolution. Heightened AT1 scrutiny post-Credit Suisse 2023 wipe-out — Tier 1 instruments now command higher yields than pre-2023.
plain: A Bank's highest-quality reserves — mostly Shareholder equity — that absorb losses while the bank keeps operating normally.

snappy: Subordinated bank debt — absorbs losses in resolution but not as going concern.
detail: Includes subordinated bonds with at least five-year maturities and other 'gone-concern' instruments. Basel III minimum (combined with Tier 1) 8 percent of RWA. Less expensive than Tier 1 capital. Banks issue Tier 2 as a cost-effective layer above subordinated debt eligibility. Tier 2 holders sit above equity and AT1 in the resolution hierarchy.
plain: A Bank's second-tier reserves — mostly Subordinated Debt — that absorb losses only when the bank is being wound down.

snappy: Option premium beyond intrinsic value — captures uncertainty and remaining time to expiry.
detail: An ATM option has zero intrinsic value; all its premium is time value. Decays through theta as expiry approaches. Time value is largest for at-the-money options (highest uncertainty about whether they'll end in-money). Time value depends on implied volatility, time to expiry, interest rates, and dividend expectations. Falls to zero precisely at expiry.
plain: The chunk of an option's price that comes from uncertainty and remaining time — separate from any value the option already has if exercised today.

snappy: Order parameter specifying how long an order stays active.
detail: GTC (Good-Till-Cancelled), DAY (cancel at session close), IOC (Immediate-or-Cancel — fill what you can, cancel rest), FOK (Fill-or-Kill — all or nothing). Different markets and broker platforms offer varying TIF options. Algos use IOC heavily to probe for liquidity at multiple venues. Retail traders mostly use DAY orders implicitly.
plain: An instruction telling your broker how long an order stays alive — for example, until end of day, or until you cancel it.
US government bonds whose principal grows with inflation — protects holders from losing purchasing power.
snappy: US Treasury bonds with principal indexed to CPI — pay real, not nominal, returns.
detail: Principal adjusts with the CPI-U index; coupon is paid on the inflated principal. At maturity, holders receive the inflation-adjusted principal (or original par if deflation prevailed). Issued in 5-, 10-, and 30-year maturities. About 2 trillion outstanding. The yield gap between regular Treasury securities and TIPS is the breakeven inflation rate — the market's implied future inflation. Pension funds and inflation-focused investors are core holders.

snappy: Dodd-Frank's derivatives provisions — central clearing, SEF trading, swap-dealer registration.
detail: Required mandatory clearing for standardised swaps, real-time public reporting, position limits, and capital and margin requirements for non-cleared derivatives. Created SD (Swap Dealer) and MSP (Major Swap Participant) registration categories. SBSD (Security-Based Swap Dealer) under SEC versus SD under CFTC by product type. Reshaped derivatives industry from 2013 onward. CFTC and SEC continue to issue clarifying guidance.
plain: The chunk of the US Dodd-Frank law that forced standardised Swap contracts onto regulated venues and into central clearing.

snappy: G-SIB requirement to hold enough capital plus eligible debt to absorb losses without taxpayer bailout.
detail: Financial Stability Board standard (2015). G-SIBs must hold TLAC of 18 percent of RWA plus the leverage-ratio component. Eligible: capital instruments plus senior subordinated debt structurally subordinated to operating-company liabilities (US holdco senior debt; EU MREL-eligible instruments). Enables resolution via bail-in rather than bailout. EU's MREL is similar but applies to all banks.
plain: A rule forcing the biggest Banks to keep enough Capital and special bonds on hand to absorb huge losses without needing a taxpayer rescue.
A proposed small tax on every foreign-exchange trade — meant to discourage short-term speculation and raise revenue.
snappy: Theoretical small tax on FX transactions — proposed to dampen short-term speculation.
detail: Proposed by Nobel laureate James Tobin in 1972 after the Bretton Woods collapse. Idea: a tax of even 0.1 percent on currency conversion would deter rapid speculative flows while leaving long-term investment unaffected. Never implemented at the global level — would require coordination to prevent traders moving to untaxed venues. The EU's Financial Transaction Tax (FTT) proposal is its closest modern relative. You'll hear Tobin Tax cited in any debate about taming currency volatility or taxing finance.

snappy: Bank of Japan's overnight benchmark — yen LIBOR replacement.
detail: Volume-weighted median of unsecured overnight yen borrowing market transactions. Replaced JPY LIBOR by end-2021. Used in yen OIS and after LIBOR was retired yen floating-rate instruments. Yen TONAR rates spent most of 2016-2024 near zero or negative due to BoJ ultra-loose policy; positive territory only after the March 2024 policy normalisation.
plain: The Bank of Japan's daily benchmark interest rate, based on actual overnight yen lending between Japanese banks — replaced yen LIBOR.
Broad market-cap-weighted index of Tokyo's main stock board — the Japanese alternative to the better-known Nikkei 225.
snappy: Broad Japanese equity benchmark — market-cap-weighted index of all TSE Prime stocks.
detail: Covers all roughly 2,150 stocks in the Tokyo stock Exchange's Prime market section. Market-cap-weighted methodology (unlike the price-weighted Nikkei 225). Tracked by Topix ETFs and futures. Underlies institutional Japanese-equity benchmarks more often than Nikkei. Toyota, Sony, Mitsubishi UFJ, Keyence are top weights. You'll hear TOPIX cited in any serious Japanese-equity analysis, with Nikkei reserved for headline media coverage.

snappy: One leg pays total return on an asset; the other pays a financing rate.
detail: Equity TRS is the most common flavour: hedge fund receives total return on a stock, pays SOFR plus spread to the bank. Lets the fund get equity exposure with bank-financing leverage and without owning shares. Used to circumvent shareholding disclosure requirements (Archegos), as a tax-efficient alternative to cash equity, and to lock in financing cost. Centrally cleared not common; mostly bilateral.
plain: A contract where one side receives a stock's full gains and Dividends while paying a financing fee — like renting equity exposure.

snappy: Order flow that consistently trades against market-makers because it has informational advantage.
detail: Market-makers lose money to toxic flow on a per-trade basis. HFT firms classify counterparties (retail, institutional, other HFT) and adjust their quotes accordingly. PFOF brokers route retail flow to market-makers specifically because it's non-toxic — retail trades aren't reliably informed. Buy-side flow from sophisticated quant funds is often the most toxic. Dark pools struggle with toxic-flow filtering.
plain: Order flow that consistently outsmarts market-makers — usually from sophisticated traders with informational edge over the firms quoting prices.

snappy: Standard deviation of return differences between a portfolio and its benchmark.
detail: Measure of active risk. Pure index funds: 0-0.2 percent tracking error. Active equity managers: 2-6 percent typical. Hedge funds and concentrated portfolios: higher still. Information Ratio = alpha divided by tracking error — measures skill per unit of active risk. Excessive tracking error in benchmark-aware portfolios attracts client scrutiny. Optimisation algorithms aim to minimise tracking error subject to other constraints.
plain: How much a fund's returns drift away from the Index it's supposed to mirror — low for passive funds, higher for active ones.

snappy: Difference between a country's exports and imports of goods and services.
detail: Trade surpluses (Germany, China, Japan historically) build FX reserves and tend to support the local currency; deficits (US, UK) require capital inflows to fund. The US has run persistent trade deficits since the 1970s, balanced by capital inflows into Treasury securities and equities. Bilateral trade balances (US-China, etc.) are politically charged but economically less meaningful than overall balances.
plain: The difference between what a country sells abroad and what it buys in — a surplus tends to support its Currency, a deficit weighs on it.

snappy: Slice of a structured product with specific priority of payment and risk.
detail: Senior tranche gets paid first, takes losses last; equity tranche gets paid last, absorbs first losses. Mezzanine sits between. Each tranche carries a separate credit rating (senior often AAA, mezzanine BBB, equity unrated). Investors choose tranches matched to their mandate: pension funds buy senior, hedge funds buy equity for higher yield. The 'waterfall' specifies the cash-flow order.
plain: One slice of a bundled-loan deal — each slice has its own risk and payoff, with senior slices safer and junior slices riskier.

snappy: Debt issued by the US Treasury Department — the world's largest fixed-income market.
detail: Includes bills, notes, bonds, TIPS, FRNs, and STRIPS. Issued via auction to primary dealers, who then distribute to the broader market. Total outstanding crossed 35 trillion in 2024. Treasury securities function as the global risk-free benchmark, collateral for repo markets, central-bank reserve holdings, and the foundation of dollar-denominated valuation. Yields on different Treasury maturities form the US yield curve.
plain: The US government's bond issuance — collectively the biggest and most-trusted bond market in the world, used as the global Risk-Free benchmark.

snappy: Repo where a custodian bank handles settlement and collateral management.
detail: BNY Mellon clears the vast majority of US tri-party repo (trillions daily). The custodian holds the collateral, marks it to market, and substitutes one piece for another as needed. Reduces operational burden on the cash lender (typically a money fund) and lets dealers fund a portfolio rather than security-by-security. Distinct from bilateral repo (direct between counterparties) and cleared repo through FICC.
plain: A repo loan where a third-party Bank handles all the paperwork — moves the collateral, marks it daily, and swaps in fresh securities as needed.

snappy: Exploits inconsistencies between cross-rate quotes and the implied rate from two majors.
detail: If EUR/USD is 1.10, USD/JPY is 150, and EUR/JPY is 166, the implied EUR/JPY via the dollar legs is 165 — and an arbitrageur buys EUR/JPY at 165 and sells at 166 for risk-free profit. Algorithms close these gaps in milliseconds, so opportunities are vanishingly small in major pairs but persist in EM and exotic crosses. Reinforces price consistency across the FX matrix.
plain: A near-instant trade that exploits tiny mismatches between three Currency pairs — algorithms close these gaps in milliseconds.

snappy: Combined return from share-price appreciation plus dividends reinvested.
detail: Standard measure of shareholder value creation over a period. Often used in executive compensation — TSR-linked performance shares pay out based on multi-year TSR versus peer group or index. Computed on a total-return basis: assume each dividend is reinvested at the ex-date price. The S&P 500 Total Return Index tracks TSR for the index. Distinguishes from price return (price-only, ignores dividends).
plain: The total payoff to a Shareholder over time — combines the rise in share price with any Dividends paid out.

snappy: Average price across equal time slices — execution algo's simpler sibling to VWAP.
detail: TWAP algos chop an order into evenly-spaced child orders over a chosen window. Used when volume forecasts are unreliable, for less-liquid names, or when minimising signalling matters more than tracking volume. Easier to model and explain than VWAP. Common in crypto and small-cap equities. Critics note TWAP is gameable by predatory algos that detect the regular slicing pattern.
plain: An automated trading style that chops a big order into equal pieces and trades them at steady intervals through the day.

full: Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities
snappy: EU regulatory framework for retail-eligible investment funds.
detail: First adopted 1985, currently UCITS V (in force 2016). Cross-border distribution within EU on a passport basis — a UCITS authorised in Luxembourg can be sold to retail in Spain or Germany. Limits on portfolio concentration, leverage, derivatives. 11 trillion euros in UCITS funds — the dominant European retail fund vehicle. Distinct from AIFMD which covers alternative funds.
plain: An EU rulebook for everyday investment funds that can be sold to retail investors across all member states — Europe's main mutual-fund framework.

snappy: Theory: high-yield currencies should depreciate to offset the rate advantage.
detail: Predicts no excess return from borrowing low-yield currencies to invest in high-yield ones. Famously fails in practice: the carry trade has historically delivered positive excess returns over decades, including during the 2002-08 yen-funded carry bonanza. UIP failure underpins the long-running 'forward premium puzzle' in academic finance. Briefly held during 2008 and 2020 crises when carry trades unwound violently.
plain: The textbook idea that high-yield currencies should weaken to cancel out the rate advantage — but in real life it routinely fails.

snappy: Asset or reference rate a derivative is based on — drives the derivative's price.
detail: Could be a single stock (Apple), an index (S&P 500), a currency pair (EUR/USD), a commodity (WTI), a rate (SOFR), or even another derivative (option on a future). Defines the contract's economics and Greeks. Derivatives draw their name from being 'derived' from underlying prices. Crypto derivatives use cryptocurrencies as underlyings; weather derivatives reference temperature or rainfall indices.
plain: The stock, bond, currency, or other asset whose price a derivative contract is tied to.
An investment bank that buys a company's new shares or bonds and resells them to investors, taking a cut for the service.
snappy: Investment bank that prices and distributes a new securities issue — and often guarantees the proceeds to the issuer.
detail: In a firm-commitment underwriting, the bank buys the entire issue and resells — taking on price risk. In best-efforts, the bank only commits to try. IPO syndicates have a lead underwriter (the bookrunner) plus co-managers, each receiving a share of the gross spread (typically 7 percent of an IPO). Bond underwriting works similarly. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan dominate top global rankings. You'll hear underwriters named in every IPO prospectus and bond pricing announcement.

plain: A Barrier option that only activates if the Underlying price rises and hits the chosen barrier level.
snappy: Knock-in barrier option that activates only if the underlying rises through the barrier level.
detail: One of four standard barrier flavours (up-and-in, up-and-out, down-and-in, down-and-out). Holder gets nothing unless the underlying touches the upper barrier before expiry; once breached, it becomes a vanilla option. A cheap way to express a directional view — pays only if the move is large enough to clear the barrier. Common in FX structured notes and equity-linked products.

plain: A Barrier option that automatically expires worthless if the Underlying price rises and hits the chosen barrier level.
snappy: Knock-out barrier option that extinguishes if the underlying rises through the barrier level.
detail: Mirror of down-and-out. Holder is happy in mild moves but loses everything if the underlying breaches the upper barrier. Used to cheapen calls when the buyer thinks a large rally is unlikely — cap-like exposure. Common in FX (sell upside above target) and equity structured notes. Hedging is tricky near the barrier — large position changes for small spot moves.

plain: A standard, no-frills option — just a strike price, an expiry date, and the right to exercise. Nothing extra.
snappy: Standard option with no exotic features — strike, expiry, exercise rights, nothing more.
detail: The reference point against which exotic options (barriers, Asians, lookbacks) are priced and contrasted. 'Vanilla' because plain and unadorned. Black-Scholes territory — closed-form pricing, fast. CBOE-listed equity options and most FX dealer options are vanilla. Anything more complex sits in structured-product land. Liquidity, transparency, and listing make vanillas the workhorse instrument.

snappy: Second-order Greek — sensitivity of delta to changes in implied volatility.
detail: Captures the interaction between delta and vega. Important for options near the wings (far OTM) where vol moves dramatically shift the delta. Quants manage vanna exposure when running large vol books. Vanna-Volga adjustment is a common FX option-pricing add-on that corrects Black-Scholes for smile effects using vanna and volga.
plain: A finer option risk measure — tracks how much the basic price sensitivity shifts when expected volatility moves.

snappy: Maximum loss expected at a given confidence level over a given horizon.
detail: A 95-percent 1-day VaR of 10 million means there's a 5-percent chance of losing more than 10 million tomorrow. Basel framework requires banks to hold capital against VaR. Three calculation methods: historical simulation (use past returns), parametric (assume normal distribution), Monte Carlo (simulate paths). Tail-risk events repeatedly exceed VaR (2008 banks losing far more than VaR suggested) — hence the shift toward Expected Shortfall.
plain: An estimate of the biggest loss a portfolio is likely to take on a normal bad day — say, the worst day in 100.
A statistical measure of how spread out a set of numbers is — the squared version of volatility, used in pricing and risk maths.
snappy: Squared standard deviation — the workhorse statistic for risk and volatility math.
detail: Variance is volatility squared. Variance swaps pay off in variance units, not volatility, because variance is easier to replicate with a portfolio of options. Realised variance (what actually happened) versus implied variance (what options prices imply) is the building block of the variance risk premium. Quant desks model variance dynamics under stochastic-vol models (Heston, SABR). The CBOE's VIX is calculated from variance, then square-rooted to quote in vol-like units.

snappy: Difference between implied volatility and subsequently realised volatility.
detail: Usually positive: implied vol trades above realised vol on average. Volatility sellers (selling options or variance swaps) capture this premium over time, with occasional crash losses. VRP collapses or inverts during stress — 2008, 2020, 2022 all saw realised vol exceed prior implied vol by wide margins. CBOE's VIX index versus subsequent S&P realised vol is the canonical VRP series.
plain: The gap between how jumpy option markets expect prices to be and how jumpy they actually turn out — usually positive.

snappy: Pure exposure to realised variance — settles on the difference between realised and agreed variance.
detail: OTC product favoured by volatility traders. Notional set in 'vega' or 'variance units'. Linear in variance (not vol), making it different from straddles which require dynamic delta-hedging to extract vol. Crashed dramatically in March 2020 when realised vol spiked far above the strike — dealers who were short var swaps took huge losses. Now mostly cleared via dealer-to-dealer arrangements.
plain: A contract that pays off based purely on how bumpy a stock's price turns out to be — letting traders bet directly on volatility itself.

snappy: Daily cash flows that settle the change in derivative mark-to-market.
detail: If a swap's value falls 100,000 dollars on a given day, the counterparty owes 100,000 in variation margin. Settled in cash or eligible collateral (Treasury securities, often) every business day. Eliminates counterparty risk on existing P&L. Cleared swaps post VM through clearing houses; bilateral swaps via CSA. The 2008 AIG failure was triggered by VM calls AIG couldn't meet.
plain: The daily cash settle-up between two sides of a derivative contract — whoever's losing money sends cash to whoever's winning, every business day.

snappy: Option's price sensitivity to a one-percent change in implied volatility.
detail: A 100-million notional option with vega of 50,000 dollars per vol point gains or loses 50,000 dollars when implied vol moves one percent. Highest for at-the-money options near expiry-equivalent vol levels. Vega-long books make money when vol rises (long vol); vega-short books profit from realised-vol below implied (the vol risk premium). Vol-trading desks manage vega the way rates desks manage DV01.
plain: How much an option's price moves when expected price wobble changes by one percentage point — the main risk measure for volatility traders.

snappy: 30-day implied volatility of S&P 500 index options — the 'fear gauge'.
detail: Calculated by CBOE from SPX options across strikes and tenors. Quoted as annualised vol in percent. Long-run average around 19; spikes above 80 during extreme stress (2008 Lehman crisis, 2020 March pandemic crash). VIX futures (/VX) and VIX options trade on CFE. Volatility ETFs (VXX, UVXY) provide retail VIX exposure with significant contango drag. The volatility benchmark for risk sentiment globally.
plain: An Index that tracks how much US stock investors expect prices to swing over the next month — nicknamed the market's fear gauge.
How jumpy volatility itself is — when markets get nervous, the size of price swings also starts swinging unpredictably.
snappy: Volatility of volatility — the second-order vol measure that drives crash-protection pricing.
detail: Captured by indices like VVIX. High vol of vol means traders expect volatility itself to move sharply — typically when crash fears rise and demand for tail hedges spikes. Stochastic-vol models like Heston and SABR explicitly parameterise vol of vol (nu in SABR). vol of vol exposure shows up in the Greek volga. Long vol of vol strategies (often via VIX call options) hedge against rapid regime shifts in market sentiment.

snappy: Statistical measure of price variability — typically annualised standard deviation of returns.
detail: Higher volatility means bigger price swings. Equity vol typically 15-20 percent annual; safe-haven currencies (CHF, JPY) lower; emerging-market FX higher. Implied vol (from options) versus realised vol (from historical prices) the basic distinction. Volatility clusters — high-vol periods follow high-vol days (the GARCH effect). Mean-reverts to long-run averages, but slowly.
plain: How sharply a price tends to swing — high volatility means big moves up and down, low volatility means calmer behaviour.

snappy: Implied vol curve plotted against strike — typically lower in the middle, higher at wings.
detail: Reflects market pricing of fat-tail risk. The 1987 crash shifted equity vol smiles permanently — out-of-money puts price in crash risk that Black-Scholes doesn't capture. FX vol surfaces have symmetric smiles in major pairs, skewed smiles in EM. Rates options have smiles dependent on the strike convention. Local volatility, stochastic volatility, and SABR models attempt to fit smile shapes consistently.
plain: The U-shaped pattern when you plot option prices across strike levels — extreme Strikes cost more, reflecting the market's fear of big surprises.
A three-dimensional chart that maps out how expensive options of every Strike Price and expiry date are at a given moment.
snappy: Implied-vol grid across strikes and maturities — the canonical option-trader's worksheet.
detail: X-axis: strike (or moneyness). Y-axis: time to expiry. Z-axis: implied volatility. Real-world surfaces aren't flat — out-of-the-money puts are usually pricier than equivalent calls (equity skew), and short-dated options often command higher volatility than long-dated (term-structure inversion in stress). Traders calibrate stochastic-volatility and local-vol models to fit the surface. You'll hear 'vol surface' cited on any options desk and in every structured-product pricing meeting.

snappy: Like a variance swap but settles on realised volatility (square root of variance) — linear in vol.
detail: Less common than variance swaps because the math is harder for dealers to replicate — vol swaps require dynamic hedging in variance space and convexity adjustments. Used when traders want straight directional vol exposure without the convexity of var swaps. Quoted OTC; small market versus var swaps but a real product, especially in single-name equity vol.
plain: A close cousin of the Variance Swap that pays off directly on realised price wobble rather than on its squared version.

snappy: Dodd-Frank provision banning banks from proprietary trading for their own profit.
detail: Section 619 of Dodd-Frank, finalised 2013, effective 2014. Banned banks from prop trading and most hedge-fund/private-equity sponsorship. Required banks to demonstrate market-making was customer-driven, not prop. 2019 'Volcker 2.0' simplifications reduced compliance burden. Sometimes credited with reducing US bank trading-revenue volatility post-2014. Named after former Fed Chair Paul Volcker, its principal advocate.
plain: A US rule banning Banks from making big speculative trades for their own profit — meant to stop deposit-taking banks gambling like hedge funds.

snappy: 1979-1982 Fed tightening that crushed inflation but caused severe recession.
detail: Fed Chair Paul Volcker took over August 1979. Federal funds rate hit 20 percent in 1981. US fell into the longest post-WWII recession (1980, 1981-82); unemployment hit 10.8 percent. CPI fell from 14 percent (1980) to 3 percent (1983). Established Fed credibility on inflation. Volcker shock remains the benchmark for understanding what extreme monetary tightening costs and achieves.
plain: The Fed's brutal late-1970s rate hikes that pushed borrowing costs above 20 percent — broke runaway inflation but caused a deep Recession.

snappy: Second-order Greek — sensitivity of vega to changes in implied volatility.
detail: Measures the curvature of option price in implied vol. Long-volga positions benefit from vol of vol moves (vol spiking from 10 to 30 more than offsets vol grinding back from 30 to 10). Important for ATM options far from expiry and for vol books. Vanna and volga are the two main 'second-order vol Greeks' that vol traders track alongside vega.
plain: A finer option risk measure — tracks how much Vega itself shifts when expected price wobble moves.
Total number of shares or contracts changing hands in a given period — a basic measure of how active a market is.
snappy: Quantity of shares or contracts traded over a given period — basic activity measure.
detail: Daily volume in S&P 500 stocks runs 10-15 billion shares total; SPY ETF alone trades 70-100 million shares daily. Volume spikes around earnings, central-bank announcements, expiration days, and stress events. High volume on price moves signals conviction; low volume moves are easier to fade. Combined with open interest in futures and options, volume tells you whether positions are being opened or closed.

snappy: Historical pattern of intraday volume distribution across a trading day.
detail: US equity volume is U-shaped: heavy in the first and last hours, light in the middle. Index rebalances spike closing-auction volume. VWAP algos slice orders to match the volume curve. Different securities have idiosyncratic curves — illiquid stocks may concentrate volume at the open. Modern algos use machine-learned curves that adapt to recent days and intraday surprises.
plain: The typical pattern of trading activity through the day — heavy at the open and close, quieter in the middle — used to time orders.

snappy: Implied volatility of VIX futures — the vol of vol.
detail: Computed by CBOE from VIX options. Captures the market's expectation of how much VIX itself will move. VVIX spikes when traders rush into VIX call options for tail-risk hedging. Typically trades 80-120, well above VIX's typical 15-25 range, reflecting how much more violent VIX moves are than equity moves. Used in long-vol-of-vol strategies and as a sentiment gauge for crash hedging demand.
plain: An Index measuring how jumpy the VIX itself is expected to be — the wobble of the wobble gauge.

snappy: Average price weighted by traded volume across the day — the execution benchmark.
detail: Resets daily. Traders measure execution quality against VWAP: 'I bought five cents inside.' Brokers offer VWAP algos that slice an order across the day proportional to expected volume, minimising market impact for big trades. Index rebalances and ETF creations often target VWAP. Distinct from arrival-price benchmarks (Implementation Shortfall) which capture timing risk too.
plain: The day's average traded price weighted by volume — the most common yardstick for judging whether a big trade got a fair deal.
Average interest rate a company pays on the mix of debt and equity that funds it — the hurdle rate any new project must beat.
snappy: Blended cost of a company's debt and equity funding — the discount rate for valuing projects and cash flows.
detail: Weighted by market value: cost of equity times equity share plus after-tax cost of debt times debt share. Used as the discount rate in DCF valuation models and the hurdle rate for capital-budgeting decisions. Cost of equity typically estimated via CAPM (risk-free rate plus beta times equity risk premium). A company creates value when ROIC exceeds WACC and destroys value below. Featured in nearly every equity research model.

snappy: Self-reinforcing dynamic where rising wages drive prices up, which drives further wage demands.
detail: 1970s textbook stagflation pattern: oil shock raises prices, unions demand cost-of-living adjustments, businesses raise prices to cover wage costs, repeat. Modern labour markets less unionised; spirals less automatic. 2021-22 inflation surge prompted wage-price-spiral concerns but didn't fully materialise — real wages mostly stayed below price growth, breaking the feedback. Central banks watch real-wage trends to assess spiral risk.
plain: A feedback loop where rising prices push workers to demand higher wages, which then push businesses to raise prices further.

snappy: Expected average time until principal is returned — like duration but for amortising securities.
detail: Most relevant for MBS and ABS where principal returns over time, not in a lump sum. WAL depends heavily on prepayment assumptions — a 30-year MBS might have a WAL of 6 years if prepayments are heavy, 20 years if slow. Quoted in years. Used to size positions in amortising securities and compare them to bullet bonds of similar duration.
plain: The average time before a bundled-loan deal's principal is paid back — like Duration but for bonds where the money trickles in over years.

snappy: Long-dated option issued by a company on its own stock.
detail: Distinct from listed equity options: warrants are issuer-created securities with multi-year tenors (5-10 typical). Used in capital raises (often attached to debt to sweeten terms), SPAC deals (warrants sweetened the early SPAC structures), and crisis-era restructurings (TARP warrants for major bank bailouts). Settles in newly-issued shares when exercised — dilutive to existing holders.
plain: A long-dated option a company issues on its own shares — when exercised, the company issues new shares, diluting existing holders.

full: World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates
snappy: USDA's monthly snapshot of global crop supply, demand, and stocks — moves ag markets.
detail: Released mid-month at noon Eastern. Updates production estimates, ending stocks, demand forecasts for major crops. Bigger-than-expected revisions move corn, soybeans, wheat 2-5 percent on release. Quarterly Grain stocks reports also significant. International equivalent: FAO Food Price Index, less market-moving but watched for macro food-price commentary.
plain: A monthly US government snapshot of global crop supply and demand — moves corn, wheat, and soybean markets when the numbers surprise.

snappy: Trade where the same party is both buyer and seller — artificially inflates volume without economic substance.
detail: Banned under exchange rules. Sometimes attempted to game volume-based metrics (tape painting), or to create misleading impressions of liquidity in thin markets. Crypto exchanges have been particularly criticised for wash trading prior to regulation. Detection: cross-trades between affiliated accounts, near-simultaneous opposing orders. Exchanges run surveillance algorithms to flag wash trades for compliance review.
plain: A bogus trade where the same trader is on both sides — illegal because it inflates volume figures and misleads other market participants.

snappy: Pre-defined order in which a structured product's cash flows are distributed across tranches.
detail: Interest waterfall: senior interest first, then mezz, then equity. Principal waterfall: usually starts with senior amortisation in a 'turbo' structure. Tests embedded in the waterfall (overcollateralisation, interest-coverage tests) redirect cash flow to seniors if performance deteriorates. The 2007-08 mortgage crisis exposed how failure of waterfall tests cascaded through CDOs. Modern deals have triggers tuned from that experience.
plain: The rule for which slice of a bundled-loan deal gets paid first from the incoming cash — senior slices at the top, junior slices last.

snappy: Agricultural commodity price risk driven by weather — drought, frost, heatwaves, flooding.
detail: El Niño and La Niña cycles affect global crop patterns predictably. The 2012 US Midwest drought spiked corn and soybean prices over 50 percent in months. Australian wheat crops sensitive to rainfall during winter. Brazilian frost has driven coffee price spikes. Weather derivatives (CME-listed) hedge specific climate-data outcomes (temperature, rainfall). Climate change intensifies tail-risk events.
plain: The danger that storms, droughts, or heatwaves disrupt crops or energy supply — drives big price swings in commodities like wheat and natural gas.

snappy: Options expiring weekly rather than monthly — most popular for major indexes and large stocks.
detail: SPX Weeklys (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday expirations) trade billions of dollars notional. Provide finer-grained expiry choice for short-dated hedging or speculation. Spurred the rise of 0-day-to-expiry (0DTE) trading. Listed by CBOE in the US, with similar products on other exchanges. Open interest concentrates around upcoming Friday expiries.
plain: Option contracts that expire every Friday rather than only once a month — give traders more precise tools for short-term bets and hedges.

snappy: Global staple grain — food, feed, industrial.
detail: Three major futures contracts: CBOT SRW (soft red winter, Chicago), KC HRW (hard red winter, Kansas City), Minneapolis HRS (hard red spring). Different protein and gluten properties suit different end uses (bread, pastry, pasta). The 2022 Russia-Ukraine invasion spiked wheat to record prices — Black Sea region produces roughly a quarter of global exports. Volatility eased as Black Sea grain initiative restored some flows.
plain: A staple grain used for bread, pasta, and animal feed — traded on US exchanges with different contracts for different protein and gluten properties.

snappy: Friendly counter-acquirer that target seeks to replace a hostile bidder.
detail: Target board prefers being bought by a white knight (often paying a higher price or offering better employment continuity) than by a hostile acquirer. The 2013 Dell going-private deal had Carl Icahn pressing for higher prices; Michael Dell partnered with Silver Lake as the white-knight option. White-knight protections include reciprocal break-up fees and lock-up arrangements.
plain: A friendly buyer that swoops in to acquire a company targeted by a hostile bidder — preferred by the board for better terms.

snappy: Daily reference exchange rate calculated from a five-minute window around 4 PM London time.
detail: Used to value FX-denominated assets, set benchmark FX returns, and rebalance index funds. The 2013 manipulation scandal exposed banks colluding to push the fix rate to profit from client orders timed around the window — leading to billions in fines and methodology overhauls. The window is now five minutes (was one), with broader data sources to reduce manipulation risk. Indispensable for asset-management plumbing.
plain: A daily snapshot of Currency exchange rates taken in a five-minute window around 4 PM London — used to value FX-linked assets worldwide.

snappy: Multilateral development bank funding poverty-reduction and infrastructure projects.
detail: Founded with IMF at Bretton Woods 1944. Five institutions: IBRD (loans to middle-income), IDA (concessional finance for poorest), IFC (private-sector lending), MIGA (guarantees), ICSID (dispute settlement). Total commitments roughly 100 billion annually. Distinct from IMF: World Bank funds projects, IMF stabilises balance of payments. Recent priorities: climate adaptation, pandemic response, conflict states.
plain: A global lender funded by member governments — makes long-term loans for development projects in poorer countries, like roads, schools, and power grids.

snappy: Counterparty credit exposure rises just when the counterparty's credit deteriorates.
detail: Classic example: bank sells CDS protection on a sovereign back to that sovereign's bank — both default trigger together. AIG's 2008 collapse: huge CDS protection sold on mortgages, hammered when housing tanked, exactly when AIG itself was failing. Basel III imposes specific WWR capital charges. Hard to model; recognition is qualitative and judgment-based.
plain: The nasty pattern where the amount you're owed by a counterparty grows precisely when that counterparty becomes more likely to default.

snappy: US benchmark crude oil grade — light, sweet, deliverable to Cushing, Oklahoma.
detail: Quoted in dollars per barrel. NYMEX-listed WTI futures (/CL) are the most-traded energy contract globally. Light (API gravity 39.6) and sweet (low sulphur) make it easier to refine into gasoline. The April 2020 negative WTI episode — front-month settled at minus 37 dollars — was a contango storage-overflow event. Delivery at Cushing creates landlocked pricing dynamics different from waterborne Brent.
plain: The main US benchmark for crude oil — light, low-sulphur barrels priced for delivery in Cushing, Oklahoma.

snappy: Collective term for CVA, DVA, FVA, KVA, MVA — adjustments to derivative fair value.
detail: Modern derivative pricing requires multiple adjustments: CVA (counterparty risk), DVA (own credit), FVA (funding), KVA (regulatory capital), MVA (initial margin funding). Dealers have dedicated XVA desks managing aggregate adjustment exposure. XVA P&L can swing dramatically with market conditions. The 'pure mid' price (Black-Scholes-perfect, no adjustments) is increasingly an academic concept — XVAs are the price.
plain: A family of pricing adjustments tacked onto derivative trades — they account for counterparty risk, funding cost, capital, and other real-world frictions.

snappy: Return a bond pays as a percentage of its price.
detail: Several flavours: current yield (coupon over price), yield-to-maturity (the discount rate equating cash flows to price), yield-to-call (assumes the issuer redeems early). Inverse to price — when rates rise, bond prices fall. The Treasury's daily yield curve, posted by the Federal Reserve, is the global benchmark. Equity 'yield' (dividend over price) is a different beast.
plain: The annual return a bond pays as a percentage of its current price — when bond prices rise, yields fall, and vice versa.

snappy: Yields plotted across maturities — the most-watched chart in markets.
detail: Usually upward-sloping: longer bonds yield more because investors demand a term premium. Inverted curve (short rates above long) has preceded every modern US recession with one false positive (1966). The 10-year-minus-2-year and 10-year-minus-3-month spreads are watched gauges. The Federal Reserve controls the short end via policy rates; the long end reflects growth and inflation expectations plus term premia. Bull steepeners, bear flatteners — every shape carries a macro meaning.
plain: A chart showing bond yields for different lengths of borrowing — its shape signals what investors expect for growth, inflation, and interest rates.

snappy: Central bank caps yields at specific maturities by committing to unlimited buying at those points.
detail: Bank of Japan implemented YCC 2016-2024, pegging the 10-year JGB yield around zero (with bands widened over time). Reserve Bank of Australia attempted YCC during COVID, abandoned painfully in 2021 when markets broke through the cap. Fed considered YCC in 2020 but didn't implement. YCC controls the price of bonds; QE controls the quantity. The BoJ exited YCC March 2024 as inflation finally returned.
plain: When a central bank promises to buy unlimited bonds at a chosen maturity to keep that yield pinned at a target level.
A fee a commercial borrower must pay to repay a mortgage early — designed to keep the lender's expected yield intact.
snappy: Prepayment penalty on commercial mortgages — compensates lender for reinvestment-rate gap.
detail: Standard in US commercial mortgage-backed securities. If a borrower repays before maturity when interest rates have fallen, the lender would otherwise have to reinvest at lower yields — yield maintenance forces the borrower to pay the present value of the lost interest. Distinct from defeasance, where Treasury collateral is substituted to replicate the cash flows. Makes commercial mortgages much less prepayment-prone than residential ones. You'll hear yield maintenance cited in any CMBS prospectus or refinancing analysis.

snappy: YTM calculated assuming the issuer redeems the bond at the earliest redemption date.
detail: Callable bonds let the issuer redeem early — typically when rates fall and the issuer can refinance cheaper. YTC computes the yield to that redemption date instead of final maturity. For premium-priced callable bonds, YTC is usually lower than YTM and is the realistic measure. The 'yield to worst' is the lower of YTC and YTM — what conservative analysts quote.
plain: The return on a bond if the issuer redeems it early at the first opportunity — usually lower than the headline yield.

snappy: Total annualised return if you buy a bond today and hold to maturity.
detail: Solves for the discount rate that equates the bond's future cash flows (coupons plus face value) to its current market price. Implicitly assumes you reinvest each coupon at the same yield. Quoted as the headline yield in bond tables. Differs from current yield (coupon over price) which ignores principal gain or loss. Bond traders quote YTM, not current yield, for anything maturity-bearing.
plain: The total annual return you'd earn if you bought a bond today and held it until it matured — the headline number quoted for any bond.

snappy: Number of standard deviations a value is from the mean.
detail: Statistical measure: (observation minus mean) divided by standard deviation. Z-score above 2 (or below -2) often used as 'unusual' threshold. Altman Z-score (1968) is the classic corporate-credit version: combines profitability, leverage, liquidity, solvency, asset-turnover ratios to predict bankruptcy. Z-score below 1.8 historically signals high distress risk. Many other Z-scores used in market regimes, sentiment, statistical anomaly detection.
plain: A simple statistic showing how unusual a number is compared to its typical range — the further from zero, the rarer the value.

snappy: Constant spread added to the Treasury zero curve that prices a bond at market.
detail: More precise than nominal yield spread (which compares to a single Treasury point) — Z-spread accounts for the timing of every cash flow. The 'zero-volatility' qualifier means no embedded option value assumed. For non-callable bonds, Z-spread equals OAS. For callable bonds, OAS subtracts the option value from Z-spread. Standard quote in IG bond markets.
plain: The extra yield a corporate bond pays over the US Treasury Yield Curve — quoted as one number pricing every cash flow's timing.

snappy: Bond with no coupon — sold at deep discount, pays face value at maturity.
detail: All return comes from the spread between purchase price and the face value paid at maturity. The longer the maturity, the steeper the discount. STRIPS — separated trading of registered interest and principal — let dealers strip Treasury notes into zero-coupon pieces. Zero-coupon bonds have higher duration than coupon bonds of the same maturity, making them powerful tools for pension liability matching.
plain: A bond that pays no Interest along the way — you buy it at a deep discount and receive the full face value at maturity.

snappy: Options expiring the same day they're traded — exploded in popularity 2022-2024.
detail: Possible because of daily SPX expirations and CBOE listing rolling weeklies. Now roughly half of all SPX options volume. Used by traders for tactical exposure, theta-harvest strategies, and gamma plays. Critics argue 0DTE creates intraday market microstructure stress: dealer gamma hedging needs accelerate, contributing to V-shaped intraday moves. Regulatory scrutiny ongoing but no major restrictions yet.
plain: An option contract that expires the same day it's traded — exploded in popularity after 2022 for tactical short-term bets on the US stock market.

snappy: Hypothetical floor on nominal interest rates around zero — limits conventional monetary policy.
detail: Fed hit the ZLB Dec 2008 - Dec 2015 and Mar 2020 - Mar 2022. ECB went below the ZLB to negative rates (-0.5 percent at deepest). The presumed ZLB at zero turned out to be slightly negative as central banks discovered they could push below zero. Once at the ZLB, central banks rely on QE, forward guidance, and credit-easing tools. Discussion of higher inflation targets (3-4 percent) partly aims to reduce ZLB frequency.
plain: The point where central banks have cut interest rates close to zero — leaving little room to ease further without unconventional tools.
